JESUS † The Complete Biography
Peter Terry
BOOK THE FIRST
Introduction
Every attempt to tell this story must begin by admitting its incapacity to
adequately encompass the life, teachings, influence and overall historical
significance of a man from Galilee who set foot upon the earth over two
millennia ago.  The principal source of our knowledge of this man are
recorded in the four gospels of the New Testament, along with the Acts of the
Apostles, the Epistles and the Apocalypse.  This attempt seeks to combine the
classical  harmony  of the  gospels,  also  called  a  lectionary,  and  which  is
probably  the  earliest  form  in  which  this  story  was  written  down  and
disseminated among the Christian faithful; with correlations and connections
to other persons and events occurring during the same time, and written
down soon afterwards or even centuries later.  These include the activities and
writings of the other Jewish people, those who did not affirm Jesus as their
Messiah -- including those preserved in the Talmud, the apocrypha, the
pseudepigrapha, the books of Titus Flavius Josephus and Philo Judaeus, and,
the so-called Dead Sea Scrolls, literature discovered in the Qumran caves and
Masada.  They also cite the life and teachings of Apollonius of Tyana, a
famous Greek-speaking contemporary, and of other Greek thinkers of the
time.  The third set of referents are those of the Romans, including rulers,
historians and philosophers.  It is not assumed that the reader is a Christian;
nor that s/he is not a Christian.  The truth will be told, as objectively as
possible, and the reader will come to his or her own conclusions.
Setting the Stage
The principal chronicles for the life of Jesus begin very differently from one
another – Matthew begins with a genealogy, of Joseph, the step-father of the
spirit-conceived Jesus, and hence only his genealogy by adoption.  It then
proceeds to the annunciation of his birth and the birth itself; Mark begans
roughly with chapter 3 of Matthew, with the baptism of Jesus by John; Luke
begins with the annunciation, of the birth of John and then of Jesus, then
proceeds to the two births with a little bit of historical context, and then cuts
to the baptism of Jesus by John, and at the end of chapter 3 the genealogy is

JESUS † The Complete Biography
inserted, a backwards geneaology, but still of Joseph rather than Jesus; and
John begins with a theological and cosmic setting of the stage, reminiscent of
the opening of Bereshit/Genesis, then cuts to John and the baptism of Jesus.
We will try to set the stage in another way, one that is more familiar perhaps
with modern readers than with the ancients.  We don’t generally begin with
genealogies or with cosmologies or jump into the story without preliminaries,
unless we intend to come back to them later.  None of the canonical gospels
does that…they never hearken back to before the beginning, except, very
briefly, Luke’s insertion of his backwards genealogy in chapter 3.  The first
readers of these chronicles were pretty familiar, from their oral histories and
from their day to day lives, with much of the detail that we don’t know about
unless  it  is  told  to  us.   So  we  will  begin  with  the  people  who  were
contemporaries of Jesus and with whom he had some kind of relationship.
We will begin with those people he came to value the most – the children, the
women, the poor, the diseased, the disabled, the possessed.  The children
were born many to each family, and perhaps a half dozen or so survived their
infancies and grew to some degree of adulthood.  They did not attend school,
they did not have toys except those they fashioned for themselves, and if they
had one set of clothes that fit and that protected their skins, they were
probably fortunate.  They walked barefoot, most likely.  Very young the girls
would help out their mothers in the field, in the kitchen, anywhere she needed
assistance.  She had no slaves and no servants, so she needed her girls to help
her, the older to take care of the younger.  The boys would help their fathers,
wherever they labored, be it fishing in the Sea of Galilee or along the banks of
the Mediterranean, farming, tending the goats and sheep and perhaps cattle if
they had the means, in the building trades, in all the varied occupations that
men engaged in to keep body and spirit together.  The children were obedient
to their parents and respectful of their elders, because it was impossible to
manage a family with multiple generations living under one roof or in one
cluster of huts without a clear chain of command and a job for every person.
Like children today, the children then were cursed and beaten by their
parents and by their older siblings and by the other bigger children in their
neighborhoods, and they had nobody to defend them.  They had early on to
learn how to defend themselves, with words, with cunning, with force if
necessary.  We might imagine that this was a bleak existence…but having
lived in a country village as a boy myself, I well recall the pleasures, the joys,
the comforts of a simple life close to nature.  Every rock, every tree, every
flower has meaning for a child who is not overwhelmed with man-made
material things.  He rejoices when it is warm, he rejoices when the wind
blows, he rejoices when the birds sing.  And he makes real friends, the friends
who share their all, their hearts, their thoughts, their sustenance.  Those who
have little, and children have the littlest of the little, share much and are
happy in the sharing.  Jesus knew many of these children, his half brothers
and half sisters, his cousins, his neighbors.  As a child, he played with them.
As a man he remembered his childhood and felt their vulnerability, their

JESUS † The Complete Biography
innocence and beauty, and he sought to protect them and cherish them.  Of all
beings created by God his Father, he loved children the most.
Women living in Judaea, in the Galilee, in Samaria, Philistina, and along the
coast of the great sea we call Mediterranean lived then as they do today…in
poor districts of Arab countries virtually untouched by modern civilization.
They were girls at their mothers’ beck and call, and then married and had
children of their own, soon after they reached puberty, most certainly by the
age of twelve or thirteen.   Since most of the families were  engaged  in
subsistence  farming,  whatever  else  they  might  be  doing  to  support
themselves, they had need of their children to help with the daily work of life.
But when it came time for them to marry, there was a change of status.  It has
been assumed that, as the custom survives to this day, each girl went to the
home of her husband, and helped her mother in law with the management of
their household; and each boy stayed home with his parents and his wife
joined him there and they raised their children in his childhood home.  But
the  Israelites  do  not  seem  to  have  followed  this  tradition.   Instead,
Bereshit/Genesis  (2:24) indicates that it  was their  custom for  men and
women alike to leave their parents and live independently of them.  Indeed,
this is confirmed by two of the gospels of Mark (10:7-8) and Matthew (19:5-
6), as well as by the stories of the patriarchs.  Hence, when they married,
women began a new life, with a husband, perhaps in the same town in which
both sets of parents resided, and perhaps not.  But her day to day work was
similar, from her girlhood to her womanhood, only now she took the lead
with the women’s work, and when she bore daughters, they became her
assistants, her apprentices in womancraft.
Not all women though followed this pattern from childhood to old age.  Some
women were born to riches, and did no laboring themselves, but their fathers
and their husbands procured slaves or hired servants to do this woman’s
work, and they could attend to other things.  For as the husband of such a
woman could have any woman he wanted, his wife would have make every
effort to be attractive to him in order to keep his loyalty.  She would have to
entertain him, delight him, seduce him, make him jealous, in order to have
him continue to provide her with her privileged status and lifestyle.  In other
words, whether she was a prostitute before she married, she almost invariably
became one once married, in order to stay married.  And if her husband
should divorce her, as moneyed people did (but rarely the poor, because the
burden of family disapproval and of singlehood was too much for any man or
woman to bear), she would whore in order to attract a new patron.  While
certainly  there  were  poor  women  who  supplemented  their  income  with
prostitution, it was rare because the village would not tolerate this treasonous
undermining of social integration…they depended upon the stable family to
ensure their survival.  And a poor woman could only earn poor wages and
never afford the luxury items that made the life of a whore attractive in the
first place.  Jesus knew women, like the Samaritan he met at the well of Yakov
who were not chaste and loyal to one man.  And he no doubt knew other

JESUS † The Complete Biography
women who were the whores of rich and powerful men, such as Salome the
daughter of Herodias who received the head of John the Baptist for her
mother’s satisfaction.  When he read and recited the words of the prophets
about whores, he knew what they were speaking about.  But he was not angry
with those women.  He understood that they were the captives of sin…the
captives of egoism, of pleasure, of addiction, of greed, of vanity, of a slave
mentality from which they did not know how to free themselves.  He had
compassion for them, not contempt; he was disposed to forgive and not to
punish; he told a woman who had been unfaithful to repent and sin no more,
rather than permitting self-righteous men to stone her to death.
Most of the people that Jesus knew were poor.  They were poor as so many of
those living in villages of the developing world are poor to this day, two
millennia after the evens depicted in this story.  They scratched together a
living, for as long as they could, doing whatever labor would earn them their
bread.  Remember the prayer Jesus taught to his disciples – “give us this day
our daily bread”2 – for subsistence is what the poor sought to provide for
themselves and their families.  They had no hope, no chance of escaping
poverty, of attaining material wealth.  They participated in an economy that
was neither socialist nor capitalist – it did not provide the security of state
welfare and universal employment, nor did it provide the freedom of trade
and of investment that can enable the rags to riches story to become a reality
for some.  It was a slave economy, and the owners of the slaves were the
political and economic masters of the situation.
In all of the regions of the land of Israel, the rulers during the lifetime of Jesus
were Romans and their Jewish allies.  These allies were descendants of King
Herod the Great (74/73/ruled 37 BCE - 4 BCE), who was ruthless towards
Sadducees and Pharisees alike, chosen his own religious hierarchy, rebuilding
the temple on a grand scale, as well as Caesaria, a port north of present day
Tel-Aviv, and fortresses at Masada and Herodium, where he was buried.  The
longest ruling was Herod Antipater (called Antipas: 20 BCE-39 CE), who
ruled Galilee from 4 BCE to 39 CE, along with his family, and their entourage.
It was this Herod who issued the order to imprison and then to behead John
the Baptist.  His second wife was Herodias, formerly spouse of Herod II, his
half-brother who never ruled at all.  Herod Antipas’ brother, called Herod
Archelaus (23 BCE – 18 CE) ruled Judaea, Samaria and Idumea (now the
border country of Jordan, on the other side of the Dead Sea), from his father’s
death, in 4 BCE to 6 CE, when he was relieved of his throne and disappeared
from  history.   He  was  confirmed  in  his  position,  when  he  ruthlessly
suppressed  dissent  in  Jerusalem…and  event  that  must  have  left  bitter
memories for all those alive at the time.  We will come back to that.
2Matthew 6:11 (variant Luke 11:3 – “Give us day by day our daily bread.”

JESUS † The Complete Biography
From 6 CE until long after the destruction of Jerusalem in 70 CE, a succession
of Roman officials ruled Herod Archelaus’ former realms: Coponius (6-9 CE),
Marcus Ambivulus (9-13 CE), Annius Rufus (13-15 CE), Valerius Gratus (15-
26 CE) and Pontius Pilatus (26-36 CE).  The Herodians were famed for their
love of all things Roman, and their frequent quarrels with the observant Jews
over whom they ruled.  The Romans were famed for their love of all things
Roman, and their ruthless incomprehension of the Jews they ruled.  The
ruling class was not well integrated with the social fabric of the country.
When Jesus speaks disparagingly of the rich, it is because the only people who
were rich in his age were determined to possess the totality of the resources,
leaving only enough to the masses to survive.  “It is easier for a camel to go
through the eye of a needle, than for a rich man to enter into the kingdom
of God”3 was not an exaggeration – this was the truth about the rich of his
time.  They ruled with iron fists, and iron swords, and iron wills.  They were
military men, but they had such power that they certainly enjoyed all of the
pleasures that scultures and paintings and stories have depicted in Pompei
and other Roman cities.  If whoring was going on in Babylonia, it was
flourishing in Rome.  It cannot be repeated often enough that the Roman
economy, its military and its entire society depended upon slavery for its
existence.  While slavery existed in ancient Israel, and there were no doubt
many slaves of many nations serving the Romans and the Herodians in their
city dwellings, the poor of Galilee, Samaria and Judaea were most of them not
outright slaves…they were serfs.  They probably owned no land and they
certainly paid taxes to support the lavish lifestyle of their rulers.  Although
most of them were not slaves of the Romans, they had no freedom.  Hence,
when Jesus spoke to them of the Jubilee and of freedom, this was novel and
appealing for a population that was accustomed to bone weary work and no
prospect of either liberty or progress.
Herod the Great was near to death, and his son by his Samaritan wife
Malthace, Herod Archelaus was acting on his behalf.  According to Titus
Flavius Josephus, who described the occurrence many years later in his
“Antiquities of the Jews” (17.6.5), Archelaus ascended the throne
and heard the crowd assembled just before Pesach in 4 BCE.
They were upset about the death penalty ordered for two of the
rabbanim and  fourty  of  their students.   They  demanded  the
replacement of the Kohen ha-gadol, as the one appointed by his
father was not sufficiently pious.  Archelaus made excuses and
left to feast with his friends.  He then sent a military envoy with
a small group under their command to tell the crowd to cease
and  desist  and  await  confirmation  from  Rome  of  Archelaus’
appointment  to  the  throne.   The  envoys  were  stoned  by the
crowd and many were killed.  The crowd then returned to the
sacrifices that preceded Pesach. Abruptly Archelaus ordered the
3Gospel of Mark 10:25

JESUS † The Complete Biography
entire army to subdue the seditious mob.  Josephus estimated
that 3000 Jews gathered for Pesah were killed in that night.
Archelaus then sent heralds about the city cancelling Pesach for
that year.  It is unimaginable that a slaughter on this scale would
be forgotten, even a decade or two later.  Jesus must have been
told this story, over and over, and it must have haunted him,
gentle soul that he was, and perhaps this tragedy impelled him
as a young man to oppose all violence, all rebellion, and even the
angry sentiments and words that are the roots of discord.
Where were we?  With the poor…and among the poor, the most destitute of
the poor are those who are ill, those who are handicapped, those who are
deranged.  A poor man or woman who is of sound body and mind can usually
fend for himself or herself and survive.  Billions of our fellow homo sapiens
have done so over the centuries and millennia.  But a man or woman who is
severely ill, who is blind before braille, deaf before sign language, possessed
before psychiatrists and exorcists (apart from the expensive magicians, who
didn’t work for the poor, but attached themselves to the courts of the rich and
powerful), this one has hardly a chance of limping on day by day.  Poverty
does not in itself bring suffering.  But those who are poor and also less than
whole, they suffer, and Jesus felt their suffering.  He couldn’t pass a suffering
soul in the street without feeling that suffering himself, in his very body and
soul.  Later he was to tell his followers that if they refused help to anyone, they
were refusing it to him.  Doubtless many of them did not understand.  He felt
this suffering acutely, personally.  And in his day suffering was out in the
open, as it is in poor countries and poor neighborhoods in rich countries
today.  There were no special clinics or hospitals or halfway houses for the
infirm.  They survived on the generosity of the poor.  The blind were leading
the blind, because the seeing wouldn’t go near them.
While the children were many and there were women all about, and the
diseased  and  deformed  and  possessed  were  in  plain  view,  there  was  a
universal condition that characterized every soul Jesus encountered, from the
very time of his birth.  We don’t know what he remembered of his childhood,
or whether, in such an extraordinary character, his childhood memories
shaped his views and his actions in later life.  But we know that every soul he
met was burdened with estrangement from God and from fellow humans.
That is what he called “sin”.  And when he called for “repentence” in later life,
it was a summons to abandon that estrangement, to come back to the loving
Creator, to return to loving fellow humans as the child loves their mother.  In
every heart there lurked the devils of disappointment, or hurt feelings, of
anger and betrayal.  In every heart there also resided the hope for redemption,
for being saved, for being liberated from this burden of estrangement, this
bringer of death, this deprivation of light and warmth that is not the darkness
of black but the absence of life.

JESUS † The Complete Biography
Jesus was not alone in his wisdom.  His most famous contemporary from the
perspective of his fellow Jews centuries later, was Hillel ben David, born in
Babylonia,  a  disciple  of Shemaia  and  Avtalion,  appointed  a  nasi  in the
Sanhedrin in Jerusalem early in the reign of King Herod the Great.  Hillel was
famous  for  his  gentle  and  peace-loving  character,  for  his  patience,  his
modesty,  his  charitable  generosity.   He  established  the  school  of  legal
interpretation  known  as  Beit  Hillel,  as  well  as  seven  rules  for  the
interpretation of the Oral Torah, later written down and called the Mishnah
and Gemara – together, the Talmud.  Hillel is most famous for two sayings
indicating his ethical minimalism (or essentialism) – one is that the essence of
the Torah is to love one’s neighbor like oneself; and the other is to take action
now and without excuses or delays.
A contemporary of Hillel was Shammai, who was the founded of the Beit
Shammai school of legal interpretation, also reported in detail in the Talmud,
and famous for his more stringent and maximalist position with regard to
most legal decisions.   He was fearless and outspoken in his disagreements
with Hillel, and also a warm-hearted person.  Other contemporaries include
Measha, Menachem, Chanania ben Hezekiah ben Gurion, and the many
disciples of Shammai and Hillel.  Disciples of Shammai included Dostal of
Kefar Yathma, Yoezer le Bira, Rav Yochanan ben ha-Horani.  The most
famous of the first generation after Hillel was Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai,
the last of Hillel’s disciples who persuaded Vespasian not to destroy the
Jewish college in Yavne.  Of the same generation as ben Zakkai were Admon
ben Gaddai, Ben Buchri, Samuel the Younger, and Chanan ben Avishalom.
Mentioned in the gospels and the Acts of the Apostles were Rav Gamaliel the
Elder, a grandson of Rav Hillel.   Others listed but without affiliation with
either Beit Shammai or Beit Hillel were Rav Chanina, Rav Yochanan ben
Gudgada, Abba Yose Choli Kufri, Menachem ben Signai, Nachum the Mede,
Nachum the Scrivener, Simon of Mitzpa, Rav Zecharia ben ha-Kazzav and
Rav  Zecharia  ben  Kavutal.  All  of  these  hachamim  (wise  men)  were
remembered in the Talmud, written down hundreds of years later.  They were
members of the rabbinical school that emerged from the Pharisees, as they
had emerged from the Hassidim in the time of the Hasmonaean dynasty.
Jesus was certainly familiar with the views of the Pharisees, and careful
comparisions of their teachings with his have demonstrated agreement on
most points.  However, the gospel chroniclers include many stories in which
Jesus took objection not to the ideology of the Pharisees but to their actions,
and lack of actions.  He wanted to see more ethical behavior emitting from
self-described righteous men and less talk about how many angels can fit on
the head of a pin.  Nevertheless, Jesus was not alone, and in Beit Hillel
especially we find much mutual resonance.
How then did the followers of the rabbanim go in one direction and the
followers of Jesus in another?  We are getting ahead of ourselves if we try to
answer those questions now, before looking at his whole life.

JESUS † The Complete Biography
To provide a foil for his story, we are including excerpts from the biography of
Apollonius of Tyana, a contemporary of Jesus who provides contrast rather
than similarity.  Too much sameness may well lull us into believing that Jesus
was not exceptional, that there were plenty of people like him with teachings
like his.  If that were the case there would not be so many millions of people
grappling  with  him  and  his  ideas  two  millennia  after  he  disappeared…
grappling and finding new life and new inspiration every day.
In the beginning God
In the first verse of the first book of the Torah, the holy book of the Jewish
people, and of Jesus and his disciples and other companions, it is written:
In the entirety of the TANAKH, there are a four references to YHWH as the
“Father” – three in the Torah: one in the second book, Shmot/Exodus, two in
the fifth book, Devarim/Deuteronomy, only one by name; nine in the Neviim
– three in Isaiah, three in Jeremiah, two in Hosea, and one in Malachi;  -- one
in  Samuel,  three  in  Chronicles,  and  and  and  one  in  the  first  book  of
Chronicles.  There are, in addition, four references to Israel and his progeny
being the sons of YHWH, one in the second book of Torah, one in the book of
Hosea, and one in the first book of Chronicles.

What is the meaning of these passages?  Is there ever a statement that the
“Father”  generated  any  individuals  or  any  entire  people  through  sexual
relations?  This is a valid question, inasmuch as the Jewish contemporaries of
Jesus were in regular contact with Greeks and Romans, and probably to some
extent also with polytheist Arabs, Egyptians, and Babylonians, and that these
other populations believed that gods and goddesses procreated in much the
same fashion as human beings, and thereby gave birth to other gods and
goddesses, as well as demi-gods and demi-goddesses who were human beings
with superhuman powers.

JESUS † The Complete Biography
The context and internal dynamics of these passages seem to point to a belief
that YHWH was the creator of all human beings, as He created the first man
and woman, Adam and Eve, and all subsequent human beings are descended
from these original parents.  Hence, He was not the personal parent of any
particular people, apart from Adam and Eve.  However, it could be affirmed
that the power of creation, of generation belonged to God alone, and hence
every new birth occurred through His creative power.  Hence, the human
parents would be the vehicles for procreation, but not the actual causes.
When the text speaks of God being the “Father” of particular peoples, the
descendants of Israel, of Efrayim, this speaks to these peoples being “chosen”
for  His  guidance  and  His  blessing,  and  also  for  shouldering  certain
responsibilities that would be theirs alone.  Finally, when it speaks of Him
being the “Father” of David, or Solomon, and of these individuals being His
“sons”, there is no suggestion that He replaced the human father of either of
these Israelite kings, but rather that He assumed a spiritual fatherhood,
selecting them to represent Him as His sons, His heirs to earthly kingship.
They were to guide the Israelites and ultimately, through Mashiach ben
David, all of humanity, as He guided the powers of the heavens and the earth,
of the sea and the rivers.  Hence, to be a “son” of this “Father” was to be His
chosen envoy among humanity.  The visit of the Queen of Sheba to King
Solomon, described in some detail, is the model for future visitations from
kings and rulers, predicted for Jerusalem in the time of Mashiach ben David.
The vision then is of a continuity of divine kingship, of the “sons” of the
“Father”, to continue beyond David and Solomon, into perpetuity.  How
ironic  then  that  the  dynasty  established  by  David  lasted  only  two
generations…that his united realm of Judaea, Samaria and Galilee did not
endure,  except  in  the  dreams  and  hopes  of  the  Jewish  people,  and
subsequently, transformed, in those of Christians.
One of the significances of the above-cited verses to this biography of Jesus is
that they demonstrate that in Biblical times (or in the collective memory of
those times), Jews referred to YHWH as their “Father”; and to themselves
collectively and to particular individuals, including David and Solomon (and
possibly of Mashiach ben David) as His “sons”.  Furthermore, YHWH is
recorded to have referred to Himself as the “Father” of individuals and
collectively of the descendants of Israel and Efrayim.  In the non-canonical
literature, its use is also rare – Apocrypha: Wisdom of Solomon 2:16; 14:3;
Tobias 13:4; Wisdom of Sirach 23:1, 4; 51:10); Pseudepigrapha: Jubilees
1:24, 28; 19:29; 3 Maccabees 5:7; 6:4, 8; Testament of Levi 18:6; Testament
of Judah 24:2; and Dead Sea Scrolls: 1 QH 9:35f.
Hence, YHWH is referred to as “Father” in texts associated with Jewish
tradition, and even in Jewish prayer.  Nevertheless, there is a much greater
concentration of references to God as “Father” in the New Testament than in
all of the citations mentioned thus far.   It is found no less than 65 times in the

JESUS † The Complete Biography
synoptic gospels, and over 100 times in the Gospel of John.  In all but one
example,  where the Aramaic  Abba is used (Mark 14:36) instead of the
Hebrew Av, it is in its Greek translation, pronounced “Pater”.
Shekhinah[Ruah Elohim]
The historical Jesus, the theological Jesus, the mystic Jesus is preceded by
the presence of God.  We will now approach Jesus as did the author of the
Gospel of John.  Before revieiwing the life story and teachings of the man
named Jesus (in Latin), Yesus (Greek), Yeshu'a (in Hebrew), we will address
the opening salvo in the Gospel of John:
1 In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word
was God.  2 The same was in the beginning with God.  3 All things were made
by him; and without him was not any thing made that was made.  4 In him was
life; and the life was the light of men.
All things were made by Whom?  God or the Word?  In Whom was life and
the light of men?  This is immediately made apparent when we read on:
6 There was a man sent from God, whose name was John.  7 The same came
for a witness, to bear witness of the Light, that all men through him might
believe.  8 He was not that Light, but was sent to bear witness of that Light.
9 That was the true Light, which lighteth every man that cometh into the
world.  10 He was in the world, and the world was made by him, and the world
knew him not.  11 He came unto his own, and his own received him not.  12 But
as many as received him, to them gave he power to become the sons of
God, even to them that believe on his name:  13 Which were born, not of
blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God.  14 And
the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, (and we beheld his glory,
the glory as of the only begotten of the Father,) full of grace and truth.
15 John bare witness of him, and cried, saying, This was he of whom I spake,
He that cometh after me is preferred before me: for he was before me.
16 And of his fulness have all we received, and grace for grace.  17 For the law
was given by Moses, but grace and truth came by Jesus Christ.  18 No man

JESUS † The Complete Biography
hath seen God at any time, the only begotten Son, which is in the bosom of
the Father, he hath declared him.
So, here are the answers to our questions:  All things were made by the Word
(1:10).  The Word was “the true light, which lighteth every man” (1:9).  The
Word was made flesh and lived with the author of this gospel and many
others (1:14), and his name was Jesus (1:17), and was called the Son of the
Father (1:18).  It is clear from these answers that the author of this gospel,
and apparently many of his fellow Christians believed that Jesus was not just
Messiah, but the incarnation of the Word of God, which created all things and
was from the beginning of the world and before its creation.  While we are
reeling from these statements so unexpected coming from a presumably
Jewish author referring to a Jewish historical person, we will now turn to
some of the statements of Jesus himself, which seem to suggest a cosmic
existence and identity.
Later in this same gospel, Jesus says: “I am the way, the truth, and the life:
no man cometh unto the Father, but by me.” (14:6)  But, at that point,
Jesus is talking with other people and he could have intended an entirely
different meaning from what the author of the gospel sought to convey in
its opening chapter.  There is every indication that Noah could have made
the same statement to his sons and descendants; that Abraham could also
have affirmed the same to his entourage and his sons; and, to fast forward
several centuries, Moses could also have affirmed that his teaching, his
Torah was “the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the
Father, but by me”.  Did Jesus actually claim a unique station for himself?
We now come to another statement attributed to him in the Gospel of John:
8:58 Verily, verily, I say unto you, Before Abraham was, I am.
Who is this "I am" that was “before Abraham”?  Was it Jesus, son of Mary,
born in Bethlehem, raised in Nazareth, during the reign of Herod Antipas in
Galilee, Herod Archelaus in Judaea, and Herod Philip in Jordan?   In order to
answer this question, we must search for this expression "I am" in the Jewish
sacred literature.  We do not find any usage of this "I am" in the Biblical
chronicle preceding Abraham, but we do find one in the Book of Exodus:
3:14  And God said unto Moses, I AM THAT I AM [ehye asher ehye]: and he
said, Thus shalt thou say unto the children of Israel, I AM [ehye] hath sent
me unto you.  3:15 And God said moreover unto Moses, Thus shalt thou say
unto the children of Israel, The Lord [YHWH] God of your fathers [elo hey
av Teychem] , the God of Abraham [elo hey avraham], the God of Isaac [elo
hey yitzkhak], the God of Jacob [ve-elo hey ya’acov], hath sent me unto

JESUS † The Complete Biography
you: this is my name for ever [zeh shmiy l’olam], and this is my memorial unto
all generations [ve zeh zikriy le dor va dor].
Is Jesus saying that he is YHWH, called "I am" and "I am that I am", which is
"my name for ever"?    Yes, even as YHWH spoke to Moses in the desert, so
YHWH spoke through Jesus, and all that Jesus said came from God.  The
Gospel of John is particularly copious with statements of Jesus affirming his
direct relationship with God:
5:19 Then answered Jesus and said unto them, Verily, verily, I say unto
you, The Son can do nothing of himself, but what he seeth the Father
do: for what things soever he doeth, these also  doeth the Son
likewise.
6:57 As the living Father hath sent me, and I live by the Father: so he
that eateth me, even he shall live by me.  10:30 I and my Father are one.
10:34 Jesus answered them, Is it not written in your law, I said, Ye are gods?
10:35 If he called them gods, unto whom the word of God came, and the
scripture cannot be broken; 10:36 Say ye of him, whom the Father hath
sanctified, and sent into the world, Thou blasphemest; because I said, I am
the Son of God? 10:37 If I do not the works of my Father, believe me not.
10:38 But if I do, though ye believe not me, believe the works: that ye may
know, and believe, that the Father is in me, and I in him.
14:5 Thomas saith unto him, Lord, we know not whither thou goest; and how
can we know the way? 14:6 Jesus saith unto him, I am the way, the truth, and
the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me. 14:7 If ye had known me,
ye should have known my Father also: and from henceforth ye know him, and
have seen him. 14:8 Philip saith unto him, Lord, shew us the Father, and it
sufficeth us. 14:9 Jesus saith unto him, Have I been so long time with you, and
yet hast thou not known me, Philip? he that hath seen me hath seen the
Father; and how sayest thou then, Shew us the Father? 14:10 Believest thou
not that I am in the Father, and the Father in me? the words that I speak unto
you I speak not of myself: but the Father that dwelleth in me, he doeth the

JESUS † The Complete Biography
works. 14:11 Believe me that I am in the Father, and the Father in me: or else

In the Gospel of John, Jesus also affirmed to his followers that he lived
and was loved by God “before the foundation of the world”, associated with
his divine Father, but not identical to Him:
17:5 And now, O Father, glorify thou me with thine own self with the glory
which I had with thee before the world was.17:24 Father…thou lovedst me
before the foundation of the world.
Inasmuch as Jesus does the Will and speaks the Word of God, he is, as the
author of the Gospel of John affirms, associated with God from the beginning
(we repeat the text as it will be compared immediately with another):
1:1 In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word
was God. 1:2 The same was in the beginning with God.  1:3 All things were made
by him; and without him was not any thing made that was made.
In Jewish tradition, this Will and Word which has been since the beginning,
which was with God and of God is depicted in the first chapter of the first
book of the Torah:
1:1 In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth.  1:2 And the earth
was without form, and void; and darkness was upon the face of the deep.
And the Spirit of God moved upon the face of the waters.  1:3 And God said,
Let there be light: and there was light.
In the Aramaic translation and commentary of the Torah and other books of
the Bible, called the Targumim, and in all rabbinical commentaries on the
Biblical text, this Will and Word is denoted the “presence” of God.  When we
study the Torah (Pentateuch) and the Neviim (Prophets) we find many
references  to  this  “presence”  of  God,  in  its  cosmic  dimension,  that  is,
manifested to prophets and other purified souls in visions and dreams.
We first encounter a depiction of this “presence” in the Book of Exodus, once
above sapphire stone and once with the appearance of fire:
24:10 And they saw the God of Israel: and there was  under his feet as it were
a paved work of a sapphire stone, and as it were the body of heaven in his
clearness…

JESUS † The Complete Biography
24:16 And the glory of the Lord abode upon mount Sinai, and the cloud
covered it six days: and the seventh day he called unto Moses out of the
midst of the cloud.  24:17 And the  sight of the glory of the Lord was like
devouring fire on the top of the mount in the eyes of the children of Israel.
In the Book of Ezekiel, He sits upon a throne, which is like a sapphire stone in
color, and has the appearance of fire:
1:26 And above the firmament that was over their heads was the likeness of a
throne, as the appearance of a sapphire stone: and upon the likeness of the
throne was the likeness as the appearance of a man above upon it.  1:27 And I
saw as the colour of amber, as the appearance of fire round about within
it, from the appearance of his loins even upward, and from the appearance
of his loins even downward, I saw as it were the appearance of fire, and it
had brightness round about. 1:28 As the appearance of the bow that is in
the cloud in the day of rain, so was the appearance of the brightness
round about.  This was the appearance of the likeness of the glory of the
Lord.
8:2 Then I beheld, and lo a likeness as the appearance of fire: from the
appearance  of his loins  even downward, fire; and from  his  loins  even
upward, as the appearance of brightness, as the colour of amber.
10:1 Then I looked, and behold, in the firmament that was above the head of
the cherubims there appeared over them as it were a sapphire stone, as the
appearance of the likeness of a throne.
In the Book of Ezekiel, He has a voice like the noise of many waters:
43:2 And, behold, the glory of the God of Israel came from the way of the
East: and his voice was like a noise of many waters: and the earth shined
with his glory.

In the Gospels we do not find Jesus claiming to be this presence of God,

The characteristics that are attributed by Moses and the lesser prophets to

Son of man.
Another dimension of the cosmic reality who was called Jesus when he

All of these passages from the Jewish and Christian Scriptures point to a
cosmic manifestation of divine light, a presence of God, and the Gospel of
John depicts this presence as having assumed the human form, and to have
been the historical person named Jesus.  This is Jesus who came down from
heaven, Jesus who was the Spirit of God, Jesus who is Emmanuel, “God with
us”.  And this is where we must begin the story of Jesus.  For Jesus the
presence of God predates the creation of the world, how much moreso the
appearance of this presence in the body and personality of Jesus of Nazareth.
Before we leaving this topic, let us consider where it may have originated.  As
we have seen, most of the references to this cosmological view of the Christ
are from the Gospel of John, with some from the Apocalpse of John, and a
few others from non-canonical literature which has classically been called
“Gnostic” by Biblical scholars.  Who was teaching such ideas at the time of
Jesus?
Much ink has been spilled on whether the writings of Philo Judaeus1 (20
BCE-50CE) influenced the Gospel of John, the church fathers, or whether
similar ideas came from a common source, albeit one that has yet to be
discovered.   Let  us  examine  Philo’s  ideas  and  compare  them  with  the
passages cited above:
"And the Father who created the universe has given to his archangelic
and most ancient Word a pre-eminent gift, to stand on the confines of
both, and separated that which had been created from the Creator.
“And this same Word is continually a suppliant to the immortal God on
behalf of the mortal race, which is exposed to affliction and misery; and is
also the ambassador, sent by the Ruler of all, to the subject race.
“And the Word rejoices in the gift, and, exulting in it, announces it and
boasts of it, saying, 'And I stood in the midst, between the Lord and You;
neither being uncreated as God, nor yet created as you, but being in the
midst  between  these  two  extremities  ...  For  I  will  proclaim  peaceful
intelligence to the creation from him who has determined to destroy
wars, namely God, who is ever the guardian of peace.' "  (Philo, Who is
the Heir of Divine Things? 42.205-6)2
And the father who created the universe has given to his archangel and
most ancient Logos a pre-eminent gift, to stand on the confines of both,
and separate that which had been created from the Creator. And this
same Logos is continually a suppliant to the immortal God on behalf of
the mortal race, which is exposed to affliction and misery; and is also the
ambassador, sent by the Ruler of all, to the subject race. And the Logos
rejoices…. saying “And I stood in the midst, between the Lord and you”
(Num. 16:48); neither being uncreated as God, nor yet created as you, but
being in the midst between these two extremities, like a hostage, as it
were, to both parties (Philo, Her. 205-206).3
