3.  Now  when  righteous  Joseph  became  a  widower,  my  mother  Mary,
blessed, holy, and pure, was already twelve years old. For her parents
offered her in the temple when she was three years of age, and she
remained in the temple of the Lord nine years. Then when the priests saw
that the virgin, holy and God-fearing, was growing up, they spoke to each
other, saying: Let us search out a man, righteous and pious, to whom Mary
may be entrusted until the time of her marriage; lest, if she remain in the
temple, it happen to her as is wont to happen to women, and lest on that
account we sin, and God be angry with us.
4. Therefore they immediately sent out, and assembled twelve old men of
the tribe of Judah. And they wrote down the names of the twelve tribes of
Israel. And the lot fell upon the pious old man, righteous Joseph. Then the
priests answered, and said to my blessed mother: Go with Joseph, and be
with him till the time of your marriage. Righteous Joseph therefore received
my mother, and led her away to his own house. And Mary found James the
Less in his father's house, broken-hearted and sad on account of the loss
of his mother, and she brought him up. Hence Mary was called the mother
of James.  Thereafter Joseph left her at home, and went away to the shop
where he wrought at his trade of a carpenter. And after the holy virgin had
spent two years in his house her age was exactly fourteen years, including
the time at which he received her.
5. And I chose her of my own will, with the concurrence of my Father, and
the counsel of the Holy Spirit. And I was made flesh of her, by a mystery
which transcends the grasp of created reason. And three months after her
conception the righteous man Joseph returned from the place where he
worked at his trade; and when he found my virgin mother pregnant, he was
greatly perplexed, and thought of sending her away secretly. But from
fear, and sorrow, and the anguish of his heart, he could endure neither to
eat nor drink that day.
6. But at mid-day there appeared to him in a dream the prince of the
angels, the holy Gabriel, furnished with a command from my Father; and he
said to him: Joseph, son of David, fear not to take Mary as thy wife: for

JESUS † The Complete Biography
she has conceived of the Holy Spirit; and she will bring forth a son, whose
name shall be called Jesus. He it is who shall rule all nations with a rod of
iron.  Having thus spoken, the angel departed from him. And Joseph rose
from his sleep, and did as the angel of the Lord had said to him; and Mary
abode with him.
The true father of Jesus was not Joseph, and his forefathers were not the
patriarch Abraham or the king David.  His true father, as he himself said so
often,was God, the Father of all.  Likewise, the father of Apollonius of
Tyana was, according to legend, none other than a god43:
His  father  was  of  the  same  name  [i.e.,  Apollonius],  and  the  family
descended from the first settlers. It excelled in wealth the surrounding
families, though the district is a rich one…Now there is near Tyana a well
sacred to Zeus, the god of paths, so they say, and they call it the well of
Asbama. Here a spring rises cold, but bubbles up like a boiling cauldron.
This water is favorable and sweet to those who keep their paths, but to
perjurers it brings hot-footed justice; for it attacks their eyes and hands
and feet, and they fall the prey of dropsy and wasting disease; and they
are not even able to go away, but are held on the spot and bemoan
themselves at the edge of the spring, acknowledging their perjuries.
The people of the country, then, say that Apollonius was the son of this
Zeus, but the sage called himself the son of Apollonius.
As this is our first encounter with Apollonius, a short biography will be
cited here44:
Apollonius of Tyana (Ancient Greek: Ἀπολλώνιος ὁ Τυανεύς; c. 15 – c. 100
AD[2]),  sometimes  also  called  Apollonios  of  Tyana,  was  a  Greek
Neopythagorean philosopher from  the  town  of  Tyana in  the  Roman
province of  Cappadocia in  Asia Minor. Being a 1st-century orator and
philosopher around the time of  Christ, he was compared with Jesus of
Nazareth by Christians in the 4th century[3] and by writers in modern
times…By far the most detailed source is the Life of Apollonius of Tyana, a
lengthy, novelistic biography written by the  sophist Philostratus at the
request of empress Julia Domna. She died in 217 AD,[8] and he completed it
after her death, probably in the 220s or 230s AD…Sossianus Hierocles

argued in the 3rd century that the doctrines and the life of Apollonius were
more valuable than those of Christ, a viewpoint reportedly held by both
Voltaire and  Charles Blount during the  Age of Enlightenment.[19] …As
James Francis put it, "the most that can be said ... is that Apollonius
appears to have been a wandering ascetic/philosopher/wonderworker of a
type common to the eastern part of the early empire."[23] What we can
safely  assume  is  that  he  was  indeed  a  Pythagorean  and  as  such,  in
conformity with the Pythagorean tradition, opposed animal sacrifice, and
lived on a frugal, strictly vegetarian diet.[24]…As for his philosophical
convictions, we have an interesting, probably authentic fragment of one of
his writings (On sacrifices) where he expresses his view that God, who is
the most beautiful being, cannot be influenced by prayers or sacrifices and
has no wish to be worshipped by humans, but can be reached by a spiritual
procedure involving nous (intellect), because he himself is pure nous and
nous is also the greatest faculty of humankind.[26]…Philostratus implies
on one occasion that Apollonius had extra-sensory perception (Book VIII,
Chapter XXVI). When emperor Domitian was murdered on September 18,
96 AD, Apollonius was said to have witnessed the event in Ephesus "about
midday" on the day it happened in Rome, and told those present "Take
heart,  gentlemen,  for  the  tyrant  has  been  slain  this  day...".  Both
Philostratus  and  renowned  historian  Cassius  Dio report  this  incident,
probably on the basis of an oral tradition.  Both state that the philosopher
welcomed the deed as a praiseworthy tyrannicide.[27]
Virgin Birth
Was Mary a virgin when she became pregnant with Jesus?   Yes, according
to the Gospel of Matthew:
1:18 Now the birth of Jesus Christ was on this wise: When as his mother Mary
was espoused to Joseph, before they came together, she was found with
child of the Holy Ghost.
Yes, according to the Gospel of Luke:
1:34 Then said Mary unto the angel, How shall this be, seeing I know not a
man? 1:35 And the angel answered and said unto her, The Holy Ghost shall
come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee:
therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the
Son of God.
While  the  virgin  birth  of  Jesus  was  only  important  enough  to  early
Christians that two out of four  of the  canonical  Gospels  refer  to  that

JESUS † The Complete Biography
occurrence, there are in fact three references to the virgin birth in three
separate Surihs of the Qur’an (19:19-22; 21:91; 66:12):
19. He said: "Nay, I am only a messenger from thy Lord, (to announce) to
thee the gift of a holy son."  20. She said: "How shall I have a son, seeing
that no man has touched me, and I am not unchaste?" 21. He said: "So (it will
be): thy Lord saith, 'That is easy for Me: and (We wish) to appoint him as a
Sign unto men and a Mercy from Us': it is a matter (so) decreed." 22. So
she conceived him, and she retired with him to a remote place…
91. And (remember) her who guarded her chastity: We breathed into her of
Our Spirit, and We made her and her son a Sign for all peoples…
12. And Mary the daughter of 'Imran, who guarded her chastity; and We
breathed into her (body) of Our spirit; and she testified to the truth of the
words of her Lord and of His Revelations, and was one of the devout
(Servants).
This indicates that the Christians who informed Muhammad about Jesus
were fully informed on this question, and it was important both to them and
apparently  to  Muhammad  to  have  been  cited  multiple  times  in  his
adaptation of the Judeo-Christian heritage for the Arab people.
Let us consider this question in the context of Biblical literature as a whole.
Adam had neither father nor mother45.  He was the creation of God alone.
Melchizedek was also “Without father, without mother, without genealogy,
having neither beginning of days nor end of life, but made like the Son of
God, he remains a priest perpetually.”46   Lest we be unsure of his meaning,
the author writes, “For this Melchizedek, king of Salem, priest of the Most
High, who met Abraham as he was returning from the slaughter of the kings
and blessed him, to whom also Abraham apportioned a tenth part of all the
spoils, was first of all, by the translation of his name, king of righteousness,
and then also king of Salem, which is king of peace.”47
Isaac was born to his mother and father when the former was 90 and the
latter was 100 years of age.48  While the Biblical text does not indicate
whether or not there were sexual relations involved, Abraham was plainly
incredulous that his wife Sarah, barren for so long, could give birth to any
child.  He was assured by God that nothing is too difficult for Him.49
Rebecca, wife of Isaac was barren and her husband prayed to God for a
child, and his prayer was answered with twins, whom they named Esau and
Jacob.50  Rachel, the wife of Jacob, was also barren and prayed for a child,
and God hearkened to her and she bore Joseph.51  Consider then that this

JESUS † The Complete Biography
entire sequence of births was miraculous – that of Isaac, that of his son
Jacob, that of his grandson Joseph.
Manoah’s wife, from Zorah, of the tribe of Dan, was barren and she was
promised a child by an angel – he was named Samson and the Holy Spirit
moved upon him.52   Hannah, the wife of Elkanah son of Jeroham, from
Ramathaim, a Zuphite from the hill country of Ephraim, was barren and she
prayed for a child and was blessed by Eli the priest and then she conceived
Samuel  the  prophet.53  It  is  specifically  written  that  she  lay  with  her
husband54,  but  nonetheless  this  was  a  miraculous  birth.   All  of  these
miraculous births were recounted in the Tanakh, in the Hebrew Scriptures.
The Book of Isaiah (7:14) is therefore not stating anything that Jews were
unacquainted with when it reads, “Behold a virgin55 shall conceive, and bear
a son, and shall call his name Emmanuel”—there had already been virgins or
barren women who had borne sons, like Isaac, Jacob, Samson and Samuel—
all holy men of God.
In the Protoevangelium of James we read an account of Mary, the mother of
Jesus being born to the aged and barren Anna, wife of Joachim, by virtue of
divine intervention.  In the Gospel of Luke we encounter John (called the
Baptist), who was born to the aged and barren Elizabeth (Elisheva) and her
aged husband Zechariah after they prayed to God for a child and were
visited by an angel announcing his birth.  Hence, immediately preceding the
miraculous birth of Jesus there is the miraculous birth of his relation, John.
So much for Biblical births of miraculous nature.  It has been discovered by
numerous students of comparative religion, that the myths and legends of
numerous cultures are replete with references to miraculous, to virgin
births.  Closest  geographically  and  historically  to  Israel  and  to  Jewish
tradition are Egypt and Greece.  In ancient Egyptian myth, Horus was said
to be the offspring of the virgin Isis, and Osiris of the virgin Ceres.   The
Egyptian Bacchus is said to have been born of a virgin named Semele, and
the Greek Bacchus is reported to have born of the virgin Minerva.  Other
virgin births reported in Greek myth include Adonis, Alcides, Dionysus,
Hercules,  Hermes,  Horace,  Jason,  Perseus,  Theseus,  Zunis,  and  a
contemporary of Jesus, Apollonius of Tyana.  Plato and Pythagoras were
both reported to have been born of virgin mothers.  In the Middle East,
Attis, Mithras, Mot-Aleyin, Tammuz and Zoroaster were accounted the
issue of virgins, and in the Far East there are accounts of Bali, Buddha,
Chang-Ti, Indra, Joa, Krishna, Mahavira, Sakia, Salivahana, Tien, Yu
being likewise conceived.  In the myths of cultures far distant from the
land of Israel, and which were most likely unknown to Jews at the time of
Jesus, there are also favorite sons who are counted as the issue of virgin
mothers,  including  Crite,  Deganawidah,  Hesus/Hu,  Huitzilopochtli,
Hunahpu, Merlin the magician, Montezuma (the Pueblo not the Aztec),
Odin,  Quetzalcoatl,  Taut,  Wittoba,  Xamolxis,  Xbalanque,  and  Zoar.
Certainly all of the cultures associated with these accounts regarded virgin
birth as miraculous and as a sign of divine favor.  While those familiar

JESUS † The Complete Biography
with one but not any other of these accounts may well have assumed that
virgin birth was peculiar to one person in all of history, certainly this was
neither the assumption of the Jew, well schooled in the stories of the
Bible, nor the assumption of the Greek, brought up in the legends of his
ancient people.
That Jesus did not regard his own conception and birth as unique is
indicated by his pointing to something altogether different from this event
as the “one sign” that would be given of his divine authority.  In the Gospel
of Matthew (12:38-12:40): “Then certain of the scribes and of the Pharisees
answered, saying, Master, we would see a sign from thee.  But he answered
and said unto them, An evil and adulterous generation seeketh after a sign;
and there shall no sign be given to it, but the sign of the prophet Jonas:
For as Jonas was three days and three nights in the whale's belly; so shall
the Son of man be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth.”
This same sign is cited in the Gospel of John (2:18-20), and the Gospel of
Luke (11:29-30).   In the Gospel of Mark (8:11-12), Jesus refuses to give a
sign, saying “Why doth this generation seek after a sign? verily I say unto
you,  There  shall  no  sign  be  given  unto  this  generation.”   This  is  an
important avowal, because it cancels out the marshalling of multiple signs
from the Gospels which has preoccupied Christian apologists seeking to
demonstrate and prove the truth of the mission of Jesus.  It specifically
cancels out the virgin birth as a sign of his divine election, setting him
apart from all other sons of God.   Nonetheless, the Gospels of Mark and
Matthew attest to the virgin birth of Jesus, and the Qur’an also refers to
the chastity of Mary  (3:47, 19:20, 21:90) and to her becoming pregnant
through the Holy Spirit (21:91, 66:12) and the Will of God (3:47, 19:21).
We take this aspect of the life of Jesus to be a matter of fact, not of myth or
dogma.  And hence the circumstances of this miraculous birth are worthy
of being studied.   Chilton (pp. 3-22) devotes an entire chapter to what he
supposes to have been the consequences for Jesus’ emotional and social
development of his mother having conceived him out of wedlock.  He
indicates that Jesus was a “mamzer” (in effect, a bastard) and that he
would have been treated as an outsider by the Jewish community as a
whole as a result.  Vermes  (pp. 226-229) has a much more nuanced
understanding of the accounts of Mary’s virgin birth.  He points out that
Philo  of  Alexandria,  a  contemporary  of  Jesus,  described  “the
postmenopausal wife of Abraham as a woman who had become a virgin for
the second time (De posteritate Caini, 134)…he characterized Isaac, the
miraculously born child of Sarah and Abraham, as the ‘son of God’ (De
mutatione  nominum,  131)…Philo  ascribes  Sarah’s  pregnancy  to  her
encounter with God…(De cherubim, 45).” (p. 228)   Unlike both Chilton
and Vermes, we regard the virgin birth as an historical occurrence and not
a cover up for an unintentional and out of wedlock insemination or a
metaphorical spiritualization of a special birth.

Bethlehem
Where was Mary when Jesus was conceived of the Holy Spirit?  In the
Gospel of Matthew, no place is designated for this event:
1:18 Now the birth of Jesus Christ was on this wise: When as his mother Mary
was espoused to Joseph, before they came together, she was found with
child of the Holy Ghost. 1:19 Then Joseph her husband, being a just man, and
not willing to make her a publick example, was minded to put her away privily.
1:20 But while he thought on these things, behold, the angel of the LORD
appeared unto him in a dream, saying, Joseph, thou son of David, fear not to
take unto thee Mary thy wife: for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy
Ghost.
The other Gospel which mentions the conception of Jesus is the Gospel of
Luke, and it indicates that the annunciation of the pregnancy of Mary took
place in Nazareth:
1:26 And in the sixth month the angel Gabriel was sent from God unto a city of
Galilee, named Nazareth, 1:27 To a virgin espoused to a man whose name was
Joseph, of the house of David; and the virgin's name was Mary.
The Qur’an (19:22-28) also refers to Mary’s pregnancy, but does not identify
the  place  where  this  began.   It indicates  that after  she  discovered  her
pregnancy she retired “to a remote place”, and it describes the circumstances
of the birth which were altogether dissimilar to any account found in the
canonical or non-canonical Gospels:
22. So she conceived him, and she retired with him to a remote place. 23. And
the pains of childbirth drove her to the trunk of a palm-tree: she cried (in her

Where was Jesus born?  Was it in the desert, apart from all people, or in the
city of David?  Was Jesus born in Bethlehem, out in “a remote place” and did
she bring him afterwards with her “to her people”?  According to the Gospel
of Matthew and the  Gospel of Luke, Jesus was born in Bethlehem of Judaea,
only six miles from Jerusalem.  The passages identifying this as his birthplace
are altogether unambiguous:
In the Gospel of Matthew:
2:1 Now when Jesus was born in Bethlehem of Judaea in the days of Herod
the king, behold, there came wise men from the east to Jerusalem, 2:2 Saying,
Where is he that is born King of the Jews? for we have seen his star in the
east, and are come to worship him.  2:3 When Herod the king had heard these
things, he was troubled, and all Jerusalem with him.  2:4 And when he had
gathered  all  the  chief  priests  and  scribes  of  the  people  together,  he
demanded of them where Christ should be born.  2:5 And they said unto him,
In Bethlehem of Judaea: for thus it is written by the prophet, 2:6 And thou
Bethlehem, in the land of Juda, art not the least among the princes of Juda:
for out of thee shall come a Governor, that shall rule my people Israel.
What Hebrew prophet has written this prophetic verse?  It is the prophet
Micah, and as he lived many centuries after the death of King David, it
clearly refers to his descendant, Mashiach ben David:
5:2  But thou, Bethlehem Ephratah,  though  thou  be little  among the
thousands of Judah, yet out of thee shall he come forth unto me that is to
be  ruler  in  Israel;  whose  goings  forth  have  been  from  of  old,  from
everlasting.
In the Gospel of Luke:
2:4 And Joseph also went up from Galilee, out of the city of Nazareth,
into Juda, unto the city of David, which is called Bethlehem; (because

JESUS † The Complete Biography
he was of the house and lineage of David:) 2:5 To be taxed with Mary
his espoused wife, being great with child.
Why  is  this  important  to  the  authors  of  two  of  the  Gospels,  and  to
countless commentators through the centuries for the precise reason that,
as indicated in the Gospel of Matthew, Mashiach ben David was to be born
in Bethlehem.  Why is Bethlehem called the “city of David”?  As recorded
in the First Book of the Prophet Samuel, King David was born in this
city:
17:12. Now David was the son of that Ephrathite, of Bethlehem Judaea,
before mentioned, whose name was Jesse, who had eight sons, and was an
old man in the days of Saul, and of great age among men.
The Gospel of Luke refers to Bethlehem as the city of David, from the
annunciation to the shepherds:
2:11  For unto you is born this day in the city of David a Saviour, which is
Christ the Lord.
Nearly every one of the references to the city of David in the Bible are to
Jerusalem, five in the First Book of Chronicles,  fourteen in the Second
Book of Chronicles, five in the Second Book of Kings, ten in the Third Book
of Kings, seven in the Fourth Book of Kings, one in the Book of Isaiah, two
in  the  Book  of  Nehemiah,  and  four  in  the  First  Book  of  Maccabees.
However, there is two references which stand out, and which confirm that
Bethlehem was also called the city of David.  In the First Book of Kings
we find the story of David,  prior  to  being proclaimed  King of Israel,
absented himself from the court of King Saul in order to participate in a
family ceremony:
20:5 And David said unto Jonathan, Behold, to morrow is the new moon,
and I should not fail to sit with the king at meat: but let me go, that I may
hide myself in the field unto the third day at even.  20:6 If thy father at all
miss me, then say, David earnestly asked leave of me that he might run to
Bethlehem his city: for there is a yearly sacrifice there for all the family…
20:27 And it came to pass on the morrow, which was the second day of the

me to go to Bethlehem: 20:29 And he said, Let me go, I pray thee; for our

table.
According to the genealogies of Jesus, in the Gospels of Matthew (1:6) and

Bruce Chilton has argued, based on geographical proximity, and not any

The traditional explanation appears to be the only one that makes sense
today, namely, that while Jesus was born in Bethlehem, he was raised and
grew to adulthood in Nazareth, and hence that it was with Nazareth that he
was associated by all who knew him.  As we have seen in the case of David,
while he was born in Bethlehem, inasmuch he established his kingdom in
the city of Jerusalem, it was this latter city that came to be known as the
city of David57.
The  Gospel of Matthew explains how Jesus came to be residing in
Nazareth rather than Bethlehem.  It says that King Herod discovered from
the wise men from the East who had come to honor the newborn King of
the Jews that Bethlehem was where this babe was to be born, and to
protect Jesus and his wife Mary, Joseph took his family and fled to Egypt.
After this flight, he did not return to Bethlehem because he was warned in
a dream not to do so:
2:22 But when he heard that Archelaus did reign in Judaea in the room of
his  father Herod,  he  was  afraid  to  go  thither:  notwithstanding,  being
warned of God in a dream, he turned aside into the parts of Galilee: 2:23
And he came and dwelt in a city called Nazareth [Ναζαρέτ·]: that it might
be  fulfilled  which  was  spoken  by  the  prophets,  He  shall  be  called  a
Nazarene [Ναζωραῖος].
What  is  the  prophecy  that  indicates  that  the  promised  messiah,  the
redeemer  of  Israel  “shall  be  called  a  Nazarene”?   It  seems  to  be  a
connection between the Hebrew word for “branch” [netser] and the name
of the town where Jesus grew up.  A relationship between [netser] and
Nazareth was proposed in the Onomasticon of Eusebius (260-341 CE),
and in Jerome's (345-420 CE) Ad Marcellam, Epist. 46:13.  The prophetic
verse which are invoked in this passage from the Gospel of Matthew is
from the Book of Isaiah:
11:1 And there shall come forth a rod out of the stem of Jesse, and a Branch
[netser in Hebrew] shall grow out of his roots:

JESUS † The Complete Biography
Similar  references  to  a  Branch employ  other  words  in  the  original
Hebrew text; it is quite evident that the reference in the Gospel of Matthew
is  to  a  Hebrew  word,  as  there  is  no  equivalent  word  in  the  Greek
Septuagint.  Hence, the following references, while referring to Messiah
son of David are not fulfilled in a literal manner by Jesus:
The Book of Jeremiah:
23:5 Behold, the days come, saith the LORD, that I will raise unto David a
righteous  Branch [ֶ֣צֶ֣צַמַמח], and a King shall reign and prosper, and shall
execute judgment and justice in the earth.  23:6 In his days Judah shall be
saved, and Israel shall dwell safely: and this is his name whereby he shall be
called, THE LORD OUR RIGHTEOUSNESS…
33:15 In those days, and at that time, will I cause the  Branch [ֶ֣צֶ֣צַמַמח] of
righteousness to grow up unto David; and he shall execute judgment and
righteousness in the land.  33:16 In those days shall Judah be saved, and
Jerusalem shall dwell safely: and this is the name wherewith she shall be
called, The LORD our righteousness.
The Book of Zechariah:
3:8 Hear now, O Joshua the high priest, thou, and thy fellows that sit
before thee: for they are men wondered at: for, behold, I will bring forth
my servant the BRANCH[ֶ֣צֶ֣צַמַמח]…

grow up out of his place, and he shall build the temple of the LORD:
Whether or not those associated with Jesus during his lifetime recognized
the double entendre involved in calling him Jesus of Nazareth, it was
certainly not lost on later generations of Christians.  Perhaps we should
accord them the benefit of the doubt, and regard it as likely that those who
saw in him the anointed one of the house of David, born in the city of
David’s  birth,  having  as  his  foster  father  a  descendant  of  David,  and
regarded by his followers as the messiah of Davidic line, was the “branch…
out of his roots” predicted by Isaiah…hence it was not accidental that Jesus
referred so often to verses in the Book of Isaiah.
Only begotten son of the Father

JESUS † The Complete Biography
In the gospels there are indications that while Jesus claimed not to have
had a human father, and his mother claimed to have been miraculously
impregnated by the Holy Spirit, that there were lots of contemporaries who
did not believe this to be the case.  Not that there is any record of them
accusing him of being a “mamzer” (bastard), that is, of his father being
someone other than the man to whom she was betrothed, that is, Joseph.
There are allegedly such doubts preserved in the Talmud, as we have
already seen in the foregoing article on “Virgin Birth”.  But the people
around Jesus assumed that Joseph was his father, and this is clearly
demonstrated in all of the canonical gospels, as will be cited:
The Gospel of Matthew:
13:54 And when he was come into his own country, he taught them in their
synagogue, insomuch that they were astonished, and said, Whence hath
this  man  this  wisdom,  and  these  mighty  works?   13:55 Is  not  this  the
carpenter's son? is not his mother called Mary? and his brethren, James,
and Joses, and Simon, and Judas?  13:13:56 And his sisters, are they not all
with us? Whence then hath this man all these things?  13:57 And they were
offended in him. But Jesus said unto them, A prophet is not without
honour, save in his own country, and in his own house.
The  Gospel of Mark:
6:2 And  when  the  sabbath  day  was  come,  he  began  to  teach  in  the
synagogue: and many hearing him were astonished, saying, From whence
hath this man these things? and what wisdom is this which is given unto him,
that even such mighty works are wrought by his hands?  6:3 Is not this the
carpenter, the son of Mary, the brother of James, and Joses, and of Juda,
and Simon? and are not his sisters here with us? And they were offended
at him.  6:4 But Jesus, said unto them, A prophet is not without honour,
but in his own country, and among his own kin, and in his own house.
The people who heard Jesus preach in his hometown, in Nazareth and
vicinity, they knew him to be the son of Joseph and Mary, with brothers
Yakov (James), Yosef (Joses), Shim’on (Simon) and Yehudah (Judas), and
unnamed sisters.  They were offended that he would act so superior to
them, as if he didn’t know his lowly place, as the son of a carpenter.

JESUS † The Complete Biography
The Gospel of Luke:
4:21 And he began to say unto them, This day is this scripture fulfilled in
your ears.  4:22 And all bare him witness, and wondered at the gracious
words  which  proceeded out  of  his mouth.  And  they said,  Is  not  this
Joseph's son?  4:23 And he said unto them, Ye will surely say unto me this
proverb,  Physician,  heal  thyself:  whatsoever  we  have  heard  done  in
Capernaum, do also here in thy country.  4:24 And he said, Verily I say
unto you, No prophet is accepted in his own country.
This version of the same story drops the names of the brothers and sisters
of Jesus, keeps the question from those who witnessed his wisdom, and
added a proverb, which he is sure that they will say to him, to encourage
him to perform healings in Nazareth as he has already done in Capernaum.
Here he is depicted as a man of wisdom, as a healer, and he calls himself a
prophet, for if he were not a prophet, why would he speak of not being
“accepted in his own land”?

The Gospel of John:
6:41 The Jews then murmured at him, because he said, I am the bread which
came down from heaven.  6:42 And they said, Is not this Jesus, the son of
Joseph, whose father and mother we know? how is it then that he saith, I
came down from heaven?  6:43 Jesus therefore answered and said unto
them, Murmur not among yourselves.  6:44 No man can come to me, except
the Father which hath sent me draw him: and I will raise him up at the last
day.
This seems to be an account also set in Nazareth but not the same as is told
in the synoptic gospels.  There is no account of him preaching in the
synagogue that inspired this question about his family origins; and his
reply is different as well – here challenging the Nazarene Jews not to hide
their doubts but to speak openly, and telling them that only those will
come to and follow him if they are attracted to him by his heavenly Father
– hence, only if they are inspired by God, by the Holy Spirit to do so.  That
one who is so attracted will be raised up “at the last day”.  If we explain
these teachings we get far ahead of ourselves.
Those who knew him and his family believed that he had a natural, a
biological father and mother, like all other children.  That Jesus had a
miraculous birth does not seem to have been known to them…and it is

JESUS † The Complete Biography
even more unlikely that it would have been known to those who did not
live in his hometown.  In fact, we may well suppose that only the few who
witnessed the events connected with his birth were truly informed about
it…and they don’t seem to have talked about it much during his lifetime, or
surely it would have become an issue discussed among his followers and
his detractors.
We come now to the description of Jesus as the “only begotten son” of the
“Father”.   We are  already familiar  with the Biblical  references to  the
“firstborn son” of God, referring to Israel (Exodus 4:22), to Ephrayim
(Jeremiah 31:9) and to David (89:27).  In Bereshit/Genesis (22:2,12,16),
there are identical references to Yitzhak (Isaac) being the “only son” of
Abraham.  The phrase in Hebrew is “et bincha et yechiydecha” ְנָך ֶאתביְדָך ִּחְיְיִ
ֶאת meaning “thy son thine only son”.  This is confirmed in the Epistle to the
Hebrews (11:17), “17 By faith Abraham, when he was tried, offered up Isaac: and
he that had received the promises offered up his only begotten son”, and the Greek
wording of “only begotten” is “monogene μονογενῆ -- while the Greek Septuagint
does not translate the Hebrew at all, the equivalent in the Masoretic text of
Genesis was “yechiydecha”.  The first son of Abraham, with his wife’s slave
Hagar, was Ishmael.  For the fourteen years he lived before the birth of Isaac,
Ishmael was the only son of Abraham.  And it was doubtful that there would be a
second son, inasmuch as Sarah banished Hagar and Sarah was barren.  How then
could Isaac be called not just the firstborn son of Abraham but the only son of
Abraham?  The meaning of these verses, in Genesis and in Hebrews is not literal,
for the literal meaning would be erroneous.  It refers to the spiritual status, the
rank, the standing of this son, of Isaac in the eyes of God and in the eyes of his
father Abraham.  He was the “only begotten son” of Abraham because he was
chosen to inherit the property of his father and the promise given to his father by
YHWH.  Of the two, clearly the second was by far the most important.  It is
integral to the covenant of YHWH with Abraham that Isaac, the son of Sarah who
was barren and ninety years of age, should succeed him.  This son was miraculous
in his birth and he was chosen prior to his birth to inherit the promise of God.  It is
in this context that we are meant, by the Jewish writers of the New Testament, to
interpret the three references to Jesus as the “only begotten son of the Father” –
John 1:18; 3:16,18; and 1 John 4:9.  We know already that to be denominated a
“son” of the “Father” was a distinction and an honor and also entailed a great
responsibility, to live according to the commandments, to be holy and consecrated
to God.  We see then that to be the “only begotten son” of God is to be accorded
the heritage destined for the “firstborn” and to inherit the covenant of God.  The
images of the Davidic and Solomonic king, and of the Abrahamic son are both
invoked, not to suggest a direct biological tie between Jesus and his heavenly
“Father” but rather to depict a uniqueness of spiritual bond.  These appear to
coaslesce  the  imagery  of  Mashiach  ben  David,  clearly  in  the  Davidic  and
Solomonic line of “sons” of God, with that of Mashiach ben Joseph, offered as a
sacrifice to God, a suffering servant as depicted by Isaiah, and hence “Ephrayim”
the “firstborn son”.

JESUS † The Complete Biography
Year of his birth
The traditional year of the birth of Jesus is the starting point of the
Gregorian calendar, used for all business and governmental transactions of
a global nature worldwide and the default calendar in most countries and
daily referred to by most people.  However, the calculation of the birth of
Jesus has been disputed on many grounds, including the following:
1)According to the Gospels of Matthew and Luke, King Herod the Great
was the reigning monarch over Bethlehem when Jesus was born.  In the
Gospel of Matthew, it is related that Joseph took Mary and Jesus to Egypt
to flee the wrath of King Herod, and that King Herod died before Jesus was
brought back to Israel from Egypt.  Upon their return, Herod Archelaus
reigned in Jerusalem.  King Herod died in 4 BCE according to Titus Flavius
Josephus,  Antiquities  of  the  Jews  (XVII,  viii,  1).  Apparently,  Herod
Antipas,  the  eldest  son,  expected  to  inherit  the  throne  of  his  father.
However, in the last will of King Herod he bequeathed the rule of Judea
and Samaria to his youngest son Archelaus, and Galilee and Pereia were
bequeathed to Herod Antipas while Ituraea and Trachonitis (east of the
Jordan River, now in Syria and Jordan) were bequeathed to Philip.  In
Judea, Herod Archelaus was affirmed as king by the army, but he would
not assume the title of tetrarch bestowed upon him and his two brothers
until his father’s will was confirmed by Caesar Augustus in Rome.  When
King  Herod  the  Great  had  fallen  ill,  two  Jewish  leaders  among  the
populace, Judas and Matthias, had incited their pupils to remove the
golden eagle from the entrance of the Temple.  Their wish was to purify the
Temple of the abomination of desolation of Roman polytheism.  According
to the Ten Commandments, it was a sin to make and worship idols.  King
Herod had these two teachers and their pupils burned alive (March 13, in 4
BCE).   Herod  Archelaus  had  to  face  an  angry  crowd  that  demanded
rehabilitation  of  these  martyrs;  some  three  thousand  Jews,  usually
described as Pharisees, were killed during the celebration of Passover.
After the slaughter, all seemed quiet, and Herod Archelaus traveled to
Rome. In his absence, there were fresh riots. The leaders were a robber
named Judas, a royal slave called Simon, a shepherd named Athronges and
his brothers.  All may have been messianic claimants. Archelaus' troops
were unable to put down their revolts, and the Roman governor of Syria,
Publius Quinctilius Varus, had to intervene. It was a major operation,
which probably involved three of the four Syrian legions (III Gallica, VI
Ferrata, X Fretensis and XII Fulminata).   Two thousand people were
crucified, but not all the leaders were caught.  In Rome his father’s will was
opposed  by  his  brother  Herod  Antipas  and  by  many  of  the  Jewish
population, who, after his behavior towards their brethren in Jerusalem,
greatly feared his cruelty.  Nevertheless, Caesar Augustus allotted to him
the greater part of the kingdom (Samaria, Judea, and Idumea) with the
title of ethnarch, and he retained this title and governing role until 6 AD

JESUS † The Complete Biography
when Hyrcanus II succeeded him.  Ultimately, Archelaus came to terms
with one of Athronges' brothers,  something that could  not have been
popular among the Jewish population.  The Gospel of Matthew implies
that Joseph and Mary were afraid to go to the territories ruled by Herod
Archelaus, and therefore settled in Galilee (Matthew 2.22).
If King Herod the Great was alive when Jesus was born, either Jesus was
born before 4 BCE or the chronology of Josephus is unreliable.  Historians
have preferred to vest their confidence in Josephus’ dating of events, and
so they have been critical of the traditional dating of the birth of Jesus.
2)There is another reason to revise the birth date of Jesus.  In the Gospel
of Luke it is indicated that Jesus was born at the time when a Roman
census was conducted throughout the Roman Empire:  “There went out a
decree  from  Caesar  Augustus,  that  all  the  [Roman]  world  should  be
registered” (Luke 2:1).   The issuing of this decree is confirmed in various
non-canonical  texts,  including
The  History  of  Joseph  the
Carpenter58:
7. Some time after that, there came forth an order from Augustus Caesar
the king, that all the habitable world should be enrolled, each man in his
own city. The old man therefore, righteous Joseph, rose up and took the
virgin Mary and came to Bethlehem, because the time of her bringing forth
was at hand. Joseph then inscribed his name in the list; for Joseph the son
of David, whose spouse Mary was, was of the tribe of Judah. And indeed
Mary, my mother, brought me forth in Bethlehem, in a cave near the tomb
of Rachel the wife of the patriarch Jacob, the mother of Joseph and
Benjamin.
Martin writes59, “There is  a reference to such a registration of all the
Roman  people  not  long  before  5  February  2  B.C.  written  by  Caesar
Augustus himself: "While I was administering my thirteenth consulship [2
B.C.] the senate and the equestrian order and the entire Roman people
gave me the title Father of my Country" (Res Gestae 35). This award was
given to Caesar Augustus on 5 February 2 B.C., therefore the registration of
citizen approval must have taken place in 3 B.C. Orosius, in the fifth
century, also said that Roman records of his time revealed that a census
was indeed held when Augustus was made "the first of men"--an apt
description of his award "Father of the Country"--at a time when all the
great nations gave an oath of obedience to Augustus (6:22, 7:2). Orosius
dated the census to 3 B.C.  And besides that, Josephus substantiates that
an oath of obedience to Augustus was required in Judea not long before

JESUS † The Complete Biography
the  death  of Herod  (Antiquities XVII:41-45).   This agrees nicely in a
chronological sense with what Luke records.  But more than that, an
inscription found in Paphlagonia (eastern Turkey), also dated to 3 B.C.,
mentions an  "oath sworn by all the people in the land at the altars of
Augustus  in  the  temples  of  Augustus  in  the  various  districts." And
dovetailing  precisely  with  this  inscription,  the  early  (fifth  century)
Armenian historian, Moses of Khoren, said the census that brought Joseph
and Mary to Bethlehem was conducted by Roman agents in Armenia
where they set up "the image of Augustus Caesar in every temple.'. The
similarity  of  this  language  is  strikingly  akin  to  the  wording  on  the
Paphlagonian  inscription  describing  the  oath  taken  in  3  B.C.  These
indications can allow us to reasonably conclude that the oath (of Josephus,
the Paphlagonian inscription, and Orosius) and the census (mentioned by
Luke, Orosius, and Moses of Khoren) were one and the same. All of these
things happened in 3 B.C.”
This does not resolve the problems of chronology however.  If the decree of
Caesar Augustus was issued in 3 BCE, and if King Herod the Great died in
4 BCE then he would not have been alive when the decree was issued and
he could not have met the wise men from the East and issued an order to
kill all firstborn sons in the town of Bethlehem.   As there are several
attestations to the dating of the census of Caesar Augustus and only one (in
Josephus) to the dating of the death of Herod and the accession of Herod
Archelaus and his brothers, one possibility we should consider is that
Jesus may have been born shortly after the decree of Caesar Augustus, in
2/3 BCE, and King Herod may have died a few months to a year later, in
1/2 BCE.   If Joseph did not respond immediately to the census of 2/3 BCE,
and if the reference to the census was a general marker cited by Luke and
not a precise indication of the time of Jesus’ birth, then it may be supposed
that Josephus’ chronology was off by as much as four years.  We may well
wonder why centuries of Church historians would have failed to correct the
chronology of the birth of Jesus if there were compelling evidence that it
took place at a considerable distance, possibly as much as four or five years
prior to what was calculated by the originators of the Gregorian calendar.
Could it be that those who established this calendar themselves calculated
wrongly?  Could they have begun their calendar a few years later than the
events cited for its origination?  When we consider the great calendar wars
that have occurred across the centuries, between the Julianites and the
Gregorianites, the Karaites and the Rabbanites, and many others, it seems
plausible that a few years could have disappeared here or there.

The story in the Qur’an contains parallels found in both the canonical and
non-canonical gospels.  What it has in common with that found in the
Gospel of Matthew is that Mary is depicted as being with her newborn
baby upon his birth with no mention of Joseph until it is time for them to
flee to Egypt.  In the Qur’an, Mary gives birth to Jesus alone and in “a
remote place” and doesn’t even know how she will survive there.  The
Protoevangelium of James spoke of Mary being led to the desert.  Then
there is the story of a voice from below that told her how she would be able
to derive nourishment from the date palms.  It is not clear whether this
voice is of an angel or of Jesus, her newborn son.  However, a comparison
of this story with the Gospel of Pseudo-Matthew, cited here, indicates
that Muhammad did not invent this story but it was conveyed to him by his
Christian informants.  Nevertheless, either the informants mixed up the
sequence of events, or Muhammad did so.  Jesus speaks to the date tree
and asks for the dates to be provided for food not immediately after his
birth, but three days into their journey from Bethlehem to Egypt63:

The birth of Apollonius of Tyana furnishes an apt comparison with that of
Jesus66:
Now he is said to have been born in a meadow, hard by which there has
been now erected a sumptuous temple to him; and let us not pass by the
manner of his birth. For just as the hour of his birth was approaching, his
mother was warned in a dream to walk out into the meadow and pluck the
flowers; and in due course she came there and her maids attended to the
flowers, scattering themselves over the meadow, while she fell asleep lying
on the grass.
Thereupon the swans who fed in the meadow set up a dance around her as
she slept, and lifting their wings, as they are wont to do, cried out aloud all
at once, for there was somewhat of a breeze blowing in the meadow. She
then leaped up at the sound of their song and bore her child, for any
sudden fright is apt to bring on a premature delivery.

disappeared aloft; and the gods thereby indicated,  I think, the great

should  transcend  all  things  upon  earth  and  approach  the  gods,  and
signified all the things that he would achieve.
Much has been made of Jesus’ relationship with his mother Mary.  Every
child has a special relationship with mother, and so did he.  She was not a
single mother, so he did not grow up feeling the lack of a father.  By all
accounts Joseph was a good man and a good father.  But Mary did not dote on
Jesus, although the annunciations of the angels in Matthew and Luke might
suggest that she would have treated him with kid gloves.  Mary had other
children to attend to as well as Jesus, and Jesus would have spent most of his
day with his father after he was old enough to follow him around and make
himself useful.  What Jesus displayed from the earliest accounts of his life, is a
sensitivity to women’s feelings that may well have been uncommon at that
time.  That is not to say that Joseph did not go out of his way to care for his
wife Mary – again, the canonical and especially the non-canonical gospels
indicate that he did.
Flight to Egypt
According to the Arabic Infancy Gospel of the Savior (paragraph 5)67
and  the  Gospel  of  Pseudo-Matthew  (chapter  15)68,  Jesus  and  his
parents did not immediately leave Bethlehem for Egypt.  His version of the
story is considerably more leisurely…after three days, they left the cave and
entered a stall, which they shared with the animals, cited above…after
another three days they entered Bethlehem, where they spent the seventh
day, and then, on the eighth day, they circumcised Jesus:
5. And the time of circumcision, that is, the eighth day, being at hand, the
child  was  to  be  circumcised  according  to  the  law.  Wherefore  they
circumcised Him in the cave. And the old Hebrew woman took the piece of
skin; but some say that she took the navel-string, and laid it past in a jar of
old oil of nard. And she had a son, a dealer in unguents, and she gave it to
him, saying: See that thou do not sell this jar of unguent of nard, even
although three hundred denarii (5) should be offered thee for it. And this
is that jar which Mary the sinner bought and poured upon the head and
feet of our Lord Jesus Christ, which thereafter she wiped with the hair of
her head. (1) Ten days after, they took Him to Jerusalem; and on the

JESUS † The Complete Biography
fortieth day (2) after His birth they carried Him into the temple, and set
Him before the Lord, and offered sacrifices for Him, according to the
command-meet of the law of Moses, which is: Every male that openeth the
womb shall be called the holy of God. (3)
CHAP. 15.--And on the sixth day they entered Bethlehem, where they
spent the seventh day. And on the eighth day they circumcised the child,
and called His name Jesus; for so He was called by the angel before He
was conceived in the womb.  Now, after the days of the purifiation of Mary

to the temple of the Lord. And when the infant had received parhithomus,

The  second  chapter  of  the  Gospel  of  Luke corroborates  the  latter
account, virtually word for word:
21And when eight days were accomplished for the circumcising of the child,
his name was called JESUS, which was so named of the angel before he
was conceived in the womb.  22And when the days of her purification
according to the law of Moses were accomplished, they brought him to
Jerusalem, to present him to the Lord; 23(As it is written in the law of the
Lord, Every male that openeth the womb shall be called holy to the Lord;)
24And to offer a sacrifice according to that which is said in the law of the
Lord, A pair of turtledoves, or two young pigeons.
According to the Torah (Vayikra/Leviticus 12:1-4), the mother is unclean
for a total of 40 days, so even though the circumcision at the temple in
Jerusalem would have occurred on the 8th day after the birth, Mary would
not have entered the temple at all, because the time of her purification was
not yet fulfilled.  Hence, the non-canonical gospel was more precise in
indicating that Joseph brought Jesus to the temple for circumcision.  As
Mary and Joseph were poor, the Torah (Vayikra/Leviticus 12:8) permitted
them to bring as an offering either a pair of turtledoves or or young
pigeons.

There are a few other non-canonical gospels which contain accounts of
Jesus’ infancy in Egypt, and they are  cited in full here for the purposes of
our study.
The second such source is the  Latin version of the  Infancy Gospel of
Thomas (Chapters 1-3)72:
1. When a commotion took place in consequence of the search made by
Herod for our Lord Jesus Christ to kill Him, then an angel said to Joseph:
Take Mary and her boy, and flee into Egypt from the face of those who
seek to kill Him. And Jesus was two years old when He went into Egypt.
And as He was walking through a field of corn, He stretched forth His
hand, and took of the ears, and put them over the fire, and rubbed them,
and began to eat.  And when they had come into Egypt, they received
hospitality in the house of a certain widow, and they remained in the same
place one year.  And Jesus was in His third year. And seeing boys playing,
He began to play with them. And He took a dried fish, and put it into a
basin, and ordered it to move about.  And it began to move about. And He
said again to the fish: Throw out thy salt which thou hast, and walk into the
water. And it so came to pass. And the neighbours, seeing what had been
done, told it to the widow woman in whose house Mary His mother lived.
And as soon as she heard it, she thrust them out of her house with great
haste.
2.  And as Jesus was walking with Mary His mother through the middle of
the city market-place, He looked and saw a schoolmaster teaching his
scholars.   And behold twelve sparrows that were quarrelling fell over the
wall into the bosom of that schoolmaster, who was teaching the boys. And
seeing this, Jesus was very much amused, and stood still. And when that
teacher, saw Him making merry, he said to his scholars with great fury: Go
and bring him to me. And when they  had carried Him to the master, he
seized Him by the ear, and said: What didst thou see, to amuse thee so
much? And He said to him: Master, see my hand full of wheat. I showed it
to them, and scattered the wheat among them, and they carry it out of the
middle of the street where they are in danger; and on this account they
fought among themselves to divide the wheat. And Jesus did not pass from

JESUS † The Complete Biography
the place until it was accomplished. And this being done, the master began
to thrust Him out of the city, along with His mother.
3.  And, lo, the angel of the Lord met Mary, and said to her: Take up the
boy, and return into the land of the Jews, for they who sought His life are
dead. And Mary rose up with Jesus; and they proceeded into the city of
Nazareth, which is among the possessions of her father. And when Joseph
went out of Egypt after the death of Herod, he kept Him in the desert until
there should be quietness in Jerusalem on the part of those who were
seeking the boy's life. And he gave thanks to God because He had given
him understanding, and because he had found favour in the presence of
the Lord God. Amen.
The Gospel  of  Pseudo-Matthew (Chapters  17-25)73 contains  many
details about this period:
CHAP. 17.--And when Herod saw that he had been made sport of by the
Magi, his heart swelled with rage, and he sent through all the roads, wishing

all; he sent anew to Bethlehem and all its borders, and slew all the male
children whom he found of two years old and under, according to the time
that he had ascertained from the Magi.
Now the day before this was done Joseph was warned in his sleep by the
angel of the Lord, who said to him: Take Mary and the child, and go into
Egypt by the way of the desert. And Joseph went according to the saying
of the angel.
CHAP. 18.--And having come to a certain cave, and wishing to rest in it, the
blessed Mary dismounted from her beast, and sat down with the child
Jesus in her bosom. And there were with Joseph three boys, and with
Mary a girl, going on the journey along with them. And, lo, suddenly there
came forth from the cave many dragons; and when the children saw them,
they cried out in great terror. Then Jesus went down from the bosom of
His mother, and stood on His feet before the dragons; and they adored
Jesus, and thereafter retired. Then was fulfilled that which was said by

JESUS † The Complete Biography
David the prophet, saying: Praise the Lord from the earth, ye dragons; ye
dragons, and all ye deeps [9] And the young child Jesus, walking before

much afraid lest the child should be hurt by the dragons. And Jesus said
to them: Do not be afraid, and do not consider me to be a little child; for I
am and always have been perfect; and all the beasts of the forest must
needs be tame before me.
CHAP. 19.--Lions and panthers adored Him likewise, and accompanied
them in the desert. Wherever Joseph and the blessed Mary went, they
went before them showing them the way, and bowing their heads; and
showing their submission by wagging their tails, they adored Him with great
reverence. Now at first, when Mary saw the lions and the panthers, and
various kinds of wild beasts, coming about them, she was very much afraid.
But the infant Jesus looked into her face with a joyful countenance, and
said: Be not afraid, mother; for they come not to do thee harm, but they
make haste to serve both thee and me. With these words He drove all fear
from her heart. And the lions kept walking with them, and with the oxen,
and the asses, and the beasts of burden which carried their baggage, and
did not hurt a single one of them, though they kept beside them; but they
were tame among the sheep and the rams which they had brought with
them from Judaea, and which they had with them. They walked among
wolves, and feared nothing; and no one of them was hurt by another. Then
was fulfilled that which was spoken by the prophet: Wolves shall feed with
lambs;  the  lion  and  the  ox  shall  eat  straw  together.  [10]  There  were
together two oxen drawing a wagon with provision for the journey, and the
lions directed them in their path.
CHAP. 20.-- And it came to pass on the third day of their journey, while
they were walking, that the blessed Mary was fatigued by the excessive
heat of the sun in the desert; and seeing a palm tree, she said to Joseph:
Let me rest a little under the shade of this tree. Joseph therefore made
haste, and led her to the palm, and made her come down from her beast.
And as the blessed Mary was sitting there, she looked up to the foliage of
the palm, and saw it full of fruit, and said to Joseph: I wish it were possible

JESUS † The Complete Biography
to get some of the fruit of this palm. And Joseph said to her: I wonder that
thou sayest this, when thou seest how high the palm tree is; and that thou
thinkest of eating of its fruit. I am thinking more of the want of water,
because the skins are now empty, and we have none wherewith to refresh
ourselves and our cattle. Then the child Jesus, with a joyful countenance,
reposing in the bosom of His mother, said to the palm: O tree, bend thy
branches, and refresh my mother with thy fruit. And immediately at these
words the palm bent its top down to the very feet of the blessed Mary; and
they gathered from it fruit, with which they were all refreshed. And after
they had gathered all its fruit, it remained bent down, waiting the order to
rise from Him who bad commanded it to stoop. Then Jesus said to it: Raise
thyself, O palm tree, and be strong, and be the companion of my trees,
which are in the paradise of my Father; and open from thy roots a vein of
water which has been hid in the earth, and let the waters flow, so that we
may be satisfied from thee. And it rose up immediately, and at its root
there began to come forth a spring of water exceedingly clear and cool
and sparkling. And when they saw the spring of water, they rejoiced with
great joy, and were satisfied, themselves and all their cattle and their
beasts. Wherefore they gave thanks to God.
CHAP. 21. -- And on the day after, when they were setting out thence, and
in the hour in which they began their journey, Jesus turned to the palm,

conquer in any contest, You have attained the palm of victory. And while

possessed with fear? Do you not know that this palm, which I have caused

place of delights, as it has been prepared for us in this place of the

JESUS † The Complete Biography
wilderness? And they were filled with joy; and being strengthened, they all
rose up.
CHAP. 22.--After this, while they were going on their journey, Joseph said

would have taken thirty days to go over, you shall accomplish in this one
day. And while they were thus speaking, behold, they looked forward, and
began to see the mountains and cities of Egypt.
And rejoicing and exulting, they came into the regions of Hermopolis, and
entered into a certain city of Egypt which is called Sotinen; and because
they knew no one there from whom they could ask hospitality, they went
into a temple which was called the Capitol of Egypt. And in this temple

on  its  own  day  divine  honours  and  sacred  rites  were  paid.  For  the
Egyptians belonging to the same city entered the Capitol, in which the
priests told them how many sacrifices were offered each day, according to
the honour in which the god was held.
CHAP. 23.--And it came to pass, when the most blessed Mary went into
the temple with the little child, that all the idols prostrated themselves on

Then was fulfilled that which was said by the prophet Isaiah: Behold, the
Lord  will  come  upon  a  swift  cloud,  and  will  enter  Egypt,  and  all  the
handiwork of the Egyptians shall be moved at His presence.
CHAP. 24.--Then Affrodosius, that governor of the city, when news of

taken on those on whose account the gods had fallen down. But when he
came into the temple, and saw all the gods lying prostrate on their faces,

JESUS † The Complete Biography
he went up to the blessed Mary, who was carrying the Lord in her bosom,
and adored Him, and said to all his army and all his friends: Unless this
were the God of our gods, our gods would not have fallen on their faces
before Him; nor would they be lying prostrate in His presence: wherefore
they silently confess that He is their Lord. Unless we, therefore, take care
to do what we have seen our gods doing, we may run the risk of His anger,
and all come to destruction, even as it happened to Pharaoh king of the
Egyptians, who, not believing in powers so mighty, was drowned in the sea,
with all his army.  Then all the people of that same city believed in the Lord
God through Jesus Christ.

land of Judah, for they are dead who sought the child's life.

boy is the Son of the living God who created the heavens and the earth:
for when he came over to us, the idol was broken, and all the gods fell, and
perished by the power of his magnificence.

we were in the land of Israel, Herod thought to put Jesus to death, and on

13. Going out thence, they came to a place where there were robbers who

14. Thereafter they came into another city, where there was a demoniac

In contrast to the story of Jesus, Apollonius of Tyana sojourned in Egypt as
an  adult,  according  to  chapters  1-10  of  book  VI  of  his  biography  by
Philostratus.   Philo Judaeus,  another  contemporary of Jesus lived his
whole life, with the exception of a visit to Rome, in Alexandria, Egypt, from
25 BCE to 50 CE75.  Titus Flavius Josephus, born in 37 CE and deceased
circa 100 CE, was of a later but overlapping generation, and he spent his
youth in Judaea and from 71 CE onwards mostly in Rome, first as a slave
and then as a freed servant of the Emperor.  He is not reported to have
spent any time in Egypt…but his third wife was an Alexandrian Jew.  He
wrote about both Jesus and Philo Judaeus but not Apollonius of Tyana, as
he is known only to have written about Jews.  He was also regarded by the
Roman Emperor of the time and a number of others as a sort of prophet:
“It was while being confined at Yodfat (Jotapata) that Josephus claimed to
have experienced a divine revelation, that later led to his speech predicting
Vespasian would become emperor. After the prediction came true, he was
released by Vespasian, who considered his gift of prophecy to be divine.
Josephus wrote that his revelation had taught him three things: that God,
the creator of the Jewish people, had decided to "punish" them, that
"fortune" had been given to the Romans, and that God had chosen him "to
announce the things that are to come"76
Jesus of Nazareth, son of Joseph
As  we  read  previously,  the  second  chapter  of  the  Gospel  of  Luke
continues with the story of Jesus when he returns from Jerusalem to
Nazareth:
2:39 And when they had performed all things according to the law of the
Lord, they returned into Galilee, to their own city Nazareth. 2:40 And the
child grew, and waxed strong in spirit, filled with wisdom: and the grace of
God was upon him.

JESUS † The Complete Biography
Without any indication of how long the family spent in Egypt, the second
chapter of the Gospel of Matthew also reports their return to Nazareth:
2:17Then  was  fulfilled  that  which  was  spoken  by  Jeremy the  prophet,
saying, 2:18 In Rama was there a voice heard, lamentation, and weeping, and
great  mourning,  Rachel  weeping for her  children,  and  would  not  be
comforted, because they are not. 2:19 But when Herod was dead, behold,
an angel of the Lord appeareth in a dream to Joseph in Egypt, 2:20
Saying, Arise, and take the young child and his mother, and go into the
land of Israel: for they are dead which sought the young child's life. 2:21
And he arose, and took the young child and his mother, and came into the
land of Israel. 2:22 But when he heard that Archelaus did reign in Judaea in
the room of his father Herod, he was afraid to go thither: notwithstanding,
being  warned  of  God  in  a  dream,  he  turned  aside  into  the  parts  of
Galilee: 2:23 And he came and dwelt in a city called Nazareth: that it might
be  fulfilled  which  was  spoken  by  the  prophets,  He  shall  be  called  a
Nazarene.
Jesus  grew  up  in  Nazareth,  this  is  agreed  upon  by  all  the  Gospels.
However, the synoptic Gospels do not call him the “son of Joseph”.  For
example,  consider  the  way  in  which  the  Gospel  of  Luke begins  its
genealogy of Jesus:
3:23 And Jesus himself began to be about thirty years of age, being (as
was supposed) the son of Joseph…
The only case in which a follower of Jesus is reported to have referred to
him  as  the  “son  of  Joseph”  is  a  single  discourse  in  which  Philip  of
Bethsaida (the hometown of Peter and his brother Andrew), describes
Jesus to Nathaniel, as described in the Gospel of John:
1:45 Philip findeth Nathanael, and saith unto him, We have found him, of
whom Moses in the law, and the prophets, did write, Jesus of Nazareth, the
son of Joseph.
There is also one case in which a group of Jews who are not followers of
Jesus, refer to him as the “son of Joseph”.  The incident takes place on the
eastern shore of the sea of Galilee (called Lake Kinneret in Israel) , and it is
reported in the Gospel of Luke:

JESUS † The Complete Biography
4:22  And they said, Is not this Joseph's son?
The same is found in the Gospel of John:
6:42 And they said, Is not this Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and
mother we know? how is it then that he saith, I came down from heaven?
In the same context,  the Gospel of Mark first and the  Gospel of
Matthew second have Jews referring to Jesus as the “son of Mary”:
6:3  Is not this the carpenter, the son of Mary, the brother of James, and
Joses, and of Juda, and Simon? and are not his sisters here with us?...
13:55  Is not this the carpenter's son? is not his mother called Mary? and his
brethren, James, and Joses, and Simon, and Judas? 13:56 And his sisters,
are they not all with us?
The  significance  of  the  father  of  Jesus  being  named  Joseph  may  be
embedded in Jewish history and eschatology.  The name Jesus in Hebrew
is  “Yeshu’a”,  meaning  “Yah  saves”.   “Yah”  is  short  for  “YHWH”,  the
virtually  unpronounced  name  of  God  referred  to  by  many  modern
observant Jews as “HaShem”, meaning “the Name”.  Hence, the meaning
of naming this particular son of Israel “Yah saves” is that he will be a savior
to the sons of Israel, even as Joshua, “Yehoshu’a” in Hebrew, meaning
“YHWH saves” was the one who lead the fractious descendants of the
twelve sons of Yakov back into their “promised land”.   Joseph, “Yosef” in
Hebrew, was the chosen son of Yakov who saved them and their father
from  starvation,  who  provided  for  the  protection  of  his  brothers  by
arranging for their emigration from the land of Israel to a particularly
fecund region in Egypt.  He also pardoned his brothers for their former
murderous treachery towards him.  He was in effect the “father” of the
Israelites living outside of Israel.
But  the  Jewish  resonance  goes  deeper…in  the  prophets  there  are
references to a “suffering Messiah”, chiefly in chapters 52 and 53 of the
Book of Isaiah.  These references seem to have led to the development of a
parallel messianic tradition, recorded  in the Talmud and later Jewish
literature,  to  the  standard  Davidic  Messiah.   This  tradition  came  to
describe their expected leader as “Mashiach ben Yosef”, the Messiah son of
Joseph, descended from the lineage perhaps and the character definitely of
the Biblical son of Yakov.  It is a very robust tradition, finding development
not  only  in  the  Talmud  but  in  the  Targum,  the  Midrash,  the  Sefer
Zerubbabel,  Testaments  of  the  Twelve  Patriarchs,  Otot  ha-Mashiach,
Nistarot Rav Shim’on ben Yohai, the Zohar, and Kol ha-Tor, among others.
Indeed, the less likely it seemed for the sons of Israel to reclaim possession

JESUS † The Complete Biography
of their land and revive their national community, the more this messianic
tradition caught on and penetrated into the souls of the Jewish people.
While most of the literature cited here postdated the gospels and the
advent of Christianity, its roots were definitely in the Book of Isaiah, which
predated the modern era by several centuries.  Furthermore, some of the
literature found in the Qumran caves was written in this tradition.  “The
poly-messianic Testimonia text 4Q175 presents a prophet similar to Moses,
a messianic figure and a priestly teacher.[8]:  89 The Testamonia contains
four  testimonium.[9] The  fourth  testimonium  is  about  Joshua and  is
generally viewed as non-messianic. However Alan Avery-Peck suggests
that given its placement in the text concerning Joshua should be read as
referencing a war messiah from Ephraim. It is dated to the early 1st
century BCE.[8]:   1QS lists a Messiah of Israel, a prophet and a priestly
Messiah of Aaron.[10] 1QS dates from around 100 BCE.77
For those Jews who were particularly attracted to this messianic tradition,
Jesus may well have appeared to be a promising contender.  Much as been
made of the references to Mashiach ben David in the canonical gospels, but
perhaps more attention should be paid to the Mashiach ben Yosef tradition
and the signs, some of the subtle and indirect, in the texts that may point
in that direction.  While there was definitely disappointment articulated by
Jewish contemporaries of Jesus, even by some of his followers, such as
Simon Peter, Boanerges (sons of Zebedee) and Simon the Zealot, that
Jesus did not fulfill their expectations of Mashiach ben David – he was not
a warrior king leading his followers to conquer all of Judaea and beyond
that to restore the united kingdom of David and Solomon.  He was not the
miraculous messiah king who would conquer the world, so that all nations
would stream to Mount Zion to pay tribute to him and to his God.  But
surely there were also contemporaries, including some of his disciples,
such as the disciple who loved him, such as Mary Magdalene, such as Mary
and Martha and Lazarus, who understood him in a different way and were
not at all disappointed.  For them perhaps he was every bit the fulfillment
of the Mashiach ben Yosef that they expected, and the dearer to their
hearts because of his gentle ways, and his emphasis on love rather than
ferocity, on persuasion rather than coercion.
Growing up in Galilee
Apart from this identification of Jesus as the “son of Joseph” and the “son
of Mary”, there are no details in the canonical Gospels about Jesus growing
up in Nazareth.   On the other hand, there are numerous non-canonical
Gospel accounts of incidents occurring during those years.
The  Infancy Gospel  of  Thomas  (Greek  text  A)78 contains  many
stories about his childhood in the Galilee:

The stories of Thomas the Israelite, the Philosopher, concerning the works
of the Childhood of the Lord.
I. I, Thomas the Israelite, tell unto you, even all the brethren that are of the
Gentiles, to make known unto you the works of the childhood of our Lord
Jesus Christ and his mighty deeds, even all that he did when he was born in
our land: whereof the beginning is thus:
II. 1 This little child Jesus when he was five years old was playing at the ford

pools, and made them straightway clean, and commanded them by his word
alone. 2 And having made soft clay, he fashioned thereof twelve sparrows.
And it was the Sabbath when he did these things (or made them). And
there were also many other little children playing with him. 3 And a certain
Jew when he saw what Jesus did, playing upon the Sabbath day, departed

he hath taken clay and fashioned twelve little birds, and hath polluted the

not lawful to do? But Jesus clapped his hands together and cried out to
the sparrows and said to them: Go! and the sparrows took their flight and
went away chirping. 5 And when the Jews saw it they were amazed, and
departed and told their chief men that which they had seen Jesus do.
III. 1 But the son of Annas the scribe was standing there with Joseph; and
he took a branch of a willow and dispersed the waters which Jesus had
gathered together. 2 And when Jesus saw what was done, he was wroth

and the waters do thee? behold, now also thou shalt be withered like a
tree, and shalt not bear leaves, neither root, nor fruit. 3 And straightway
that lad withered up wholly, but Jesus departed and went unto Joseph's
house. But the parents of him that was withered took him up, bewailing his
youth, and brought him to Joseph, and accused him 'for that thou hast
such a child which doeth such deeds.'

IV. 1 After that again he went through the village, and a child ran and

V. 1 And Joseph called the young child apart and admonished him, saying:

the  Beta.  Then  began  he  to  confound  the  mouth  of  the  teacher

[what follows is really unintelligible in this and in all the parallel texts: a

VII. 1 Now when Zacchaeus the teacher heard such and so many allegories

The Infancy Gospel of Thomas (Greek text B)79 contains nothing
apart from stories about his childhood in the Galilee:
The Writing of the holy Apostle Thomas concerning the conversation of
the Lord in his childhood.
I. I, Thomas the Israelite, have thought it needful to make known unto all
the brethren that are of the Gentiles the mighty works of childhood which
our Lord Jesus Christ wrought when he was conversant in the body, and
came unto the city of Nazareth in the fifth year of his age.
II. 1 On a certain day when there had fallen a shower of rain he went forth
of the house where his mother was and played upon the ground where the
waters were running: and he made pools, and the waters flowed down, and
the pools were filled with water. Then saith he: I will that ye become clean
and wholesome waters. And straightway they did so. 2 But a certain son of
Annas the scribe passed by bearing a branch of willow, and he overthrew
the pools with the branch, and the waters were poured out. And Jesus
turned about and said unto him: O ungodly and disobedient one, what
hurt have the pools done thee that thou hast emptied them? Thou shalt
not finish thy course, and thou shalt be withered up even as the branch
which thou hast in hand. 3 And he went on, and after a little he fell and
gave up the ghost. And when the young children that played with him saw
it, they marvelled and departed and told the father of him that was dead.
And he ran and found the child dead, and went and accused Joseph.
III. 1 Now Jesus made of that clay twelve sparrows: and it was the Sabbath
day. And a child ran and told Joseph, saying: Behold, thy child playeth
about the brook, and hath made sparrows of the clay, which is not lawful. 2
And he when he heard it went and said to the child: Wherefore doest thou
so and profaneth the Sabbath? But Jesus answered him not, but looked

JESUS † The Complete Biography
upon the sparrows and said: Go ye, take your flight, and remember me in
your life. And at the word they took flight and went up into the air. And
when Joseph saw it he was astonished.
IV. 1 And after certain days, as Jesus passed through the midst of the city,
a certain child cast a stone at him and smote his shoulder. And Jesus said
unto him: Thou shalt not finish thy course. And straightway he also fell
down and died. And they that were there were amazed, saying: From
whence  is  this  child,  that  every  word  which  he  speaketh  becometh  a
perfect work? 2 But they also departed and accused Joseph, saying:
Thou wilt not be able to dwell with us in this city: but if thou wilt, teach thy
child to bless and not to curse: for verily he slayeth our children: and every
thing that he saith becometh a perfect work.
V. And as Joseph sat upon his seat, the child stood before him; and he
took hold upon his ear and pinched it sore. But Jesus looked upon him
earnestly and said: It sufficeth thee.
VI. 1 And on the morrow he took him by the hand and led him to a certain
teacher, Zacchaeus by name, and said unto him: Take this child, O master,
and teach him letters. And the other said: Deliver him unto me, my brother,
and I will teach him the scripture, and I will persuade him to bless all men
and not to curse them. 2 And when Jesus heard that he laughed and said
unto them: Ye speak that ye know, but I have knowledge more than you,
for I am before the worlds. And I know when the fathers of your fathers
were begotten, and I know how many are the years of your life. And every
one that heard it was amazed. 3 And again saith Jesus unto them: Marvel
ye because I said unto you that I know how many are the years of your life?
Of a truth I know when the world was created. Behold, now ye believe me
not: when ye shall see my cross then will ye believe that I speak truth. And
they were astonished when they heard all these things.
VII. 1 Now Zacchaeus wrote the alphabet in Hebrew, and saith unto him:
Alpha. And the young child said: Alpha. And again the master said: Alpha,
and the young child likewise. Then again the third time the master said:

JESUS † The Complete Biography
Alpha. Then Jesus looked upon the teacher and said: Thou that knowest
not the Alpha, how canst thou teach another the Beta? And the child
beginning at the Alpha said of his own accord the two and twenty letters. 2

VIII. 1 And after these things one day Jesus was playing with other boys

thou didst make me alive.
IX. 1 And a few days after one of the neighbours was cleaving wood and did

he arose and worshipped him, giving thanks, and cleft the wood. Likewise

X. Now when he was six years old, Mary his mother sent him to fetch water

JESUS † The Complete Biography
spring and spread out his upper garment and drew water out of the spring

XI. 1 And when he came to the eighth year of his age Joseph was required
by a certain rich man to build him a bed, for he was a carpenter. And he
went forth into the field to gather wood, and Jesus also went with him. And
he cut two beams of wood and wrought them with the axe, and set one

given me such a son. 3 And when they departed into the city Joseph told it
to Mary, and she when she heard and saw the wonderful mighty works of
her son rejoiced, glorifying him with the Father and the Holy Spirit now and
for ever and world without end. Amen.

IV. What Jesus did in the city of Nazareth.
It is a glorious work for Thomas the Israelite (Ismaelite) the apostle of the
Lord to tell of the works of Jesus after he came out of Egypt unto
Nazareth. Hear (understand) therefore all of you beloved brethren, the
signs which the Lord Jesus did when he was in the city of Nazareth: as it is
said in the first chapter.
1 Now when Jesus was five years old there was a great rain upon the earth,
and the child Jesus walked about therein. And the rain was very terrible:
and he gathered the water together into a pool and commanded with a
word that it should become clear: and forthwith it did so.
2 Again, he took of the clay which came of that pool and made thereof to
the number of twelve sparrows. Now it was the Sabbath day when Jesus
did this among the children  of the Hebrews: and the children  of the
Hebrews went and said unto Joseph his father: Lo, thy son was playing
with us and he took clay and made sparrows which it was not right to do
upon the Sabbath, and he hath broken it. And Joseph went to the child

JESUS † The Complete Biography
Jesus, and said unto him: Wherefore hast thou done this which it was not
right to do on the Sabbath? But Jesus spread forth (opened) his hands
and commanded the sparrows, saying: Go forth into the height and fly: ye
shall not meet death at any man's hands. And they flew and began to cry
out and praise almighty God. But when the Jews saw what was done they
marvelled and departed, proclaiming the signs which Jesus did.
3 But a Pharisee which was with Jesus took a branch of an olive tree and
began to empty the pool which Jesus had made. And when Jesus saw it he
was vexed and said to him: O thou of Sodom, ungodly and ignorant, what
hurt did the fountain of water do thee, which I made? Lo, thou shalt
become like a dry tree which hath neither roots nor leaf nor fruit. And
straightway he was dried up and fell to the earth and died: but his parents
carried him away dead and reviled Joseph, saying: Behold what thy son
hath done: teach thou him to pray and not to blaspheme.
V. How the people of the city were grieved against Joseph because of that
which Jesus did.
1 And after some days as Jesus walked with Joseph through the city, there
ran one of the children and smote Jesus on the arms: but Jesus said unto
him: So finish thou thy course. And immediately he fell to the earth and
died. But they when they saw this wonder, cried out saying: From whence
cometh this child? And they said unto Joseph: It is not right that such a
child should be among us. And he departed and took him with him. And
they said to him: Depart out of this place; and if thou must be with us,
teach him to pray and not to blaspheme: for our sons are put to death by
him (lit. lose their senses). 2 And Joseph called Jesus and began to
