Apollonius also spoke to the priests in a temple, and he seems also to have
been  young  at  the  time.   If  we  admit  the  chronological  order  of
Philastratus’ Biography, then he was scarcely 20 when this occurred [S13].
Here are his purported words to the priests89:
[§9] Now it is well that I should not pass over what happened in the Temple,
while relating the life of a man who was held in esteem even by the gods.
For an Assyrian stripling came to Asclepius, and though he was sick, yet he
lived the life of luxury, and being continually drunk, I will not say he lived,
rather he was ever dying. He suffered then from dropsy, and finding his
pleasure in drunkenness took no care to dry up his malady. On this
account then Asclepius took no care of him, and did not visit him even in a
dream.[3]
The youth grumbled at this, and thereupon the god, standing over him,
said, "If you were to consult Apollonius you would be easier."
He therefore went to Apollonius, and said: "What is there in your wisdom
that I can profit by? for Asclepius bids me consult you."

JESUS † The Complete Biography
And he replied: "I can advise you of what, under the circumstances, will be
most valuable to you; for I suppose you want to get well."
"Yes, by Zeus," answered the other, "I want the health which Asclepius
promises, but never gives."
"Hush," said the other, "for he gives to those who desire it, but you do
things that irritate and aggravate your disease, for you give yourself up to
luxury, and you accumulate delicate viands upon your water-logged and
worn-out stomach, and as it were, choke water with a flood of mud."
This was a clearer response, in my opinion, than Heraclitus, in his wisdom,
gave. For he said when he was visited by this affection that what he needed
was  someone  to  substitute  a  drought  for  a  rainy  weather,  a  very
unintelligible remark, it appears to me, and by no means clear; but the sage
restored the youth to health by a clear interpretation of the wise saw.
[§10] One day he saw a flood of blood upon the altar, and there were
victims laid out upon it, Egyptian bulls that had been sacrificed and great
hogs, and some of them were being flayed and others were being cut up;
and two gold vases had been dedicated set with jewels, the rarest and most
beautiful that India can provide. So he went to the priest and said: "What is
all this; for someone is making a very handsome gift to the god?"
And the priest replied: "You may rather be surprised at a man's offering all
this without having first put up a prayer in our fane, and without having
stayed with us as long as other people do, and without having gained his
health from the god, and without obtaining all the things he came to ask
for. For he appears to have come only yesterday, yet he is sacrificing on
this lavish scale. And he declares that he will sacrifice more victims, and
dedicate more gifts, if Asclepius will hearken to him. And he is one of the
richest men in existence; at any rate he owns in Cilicia an estate bigger than
all the Cilicians together possess. And he is supplicating the god to restore
to him one of his eyes that has fallen out."

JESUS † The Complete Biography
But Apollonius fixed his eyes upon the ground, as he was accustomed to
do in later life, and asked: "What is his name?"
And when he heard it, he said: "It seems to me, O Priest, that we ought not
to welcome this fellow in the Temple: for he is some ruffian who has come
here, and that he is afflicted in this way is due to some sinister reason: nay,
his very conduct in sacrificing on such a magnificent scale before he has
gained anything from the god is not that of a genuine votary, but rather of
a man who is begging himself off for the penalty of some horrible and cruel
deed."
This was what Apollonius said: and Asclepius appeared to the priest by
night, and said: "Send away so and so at once with all his possessions, and
let him keep them, for he deserves to lose the other eye as well."
The priest accordingly made inquiries about the Cilician and learned that
his wife by a former marriage borne a daughter, and he had fallen in love
with the maiden and had seduced her, and was living with her in open sin.
For the mother had surprised the two in bed, and had put out both her
eyes and one of his by stabbing them with her brooch-pin.
[§11] Again he inculcated the wise rule that in our sacrifices or dedications
we should no go beyond the just mean, in the following way. On one
occasion several people had flocked to the Temple, not long after the
expulsion of the Cilician, and he took the occasion to ask the priest the
following questions: "Are then," he said, "the gods just?"
"Why, of course, most just," answered the priest.
"Well, and are they wise?"
"And what," said the other, "can be wiser than the godhead?"
"But do they know the affairs of men, or are they without experience of
them?"
"Why,"  said  the  other,  "this  is  just  the  point  in  which  the  gods  excel
mankind, for the latter, because of their frailty, do not understand their

JESUS † The Complete Biography
own concerns, whereas the gods have the privilege of understanding the
affairs both of men and of themselves."
"All your answers," said Apollonius, "are excellent, O Priest, and very true.
Since then, they know everything, it appears to me that a person who
comes to the house of God and has a good conscience, should put up the
following prayer:
'O ye gods, grant unto me that which I deserve.'
For," he went on, "the holy, O Priest, surely deserve to receive blessings,
and the wicked the contrary. Therefore the gods, as they are beneficent, if
they find anyone who is healthy and whole and unscarred by vice, will send
him on his way, surely, after crowning him, not with golden crowns, but with
all sorts of blessings; but if they find a man branded with sin and utterly
corrupt, they will hand him over and leave him to justice, after inflicting their
wrath upon him all the more, because he dared to invade their Temple
without being pure."
And at the same moment he looked towards Asclepius, and said: "O
Asclepius, the philosophy you teach is secret and congenial to yourself, in
that you suffer not the wicked to come hither, not even if they pour into
your lap all the wealth of India and Sardes. For it is not out of reverence
for  the  divinity  that  they  sacrifice  these  victims  and  suspend  these
offerings, but in order to purchase a verdict, which you will not concede to
them in your perfect justice."
And much similar wisdom he delivered himself of in this Temple, while he
was still a youth.
Jesus as an adult – the missing years
After Jesus impresses the men gathered at the Temple, at age twelve, and
before he reappears in the gospel narrative, at age thirty (Luke 3:23) or
nearly fifty  (John 8:57), there is a gap.  We know nothing at all about his
whereabouts  and  his  doings  and  his  associations…nothing.    Various
authors impatient with this gap have sought to fill it, but their efforts are
speculative at best and often stray far from what we do know about the
man and his character.

JESUS † The Complete Biography
In the biography of Apollonius of Tyana by Philostratus, there is also a gap,
for the better part of twenty or twenty-five years90:
So far, apparently, Philostratus has been dependent upon the account of
Maximus of Ægæ, or perhaps only up to the time of Apollonius’ quitting
Ægæ. There is now a considerable gap in the narrative, and two short
chapters  of  vague  generalities  (i  16,  17)  are  all  that  Philostratus  can
produce as the record of some fifteen or twenty [I am inclined to think,
however, that Apollonius was still a youngish man when he set out on his
Indian  travels,  instead  of  being  forty-six,  as  some  suppose.  But  the
difficulties of most of the chronology are insurmountable.] years, until
Damis’ notes begin.
After the five years of silence, we find Apollonius at Antioch, but this
seems to be only an incident in a long round of travel and work, and it is
probable that Philostratus brings Antioch into prominence merely because
what little he had learnt of this period of Apollonius’ life, he picked up in
this  much-frequented  city.  Even  from  Philostratus  himself  we  learn
incidentally later on (i 20; iv 38) that Apollonius had spent some time
among the Arabians, and had been instructed by them.
In comparison with the gospels on Jesus, the biography of Philostratus is
far more detailed in its account of the adult life of Apollonius.  Hence there
is much more material, either to fill out the legend or to detail the actual
life of the Pythagorean.  Whereas apart from one journey to Egypt as an
infant, the only places Jesus is recorded to have visited were in Judaea,
Samaria,  the  Galilee  and  possibly  Idumaea  (when  he  repairs  to  the
wilderness, as it is just east of Jerusalem and other towns in eastern
Judaea), Apollonius travels a great deal.  In Book One he journeys to
Pamphylia, Lycia and Antioch, to Mesopotamia, Iran, Cissia, Babylonia
and Ecbatana.  In Book Two he journeys through the Caucasus to India.  In
Book Three he visits the Hindu sages in India.  In Book Four he visits
Greek cities, then Italy for the first time, and departs for Spain.  IN Book
Five he visits Spain, the travels to Sicily, Athens and Rhodes and reaches
Alexandria, Egypt.  In Book Six he sojours in Ethiopia, in Book Seven he
visits Rome, and in Book Eight he visits Greece, Ionia, including Smyrna
and Ephesus, and soon after he disappears.  Clearly a jet setter for his time.
Whereas Apollonius went to many of these places to learn from the wise
men reputed to live there and to oppose oppressive rulers twice in Rome –
Nero and then Domitian – Jesus claims to receive his wisdom directly
from God, and he does not challenge the rule of any earthly ruler.  A

JESUS † The Complete Biography
summary  of  his  attitude  towards  such  temporal  administration  is
epitomized in the famous saying, regarding taxation – “Render therefore
unto Caesar the things which are Caesar's; and unto God the things that
are God's.”91
Though virtually all Jewish men of the time – even of our time – are
married by the age of twenty, Jesus was not.  How can I assert that so
definitely, without any doubt?  For many reasons…let’s look at them one by
one.  Jesus did not marry because he was aware that at some time he was
going to engage in a lifestyle that would be hazardous to a family, deeply
hurtful to a spouse, and neglectful of children.  He knew that the outcome
of the teachings he would utter would be death.  That death in fact could
have come at any time after he began to teach.  He knew this from Jewish
history, from the stories of the Biblical prophets, several of whom were
killed because of what they said – Isaiah, Joel, Amos, Habbakuk, Ezekiel,
Zechariah  among  them.   He  knew  this  from  the  stories  told  of  the
Hassidim under Alexander Jannaeus, who, though a Jewish monarch,
hated and killed as many of the observant Jews as he could get his hands
on...rather like the Herodians of Jesus’ time.   He knew this from the
killing  of  those  they  considered  to  be  competitors  to  the  absolute
sovereignty and autocratic control of the Romans and their proxies over
Judaea, Galilee and Samaria, including Simon of Paraea and Ahtronges.
He knew that, like so many other men who have died martyrs, their
families would be slaughtered as well, for that was considered to be the
best way root out a problem – kill everyone.
Jesus didn’t marry because he knew that if he were to marry, and if he
were not to be martyred or if his family was spared, it would bring about
favoritism.  To be blunt, he didn’t want his blood relatives to be his
inheritors…he wanted his followers to be his family.  He made that very
clear when he said, in the Gospel of Matthew (19:29; also see Mark 10:29-
30, Luke 14:26): “And every one that hath forsaken houses, or brethren, or
sisters, or father, or mother, or wife, or children, or lands, for my name's
sake, shall receive an hundredfold, and shall inherit everlasting life.”  And
he made the point even more emphatically when he related it to his own
relations, in the Gospel of Matthew (12:47-50; also see Mark 3:33-35, Luke
8:21): “47 Then one said unto him, Behold, thy mother and thy brethren
stand without, desiring to speak with thee.  48 But he answered and said
unto him that told him, Who is my mother? and who are my brethren?
49 And he stretched forth his hand toward his disciples, and said, Behold
my mother and my brethren!  50For whosoever shall do the will of  my
Father which is in heaven, the same is my brother, and sister, and mother.”
What woman would want to marry a man with that attitude?  What son
would want his father to feel that way about him?  Jesus understood the
personal, proprietary, possessive love of family…and avoided it like the
plague.  If he had allowed that kind of love to assume its rightful priority in

JESUS † The Complete Biography
his life, it would have been impossible for him to have devoted himself
entirely to such a radical mission as he felt called to by God.
Jesus didn’t marry because his studies as a young man, and later his
itinerant preaching and healing as a mature adult did not allow him to
think of his own pleasure, of his own benefit.  They required his complete
dedication and nothing less.  Hence, in the Gospel of Matthew (8:20; and
Luke 9:58), he says:  “And Jesus saith unto him, The foxes have holes, and
the birds of the air have nests; but the Son of man hath not where to lay his
head.”  Nor could he pledge himself wholly to one woman, when the nature
of his ministry was to be available to all women who crossed his path, not
sexually, but emotionally, and in a most intimate manner.  This intimacy
would make virtually any wife feel anxious and jealous, lest she were to be
as saintly as he.  St. Francis and St. Claire figured out a way to remain in
love and still devoted entirely to God – it was with both of them opting out
of marriage, into lifelong celibacy, and a vigorous monastic life.  While it is
certainly possible that Jesus had feelings for a particular woman, but if
they were not purely spiritual, he knew he had to keep them to himself, a
secret in his own heart, known only to him and God; anything less would
wreck havoc on the community of his followers.  Anything else would
unleash  a  miasma  of  hurt  feelings,  misunderstandings,  hopeless
aspirations…a  thousand  times  worse  than  anything  an  adolescent  has
experienced.
And how do we know that Jesus didn’t marry?  Because we have not only
the canonical gospels but many non-canonical gospels as well, and none of
them say that he married.  A few scholars have recently argued that this or
that word in this or that gnostic gospel might be interpreted to mean that
Jesus had an exclusive relationship with Mary Magdalene, one that might
well have had an erotic dimension, and could have been formalized and
presumably sacralized in marriage.  Poppycock!  If that were the case, his
relationship would not have remained secret for two millennia…it would
have been the model for all Christian marriages.  Millons of Christians
celibates would not have embraced celibacy if matrimony was the pattern
of life embraced by Jesus and enjoined by him through his actions and not
just his words.  If he had been married, his spouse and his children would
have  assumed  positions  of  great  importance  in  the  early  Christian
community.  If they followed him in their holiness they would be considerd
saints and entreated in prayer every day by Christians seeking empathetic
intermediaries to approach the throne of God.  And finally, if he had been
married, and if he had children, for sure the Jewish memory would have
preserved traces of this lineage.  Jews keep track of their families, even
when they consider members of them to be heretics.
We pause for a moment to compare Jesus once more with Apollonius of
Tyana,  who,  following  his  master  Pythagoras,  and  exceeding  him  in
virtuous self-sacrifice and chastity, never had a lover and never married92:

JESUS † The Complete Biography
And as Pythagoras was commended for his saying that "a man should have
no  intercourse  except  with  his  own  wife,"  he  declared  that  this  was
intended by Pythagoras for others than himself, for that he was resolved
never to wed nor have any connexion whatever with women. In laying such
restraint  on  himself  he  surpassed  Sophocles,  who  only  said  that  in
reaching  old  age  he  had  escaped  from  a  mad  and  cruel  master;  but
Apollonius by dint of virtue and temperance never even in his youth was so
overcome. While still a mere stripling, in full enjoyment of his bodily vigor,
he mastered and gained control of the maddening passion.[the editor
notes: “Sexual abstinence is almost unheard-off in ancient philosophy.”]
And yet there are those who accuse him falsely of an addiction to venery,
alleging that he fell a victim of such sins and spent a whole year in their
indulgence among the Scythians, the facts being that he never once visited
Scythia nor was ever carried away by such passions. Not even [his rival]
Euphrates ever accused the sage of venery, though he traduced him
otherwise and composed lying treatises against him, as we shall show when
we come to speak of him below. And his quarrel with Apollonius was that
the latter rallied him for doing anything for money and tried to wean him of
his love of filthy lucre and of huckstering his wisdom. But these matters I
must defer to the times to which they belong.
What else do we know that Jesus did not do?  He didn’t sit around at home
and watch TV for the first few decades of his life.  He was active, and we
can surmise in what way that activity took shape.  He was clearly very
familiar with the Torah, the Ketuvim and Neviim, as he quotes from these
texts in his talks, and his quotes demonstrate a grasp of the inner message
of scripture and not just the literal outward meaning.  This means that he
would have been fluent in whatever languages were required of a talmid
Torah…while  he  sometimes  quotes  from  the  Septuagint,  there  are
instances when he seems to have quoted from a Syriac translation of the
Bible (see my essay on the Last Words of Jesus), and in a synagogue in
Galilee he read from the sefer Torah, which was probably in Hebrew.  I will
propose that he was fluent in Greek, Syriac, Hebrew and probably Aramaic
as well.  Since he held converse with Romans – a centurion in Galilee, and
Pontius Pilate in Jerusalem – he may well have been fluent in Latin as
well.

JESUS † The Complete Biography
There are lots of books that assert that Jesus spent his early manhood with
the Essenes, either adjacent to the Dead Sea, or in Jerusalem or some
other location.  That is possible, but by no means is it evident that he
adopted Essene views.  Hence, in order to become well informed about this
important group of Jewish believers of his day, he may well have lived with
Essenes and read their literature for a period.  That would make him
intellectually curious, not a devoted sectarian at odd with the status quo.
He certainly had ample opportunity to associate with Sadducees, scribes
and Pharisees, who are spoken of separately in the canonical gospels, and
are members of three distinct groups within the Jewish community of his
time.   It is unlikely, given his family’s poverty and his predilection for a
simple  and  unadorned  lifestyle,  that  he  would  have  been  closely
acquainted with Sadducees, but nevertheless they crossed paths, he was
familiar with their theological peculiarities and with their legal positions.
And he was critical of them.  His knowledge of the Pharisees (perisim) and
scribes (sofrim) was much deeper and presumably he had more contact
with them, both in Galilee and in Jerusalem.  We may suppose that he
spent a fair amount of his time as a young man in the synagogue, praying
and reading and studying Torah and haftorah, and in discussion with those
who enjoy discourse about religious teachings and law.  The gospels speak
of  him  addressing  multiple  congregations...in  fact  synagogues  are
mentioned  5 times in the Gospel of John, 9 times in the Gospel of
Matthew, 12 times in the Gospel of Mark, 17 times in the Gospel of Luke!
To cite just the Gospel of Matthew: “And Jesus went about all Galilee,
teaching in their synagogues” (4:23), “And Jesus went about all the cities
and villages, teaching in their  synagogues” (9:35), “And when he was
departed thence, he went into their synagogue” (12:9), “And when he was
come into his own country, he taught them in their  synagogue” (13:54).
The anti-Semitic and idiotic aversion of Christians to entering and praying
in synagogues is without foundation in the actions of Jesus.  On the
contrary, he probably spent most of his adult life in synagogues, because
that was where the sefarim were kept, and it was the Word of God that
particularly interested him.
From his disagreements with Sadducees, scribes and Pharisees on various
legal and doctrinal issues, and in particular his familiarity with those
practices that had no basis in the written Torah, but were either part of the
oral Torah or of the minhag (custom) of the community, we know that
Jesus knew the literature backwards and forwards.  While he is reported to
have been gifted with quite remarkable intuition, as in his divining that the
Samaritan woman he met at Yakov’s well had been married multiple times
and was currently with a man she was not married to (see John 4:18), this
does not suggest that Jesus had no knowledge acquired from reading, from
study, from the normal human process of learning.  He never claimed to
have omniscience, and often demonstrated his humanity, and even his

JESUS † The Complete Biography
vulnerability.  Consider, for example, his cry to God in the Gospel of
Matthew, not once but twice: “And he went a little farther, and fell on his
face, and prayed, saying, O my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass
from me: nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt” (26:39) and “He went
away again the second time, and prayed, saying, O my Father, if this cup
may not pass away from me, except I drink it, thy will be done.” (26:42)
Consider also his tears when he sees the suffering of his friends Mary and
Martha at the death of their brother Lazarus, in the Gospel of John (11:34-
36): “34 And said, Where have ye laid him? They said unto him, Lord, come
and see. 35 Jesus wept. 36 Then said the Jews, Behold how he loved him!”
For a final example, consider the tender humanity of this plea from the
cross, in the Gospel of Luke (23:34): “Father, forgive them; for they know
not what they do.”
Jesus was very comfortable with women and children.  We know that there
were several women followers who were closely associated with him, once
he began his real work.  It must be assumed, without evidence to the
contrary, that he had long association with women apart from his mother
and sisters prior to this.  In his relations with Mary and Martha there is no
trace of preference for either one, nor of formality or disapproval.  He
freely permits a woman with whom he has no family tie and whose touch
would presumably be taboo, considering the Jewish concerns about ritual
purity and the requirements of niddah, as well as the spiritual pollution
connected with fornication and adultery and prostitution – to anoint him
with expensive ointment, not with a brush but with her hair.  This is the
sort of intimacy one would imagine between happily married couples, not
between a profligate and a holy man.  The women who followed him on his
itinerant preaching, caring for him and his disciples –some of them were
married, others were not.  They prepared his body for burial as if they were
close  relations.   With  women  he  is  forgiving  and  direct.   And  he
emphasizes the love for God and love for one’s neighbor, and these words
are understood by women.  The intellectuals who quizzed him on his
teachings  may  compartmentalize  them  and  effectively  insultate  their
hearts  from  putting  the  Word  into  practice,  but  the  women  in  his
community,  like  women  everywhere,  were  impressed  with  action,  not
words.
Nor is he haughty or imperious with children.   In the Gospel of Mark
(9:36-37), Jesus speaks to his disciples in candid terms, after they have
asked him about their pecking order:  “36 And he took a child, and set him
in the midst of them: and when he had taken him in his arms, he said unto
them,  37 Whosoever  shall  receive  one  of  such  children  in  my  name,
receiveth me: and whosoever shall receive me, receiveth not me, but him
that sent me.”  Let me get that straight – whoever brings one child to
Jesus, he is accounted as a true believer, not just in Jesus but in God.  It is
through this action of spiritually adopting a child, one child, that one

JESUS † The Complete Biography
receives the kingdom of God.  In the Gospel of Matthew (19:13-15; 10:13-
15), we read: “13 Then were there brought unto him little children, that he
should put his hands on them, and pray: and the disciples rebuked them.
14 But Jesus said, Suffer little children, and forbid them not, to come unto
me: for of such is the kingdom of heaven. 15 And he laid his hands on them,
and departed thence.”  The Gospel of Luke (18:15-17) 15 And they brought
unto him also infants, that he would touch them: but when his disciples
saw it, they rebuked them.  16 But Jesus called them unto him, and said,
Suffer little children to come unto me, and forbid them not: for of such is
the kingdom of God. 17 Verily I say unto you, Whosoever shall not receive
the kingdom of God as a little child shall in no wise enter therein.”  Like
most adults, his disciples were going to shew the children away.   They had
important, adult business to attend to, and had no time for children.
Besides, the children that were drawn to Jesus were probably not the
offspring of the rich folks, but the riffraff off the street, the poor kids…
dirty, noisy, some of them diseased and deformed.  They wanted to protect
their master from these good for nothing kids…and themselves.  They
believed implicitly that association with their inferiors would rub off and
make them inferior.  They were out of touch with the reality Jesus sought
to inculcate.  Not only did he love children, but he said that anyone who
wanted entry into the kingdom of heaven, of God, the whole purpose of his
teaching, of his sacrifice of a normal life to preach and heal his fellow Jews,
anyone at all must become like little children, like infants…what are these
little ones like?  Pure in heart, honest, spontaneous.
He demonstrated to his disciples this principle in another way, in the
Gospel of Matthew (18:1-6), in another interaction with a child: “18 At the
same time came the disciples unto Jesus, saying, Who is the greatest in the
kingdom of heaven?  2 And Jesus called a little child unto him, and set him
in the midst of them,  3 And said, Verily I say unto you, Except ye be
converted,  and  become  as  little  children,  ye  shall  not  enter  into  the
kingdom of heaven.  4 Whosoever therefore shall humble himself as this
little child, the same is greatest in the kingdom of heaven.  5 And whoso
shall receive one such little child in my name receiveth me.  6 But whoso
shall offend one of these little ones which believe in me, it were better for
him  that  a  millstone  were  hanged  about  his  neck,  and  that  he  were
drowned in the depth of the sea.”  This is at the very heart of his teaching,
so radical as to upend all of human civilization.  There is no society, apart
from the society of some women perhaps, in which children have been
treated consistently as Jesus describes here.  A kindergarten, a nursery
school, a daycare center is where the kingdom of heaven begins and ends.
To humble oneself so as to be able to care for these little ones who are
entrusted to us, this is the most important task of all.  But Jesus does not
stop here.  The rest of his sermon reinforces this teaching with power and
without compromise: “7 Woe unto the world because of offences! for it
must needs be that offences come; but woe to that man by whom the
offence cometh!”  Surely he is speaking here of offences against children,

JESUS † The Complete Biography
for they are more egregious than any towards adults.  Later on in the same
sermon  he  will  speak  of  how  two  adults  can  reconcile  after  one  has
wronged the other – but if an adult wrongs a child, this is a much graver
offence, for the child is innocent.  “8 Wherefore if thy hand or thy foot
offend thee, cut them off, and cast them from thee: it is better for thee to
enter into life halt or maimed, rather than having two hands or two feet to
be cast into everlasting fire.”  This is graphic language to get across an
essential teaching – it would be better to cut off the hand that strikes or the
foot that kicks a child than go to hell for having hurt a child. “ 9 And if thine
eye offend thee, pluck it out, and cast it from thee: it is better for thee to
enter into life with one eye, rather than having two eyes to be cast into hell
fire.”  Yes, if you look upon a child with lust, it is better to take out your eye
than to go to hell for continuing to have such thoughts.  For the sexual
exploitation of children did not begin yesterday – it was going on in Jesus’
time and he disapproved of it more than any other crime.  Offences against
a fellow adult could be forgiven, but towards children, only if drastic
measures were taken to prevent reoccurrence.  His use of this explicit
language here is not to shock or to allegorize – it is to state that there must
be  no  reoccurrence  of  such  acts  against  children.   There  must  be
restitution,  but  there  must  also  be  renunciation  and  repentence.
Otherwise, the offender is going to the fire, to be burnt as if he were a dry
tree without fruit. “10 Take heed that ye despise not one of these little ones;
for I say unto you, That in heaven their angels do always behold the face of
my Father which is in heaven.” The angels of the little children, they are
the perpetual consorts of God Himself.  The disciples wanted to know who
would have the honor of sitting at the right hand of Jesus in heaven (we’ll
come back to that), and here Jesus tells them that the little children are
reserved that place closest to God. “11 For the Son of man is come to save
that which was lost.  12 How think ye? if a man have an hundred sheep, and
one of them be gone astray, doth he not leave the ninety and nine, and
goeth into the mountains, and seeketh that which is gone astray?  13 And if
so be that he find it, verily I say unto you, he rejoiceth more of that sheep,
than of the ninety and nine which went not astray.  14 Even so it is not the
will of your Father which is in heaven, that one of these little ones should
perish.”  These little children are the sheep who are lost and will perish if
they are not brought to their true shepherd, who alone can protect them
from the snake, the wolf, and particularly the wolf disguised as a lamb.
Jesus makes it his highest priority to save children.  That translates into
making education, from birth, in the family and the synagogue and the
village and the town, the focus of Christian dedication.  Not education to
become famous and rich but education to become angels which “do always
behold the face of my Father which is in heaven.”
Jesus does not neglect men.  He must have spent a great deal of his time
with men during his adult years, because he is a very effective leader.  He
leads through his wisdom and through his actions.  Rich and powerful men

JESUS † The Complete Biography
do not like him, do not see his value.  That much we can be sure of.  He
obviously did not spend much time learning how to placate or manipulate
the rich and powerful.  We already know that his focus was on the very
opposite of the spectrum – the little children, the poor, the lost and the
diseased and possessed.  We have already considered the children, but in
many of his addresses he speaks of the poor. “Blessed are the  poor in
spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.” (Gospel of Matthew 5:3)
“Blessed be ye  poor: for yours is the kingdom of God.” (Gospel of Luke
6:20)  “The blind receive their sight, and the lame walk, the lepers are
cleansed, and the deaf hear, the dead are raised up, and the poor have the
gospel preached to them.” (Gospel of Matthew 11:5; see Gospel of Luke
4:18, 7:22)  “Then Jesus beholding him loved him, and said unto him, One
thing thou lackest: go thy way, sell whatsoever thou hast, and give to the
poor, and thou shalt have treasure in heaven: and come, take up the cross,
and follow me.” (Gospel of Mark 10:21; see Gospel of Matthew 19:21)
There are many other references to the love Jesus bore for the poor, and
his insistence that all those who sought to enter the kingdom of God
demonstrate their complete severance from the grip of materialism and
their generosity with those in need.  But we should also pay close attention
to the other signs of this kingdom of God: “The blind receive their sight,
and the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, and the deaf hear, the dead are
raised up” and the crazy folk are released from the possession of their
demons.  Mary Magadalene, freed from seven demons.  Legion, from one
hundred demons.  The wholescale healing and liberation is what his gospel
is all about.  While he didn’t have any followers and didn’t make known his
teachings until after his baptism by John, his cousin, he must have been
thinking these thoughts and living by these principles from his early years.
Towards his fellow men, working men like himself, the sons and fathers of
carpenters and masons, of fishermen and farmers, or shopkeepers and tax
collectors, Jesus is honest and affectionate, and he does not rebuff genuine
affection.  Think of the disciple who loved him, leaning on his breast at his
last supper.  This disciple did not know that his beloved teacher would
never sup with him again, that he would soon be torn from their midst,
crucified, and then resurrected.  But in that intimate moment of a shared
inner, Jesus does not stiffen and reject the love of his disciple.  He is not so
unsure of himself and of his manhood that he would reject the love of
another  man.   He  would  not  assume  that  such  love  was  sexual…for
sexuality is selfish if it is not dedicated to new life, and that new life are the
little children Jesus loved and sought to protect.  Jesus inspires the very
same love in his true disciples after his death as he did while he was alive.
That is one of the lessons of the resurrection.  He demonstrated that he is
deathless, and they demonstrated that their love for him was deathless.
That link is precisely what the Gospel of John teaches page after page.
“God so loved the world that He gave His only-begotten son…”  “I give you
a new commandment, that ye love one another as I have loved you…”  “If

JESUS † The Complete Biography
ye love me, ye must follow my commandments…”  And if this sounds fuzzy
and  comforting  but  not  operational,  consider  what  Jesus  says  about
leadership: “25 And he said unto them, The kings of the Gentiles exercise
lordship over them; and they that exercise authority upon them are called
benefactors. 26 But ye shall not be so: but he that is greatest among you, let
him be as the younger; and he that is chief, as he that doth serve. 27 For
whether is greater, he that sitteth at meat, or he that serveth? is not he that
sitteth at meat? but I am among you as he that serveth.” (Gospel of Luke
22:25-27)  “34 But they held their peace: for by the way they had disputed
among themselves, who should be the greatest.  35 And he sat down, and
called the twelve, and saith unto them, If any man desire to be first, the
same shall be last of all, and servant of all.”  This is difficult for the rich and
famous, the powerful and comfortable to understand.  But it is easy for
women and children to grasp, for they have no access to such material
advantages, they derived all of their sustenance from men, and so they
know that serving others is how to show one’s humanity and that this
humanity is the true sign of spiritual stature.
If the writers of the gospels are correct, in identifying Jesus as a savior
designated before the creation of the worlds, the incarnation of the Word
that created all things, and known as such to some from his conception and
many more from his birth, then we can be sure that his adulthood was full
of incidents that manifested these supernal gifts.  Why then is there no
record of these manifestations, from age twelve to thirty or fifty?  The
answer to this question is not that obscure…countless persons have lived
over  the  course  of  centuries  and  millennia,  and  which  of  them  are
described  in  the  chronicles,  the  epic  poetry,  the  other  traces  of  our
ancestors?  It is the kings and the prophets, the wars and the conversions…
the  children,  the  women,  the  poor,  the  diseased,  the  deformed,  the
possessed,  they  are  forgotten.   Their  names  are  mostly  missing  from
history.   The Israelites are a peculiar people, because they have chronicled
their prophets for many hundreds of years.  Most civilizations preserved
only fragments of the lives of their spiritual directors, but then wrote
volumes about their kings, and more of those volumes have been lost than
the many that has survived.  We don’t know what Jesus was doing as an
adult  because  nobody  wrote  down  that  story  or  the  document  that
preserved that story was lost or destroyed.  But Josephus wrote plenty
about the kings of his time, as did Suetonius and Caesar and Tacitus and
we could continue to drop the names of many other chroniclers, but to no
avail.  None of the contemporaries of Jesus bothered to write about any of
the ordinary people living in the land of Israel, except got for the authors of
the gospels.
We know quite a bit about Jesus from the first part of his life told here.  We
know  he  was  exceptionally  intelligent,  intuitive,  a  healer,  a  miracle
worker…poor, residing in Nazareth, probably working as a carpenter like

JESUS † The Complete Biography
his father, with his father.  Jewish, a student of scripture and halacha,
friend  to  men,  women,  children.   Living  a  largely  unremarkable  life
probably focused on the moment, even as children, women, the poor, the
diseased, the deformed, the possessed tend to be.  Building his character,
he tarried for the right moment to make his mark.
BOOK THE SECOND
Jesus joins his cousin John
Elizabeth was the cousin of Mary (Luke 1:36), so their two sons were
second  cousins.   They  do  not  seem  to  have  had  a  close  personal
relationship however.   Perhaps this was in part because Elizabeth and her
husband Zacharias raised their son John in Jerusalem, where Zacharias
was a priest [kohen] serving in the Temple [beit Knesset ha-gadol] (Luke
1:8-9), whereas Mary and her husband Joseph lived in Nazareth, in the
Galilee.  Nevertheless, Jesus and his family visited Jerusalem at least once
a year, for the festival of Pesach, as already discussed.  Surely during those
visits  they  stayed  with  Elizabeth  and  Zacharias  and  met  with  other
relatives as well.
Inasmuch  as  Jesus  accompanied  his  parents  on  an  annual  visit  to
Jerusalem and in particular the Temple during the feast of Passover, it may
be surmised that the two second cousins came into contact every year,
possibly into their adult years.   There are, however, no stories that have
survived the centuries about their relations during those visits.   It is likely
that Jesus would have been aware of the preaching of John, as he was
famous and infamous throughout Judaea.  In the Gospel of Matthew,
the preaching of John is pointed out as a fulfillment of prophecy from the
Book of Isaiah:
3:1 In those days came John the Baptist, preaching in the wilderness
of Judaea, 3:2 And saying, Repent ye: for the kingdom of heaven is
at hand.  3:3 For this is he that was spoken of by the prophet
Esaias, saying, The voice of one crying in the wilderness, Prepare
ye the way of the Lord, make his paths straight.  3:4 And the same

John had his raiment of camel's hair, and a leathern girdle about his
loins; and his meat was locusts and wild honey.  3:5 Then went out to
him  Jerusalem, and all  Judaea,  and  all  the  region  round about
Jordan, 3:6 And were baptized of him in Jordan, confessing their
sins.
Likewise in the Gospel of Mark:
1:2 As it is written in the prophets,  Behold, I send my messenger
before thy face, which shall prepare thy way before thee.  1:3 The

What all four of the canonical Gospels cite are from among these verses

40:3 The voice of him that crieth in the wilderness, Prepare ye the

What precedes this quotation in the  Gospel of Mark is the following

This verse is also found cited elsewhere in the  Gospel of Luke, where

What was the substance of John’s sermons?  We find snippets of them in
the canonical Gospels, beginning with the Gospel of Matthew:

The Gospel of Luke tells the same story, but in much greater detail:

Why would John call the people of his time a “generation of vipers”, which
was reiterated by Jesus (Gospel of Matthew 12:34 and 23:33) in at least
two  of  his  discourses?  The  Greek  word  translated  in  the  KJV  as
“generation” implies illegitimacy, and the word translated as “vipers” most
like refers to the first serpent himself, the snake in the Garden of Eden.
Hence, the “children of Satan” is most likely what he had in mind.   The
First  Epistle  of  John  indeed  refers  to  “the  children  of  God”  and  the
“children of the devil” (3:10), and in the Gospel of Matthew (13:38), Jesus
calls them “the children of the kingdom” and the “children of the wicked
one”.  In the Gospel of John, Jesus answers his critics as follows:

JESUS † The Complete Biography
8:44 Ye are of your father the devil, and the lusts of your father ye will do.
He  was  a  murderer  from  the  beginning,  and  abode  not  in  the  truth,
because there is no truth in him. When he speaketh a lie, he speaketh of his
own: for he is a liar, and the father of it.
The first time we hear of any contact between Jesus and John is in the
baptism of Jesus by John, which we may presume, from the account cited
above, to have occurred after the death of Joseph.   The Gospel of Mark
tells the story of the baptism of Jesus, and indicates that as he emerged

up out of the water, he saw the heavens opened, and the Spirit like a dove
descending upon him: 1:11 And there came a voice from heaven, saying,
Thou art my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.
The  Gospel of Matthew tells the same story, but elaborates…in this
version, John does not want to baptize Jesus because he discerns the

3:13 Then cometh Jesus from Galilee to Jordan unto John, to be baptized
of him.  3:14 But John forbad him, saying, I have need to be baptized of
thee, and comest thou to me? 3:15 And Jesus answering said unto him,

am well pleased.

When Jesus went down to the water, fire was kindled in the Jordan; and

Another source attests to John baptizing, that is, Titus Flavius Josephus
Judaeus  (that  is  his  Roman  name,  assumed  upon  being  conferred
citizenship; his original name in Hebrew was Yosef ben Matityahu98), in
The Antiquities of the Jews, 18. 116–117:
…John, that was called the Baptist….was a good man, and commanded
the Jews to exercise virtue, both as to righteousness towards one another,
and piety towards God, and so to come to baptism; for that the washing
[with water] would be acceptable to him, if they made use of it, not in order
to the putting away [or the remission] of some sins [only], but for the
purification of the body; supposing still that the soul was thoroughly
purified beforehand by righteousness.99
The “voice from heaven” in these canonical and non-canonical Gospel
accounts has traditionally been said by Christian theologians to refer to
these verses from a psalm attributed to David:
2:6 Yet have I set my king upon my holy hill of Zion.  2:7 I will declare the
decree: the LORD hath said unto me, Thou art my Son; this day have I
begotten thee.
The identification of this psalm with the words spoken by the “voice of
heaven” is by virtue of two features…first of all, in the psalm God is
addressing David, and the name David means “beloved”; secondly, the
ministry of Jesus begins with his baptism by John, and in that sense he is
begotten in that moment.  As we will soon discover, at the core of the
message of Jesus was that every soul must be reborn in the spirit, and
hence it is fitting that his rebirth should occur at the moment of his
baptism,  perpetually  associating  baptism  with  spiritual  nascence.   It
appears, then, that it was the moment of his baptism that signaled the
commencement of the ministry of Jesus, and that this was experienced by
Jesus, and perhaps also by John and others, in the form of a vision and a
voice from heaven.
This private announcement of his Davidic messianic station is reported at
a later juncture in the life of Jesus in the Gospel of Matthew, when the
“voice out of the cloud” makes the same statement to Jesus in the company
of Peter, James and John the brother of James:

JESUS † The Complete Biography
17:1 And after six days Jesus taketh Peter, James, and John his brother,
and  bringeth  them  up  into  an  high  mountain  apart,  17:2  And  was
transfigured before them: and his face did shine as the sun, and his raiment
was white as the light.  17:3 And, behold, there appeared unto them Moses
and Elias talking with him.  17:4 Then answered Peter, and said unto Jesus,
Lord, it is good for us to be here: if thou wilt, let us make here three
tabernacles; one for thee, and one for Moses, and one for Elias.  17:5 While
he yet spake, behold, a bright cloud overshadowed them: and behold a
voice out of the cloud, which said, This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well
pleased; hear ye him.
This latter visitation is recalled in the Second Epistle of Peter:
1:16 For we have not followed cunningly devised fables, when we made
known unto you the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, but were
eyewitnesses of his majesty.  1:17 For he received from God the Father
honour and glory, when there came such a voice to him from the excellent
glory, This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.  1:18 And this voice
which came from heaven we heard, when we were with him in the holy
mount.
The canonical Gospels indicate that John was aware of the superlative

and he will throughly purge his floor, and gather his wheat into the garner;
but he will burn up the chaff with unquenchable fire.
The Gospel of Mark quotes John likewise but more concisely:
1:7 And preached, saying, There cometh one mightier than I after me, the

Holy Ghost.

Jesus commented on the rank and function of his cousin John, confirming
that he was the one designated by John as “coming after me” who “is
preferred before me, whose shoe’s latchet I am not worthy to unloose”, in

11:2 Now when John had heard in the prison the works of Christ, he sent

and shew John again those things which ye do hear and see: 11:5 The blind

hear, the dead are raised up, and the poor have the gospel preached to
them.100 11:6 And blessed is he, whosoever shall not be offended in me.
The Gospel of Luke adds a few details to the account:

many that were blind he gave sight. 7:22 Then Jesus answering said unto
them, Go your way, and tell John what things ye have seen and heard; how

the dead are raised, to the poor the gospel is preached. 7:23 And blessed
is he, whosoever shall not be offended in me.

In contrast to the behavior of John the Baptist, who is reported to have

belly, and goeth out into the draught, purging all meats? 7:20 And he said,

In  contrast  to  this  teaching  is  the  practice  and  instruction  of  his
contemporary, Apollonius of Tyana, who was meticulous about his diet and
about his dietary prescriptions for others112:
Notwithstanding he [Apollonius of Tyana] did not cease to love Euxenus,
nay, he persuaded his father to present him with a villa outside the town,
where there were tender groves and fountains, and he said to him: "Now
you live there your own life, but I will live that of Pythagoras."113
[§8] Now Euxenus realized that he was attached to a lofty ideal, and asked
him at what point he would begin it. Apollonius answered: "At the point at
which physicians begin, for they, by purging the bowels of their patients
prevent some from being ill at all, and heal others."
And having said this he declined to live upon a flesh diet, on the ground
that it was unclean, and also that it made the mind gross; so he partook
only of dried fruits and vegetables, for he said that all the fruits of the
earth are clean. And of wine he said that it was a clean drink because it is
yielded to men by so well-domesticated a plant as the vine; but he declared
that it endangered the mental balance and system and darkened, as with
mud, the ether which is in the soul.
After then having thus purged his interior, he took to walking without
shoes by way of adornment and clad himself in linen raiment, declining to
wear any animal product; and he let his hair grow long and lived in the
Temple.  And  the  people  round  about  the  Temple  were  struck  with
admiration for him, and the god Asclepius114 one day said to the priest that
he was delighted to have Apollonius as witness of his cures of the sick; and

JESUS † The Complete Biography
such was his reputation that the Cilicians115 themselves and the people all
around flocked to Aegae116 to visit him. Hence the Cilician proverb: "Whither
runnest thou? Is it to see the stripling?"
Such was the saying that arose about him, and it gained the distinction of
becoming a proverb.
[§9] Now it is well that I should not pass over what happened in the Temple,
while relating the life of a man who was held in esteem even by the gods.
For an Assyrian117 stripling came to Asclepius, and though he was sick, yet
he lived the life of luxury, and being continually drunk, I will not say he
lived, rather he was ever dying. He suffered then from dropsy, and finding
his pleasure in drunkenness took no care to dry up his malady. On this
account then Asclepius took no care of him, and did not visit him even in a
dream118.
The youth grumbled at this, and thereupon the god, standing over him,
said, "If you were to consult Apollonius you would be easier."
He therefore went to Apollonius, and said: "What is there in your wisdom
that I can profit by? for Asclepius bids me consult you."
And he replied: "I can advise you of what, under the circumstances, will be
most valuable to you; for I suppose you want to get well."
"Yes, by Zeus," answered the other, "I want the health which Asclepius
promises, but never gives."
"Hush," said the other, "for he gives to those who desire it, but you do
things that irritate and aggravate your disease, for you give yourself up to
luxury, and you accumulate delicate viands upon your water-logged and
worn-out stomach, and as it were, choke water with a flood of mud."
This was a clearer response, in my opinion, than Heraclitus119, in his wisdom,
gave. For he said when he was visited by this affection that what he needed
was  someone  to  substitute  a  drought  for  a  rainy  weather,  a  very

JESUS † The Complete Biography
unintelligible remark, it appears to me, and by no means clear; but the sage
restored the youth to health by a clear interpretation of the wise saw.
[§10] One day he saw a flood of blood upon the altar, and there were
victims laid out upon it, Egyptian bulls that had been sacrificed and great
hogs, and some of them were being flayed and others were being cut up;
and two gold vases had been dedicated set with jewels, the rarest and most
beautiful that India can provide. So he went to the priest and said: "What is
all this; for someone is making a very handsome gift to the god?"
And the priest replied: "You may rather be surprised at a man's offering all
this without having first put up a prayer in our fane, and without having
stayed with us as long as other people do, and without having gained his
health from the god, and without obtaining all the things he came to ask
for. For he appears to have come only yesterday, yet he is sacrificing on
this lavish scale. And he declares that he will sacrifice more victims, and
dedicate more gifts, if Asclepius will hearken to him. And he is one of the
richest men in existence; at any rate he owns in Cilicia an estate bigger than
all the Cilicians together possess. And he is supplicating the god to restore
to him one of his eyes that has fallen out."
But Apollonius fixed his eyes upon the ground, as he was accustomed to
do in later life, and asked: "What is his name?"
And when he heard it, he said: "It seems to me, O Priest, that we ought not
to welcome this fellow in the Temple: for he is some ruffian who has come
here, and that he is afflicted in this way is due to some sinister reason: nay,
his very conduct in sacrificing on such a magnificent scale before he has
gained anything from the god is not that of a genuine votary, but rather of
a man who is begging himself off for the penalty of some horrible and cruel
deed."
This was what Apollonius said: and Asclepius appeared to the priest by
night, and said: "Send away so and so at once with all his possessions, and
let him keep them, for he deserves to lose the other eye as well."

Jesus goes into the desert
Jesus rises up from his baptism, from the purification of the mikvah and
the next scene according to the synoptic Gospels, Matthew, Mark and
Luke, is his solo sojourn in the wilderness:
4:1 Then was Jesus led up of the spirit into the wilderness to be tempted of
the devil.  4:2 And when he had fasted forty days and forty nights, he was
afterward an hungred.
1:12 And immediately the spirit driveth him into the wilderness.  1:13 And he
was there in the wilderness forty days, tempted of Satan; and was with the
wild beasts; and the angels ministered unto him.
4:1 And Jesus being full of the Holy Ghost returned from Jordan, and was
led by the Spirit into the wilderness,  4:2 Being forty days tempted of the
devil. And in those days he did eat nothing: and when they were ended, he
afterward hungered.
The story of his sojourn in the wilderness reminds the reader immediately
of the 40 years Moses and the Israelites spent wandering in the wilderness
of Sinai, according to the principle of scripture, stated in The  Book of
Numbers:
14:34 After the number of the days in which ye searched the land, even
forty days, each day for a year, shall ye bear your iniquities, even forty
years, and ye shall know my breach of promise.
It is also reminiscent of the story of Noah, and the rain that endured 40
days and 40 nights (Genesis 7:4, 12; 8:6).  Noah was set apart from the
world of humanity, and took only what was needed with him.  This setting
apart was the prelude to his re-establishment of God’s covenant on earth.

JESUS † The Complete Biography
Above all this sojourn recalls the story of Elijah in the wilderness, as told in
the Third Book of Kings:

and Elisha the son of Shaphat of Abelmeholah shalt thou anoint to be

Moses had come to the wilderness of Judaea, to the Jordan River, and he
did not cross over.  Whether with the memory of the 40 years of Moses or
the 40 days and nights of Elijah, Jesus set forth into the wilderness, the
dwelling place of the outcasts of society and the wildbeasts and evil spirits
eschewed by the faithful.  It  was in the wilderness that he would be
fortified, prepared for the ministry that he was thenceforth to pursue.  It
was in the wilderness that his first dialogue occurs, between the self and
the soul, between satan and the angel of the Lord.
The Gospel of Matthew tells the story of this dialogue, which recalls the
dialogues in the Book of Job:
4:3 And when the tempter came to him, he said, If thou be the Son of God,
command that these stones be made bread.  4:4 But he answered and
said, It is written, Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that
proceedeth out of the mouth of God.  4:5 Then the devil taketh him up
into the holy city, and setteth him on a pinnacle of the temple, 4:6 And
saith unto him,  If thou be the Son of God, cast thyself down: for it is
written, He shall give his angels charge concerning thee: and in their hands
they shall bear thee up, lest at any time thou dash thy foot against a stone.
4:7 Jesus said unto him, It is written again, Thou shalt not tempt the Lord
thy  God.  4:8 Again,  the  devil  taketh  him  up  into  an  exceeding high
mountain, and sheweth him all the kingdoms of the world, and the glory of
them; 4:9 And saith unto him, All these things will I give thee, if thou wilt fall
down and worship me.  4:10 Then saith Jesus unto him, Get thee hence,
Satan: for it is written, Thou shalt worship the Lord thy God, and him only
shalt thou serve.  4:11 Then the devil leaveth him, and, behold, angels came
and ministered unto him.
The Gospel of Luke tells the story in virtually identical terms:

Fragments of this story are also found in the Gospel according to the
Hebrews, cited by Jerome and by Origen:
The Jewish copy has not “to the holy city”, but “to Jerusalem”.120
Then my mother, the Holy Spirit, took me by oe of my hairs, and carried me
to Mount Tabor.121
What is the purpose of this story?  Who could have witnessed it?   The only
witness to this story was Jesus.  It was Jesus who sojourned alone in the
wilderness.  Even as the story of his baptism was, according to two of the
accounts,  witnessed  in  its  spiritual  dimensions  by  Jesus  alone,  and,
according to the third account by John as well as Jesus, and not by anyone
else, so also this dialogue between the devil and the Son of God was his
experience alone.  And in this story are found the hidden words wherein
his  teachings  are  enshrined.   In  dialogue  form  they  constitute  the
contrasted  teachings  of  the  world  and  its  powers  and  principalities,
represented here by the devil, with the teachings of the divine prophets
and angels of the Lord.  The one side sees only the material dimension, and
calls upon the Son of God to exercise physical powers to satisfy his physical
hunger, to do magic in order to demonstrate his control over the elements

JESUS † The Complete Biography
and to satisfy his appetites.  He answers that with the teaching he would
reiterate throughout his ministry, that “man shall not live by bread alone,
but by every word of God”.   This is a direct quote from the  Book of
Devarim (Deuteronomy), wherein Moses is speaking to the Israelites
near Horeb (5:2), the very Horeb where Elijah dwelt for 40 days:
8:3 And he humbled thee, and suffered thee to hunger, and fed thee with
manna, which thou knewest not, neither did thy fathers know; that he might
make thee know that man doth not live by bread only, but by every word
that proceedeth out of the mouth of the LORD doth man live.
The second temptation reported above in the  Gospel of Matthew and
the third temptation in the  Gospel of Luke, is not to rely upon the
miraculous intervention of God, and to act as if one is invulnerable, rather
than in need of His help.  It is to believe oneself to be physically impervious
to damage or death, and to value such physical prowess as was related of
the heroes and gods of many nations.
While there is indeed a promise found in the Psalms that God:
91:9 Because thou hast made the LORD, which is my refuge, even the most
High, thy habitation; 91:10 There shall no evil befall thee, neither shall any
plague come nigh thy dwelling. 91:11 For he shall give his angels charge over
thee, to keep thee in all thy ways. 91:12 They shall bear thee up in their
hands, lest thou dash thy foot against a stone.
Notwithstanding, Jesus is firm in noting that it is for God to test His
servants  and  not the  converse,  as  he  invoked  by  citing  the  Book  of
Deuteronomy/Devarim:
6:16 Ye shall not tempt the LORD your God, as ye tempted him in Massah.
The third temptation in the Gospel of Matthew and the second in the
Gospel of Luke is to possess everything, to have all the kingdoms of the
earth, and in exchange to worship the opponent of God, to worship what
Jesus would later call Mammon, when he taught, “Ye cannot serve God
and mammon” (Matthew 6:24; Luke 16:13).  To this Jesus replies with
what  classical  Judaism  calls  the  Shemah122,  “Shema  Yisrael,  adonai
eloheinu, adonai echad.”  (Hear, O Israel, the Lord our God, the Lord is
one) is immediately followed by this commandment (and its reiterations),
which is to be found in the Book of Deuteronomy/Devarim:

his name.

his statutes, and his judgments, and his commandments, alway.

As in the Book of Job, where Satan dialogues with the Lord, and then the
Lord dialogues with Job, and Job with his friends, the dialogue of Satan
with Jesus is a story that contrasts evil and good, a morality play.  Jesus
must have related this dialogue many times to his followers, each time
aligning it with the powerful symbolism of a sojourn in the wilderness for
40 days and 40 nights.  Like the confrontations of Elijah with the prophets
of Baal, Jesus meets every challenge from the devil with truth.  He is
inflexible, unwavering, unswayed.  These are the qualities he encouraged
in his true followers. Only such determination could establish the kingdom
of God, on earth, as it is in heaven.

reference to some distant age, but to his own time, his own experience.
Disciples of John become disciples of Jesus
The chronology of events in the Gospels is not consistent from one to the
other, and there are gaps in every account.  The Gospel of John does not
describe the baptism of Jesus by John, but it relates his telling his disciples
about that baptism…this could only have occurred after the baptism.  I
suggest this took place after Jesus returned from the Judaean desert.
In the Gospel of John, it is recorded that John was preaching one day in
Judaea:
1:19 And this is the record of John, when the Jews sent priests and Levites
from Jerusalem to ask him,  Who art thou? 1:20 And he confessed, and
denied not; but confessed, I am not the Christ. 1:21 And they asked him,
What then? Art thou Elias [Elijah]? And he saith, I am not. Art thou that
prophet [Deut 18:15,18]?  And he answered,  No. 1:22 Then said they unto
him, Who art thou? that we may give an answer to them that sent us. What
sayest thou of thyself? 1:23 He said,  I am the voice of one crying in the
wilderness, Make straight the way of the Lord, as said the prophet Esaias
[Elijah]. 1:24 And they which were sent were of the Pharisees. 1:25 And
they asked him, and said unto him, Why baptizest thou then, if thou be not
that Christ [Mashiach ben David], nor Elias [Elijah], neither that prophet
[Deut 18:15,18]? 1:26 John answered them, saying, I baptize with water: but

JESUS † The Complete Biography
there standeth one among you, whom ye know not; 1:27 He it is, who coming
after me is preferred before me, whose shoe's latchet I am not worthy to
unloose.  1:28 These things were done in Bethabara beyond Jordan, where
John was baptizing.
The  Gospel of  John continues the  story,  and  John tells  two  of his
followers that Jesus is the one to which his prophecies refer, and the
circumstances of his baptism:
1:29 The next day John seeth Jesus coming unto him, and saith, Behold the
Lamb of God123, which taketh away the sin of the world. 1:30 This is he of
whom I said, After me cometh a man which is preferred before me: for he
was before me. 1:31 And I knew him not: but that he should be made
manifest to Israel, therefore am I come baptizing with water. 1:32 And John
bare record, saying, I saw the Spirit descending from heaven like a dove,
and it abode upon him. 1:33 And I knew him not: but he that sent me to
baptize with water, the same said unto me, Upon whom thou shalt see the
Spirit descending, and remaining on him, the same is he which baptizeth
with the Holy Ghost. 1:34 And I saw, and bare record that this is the Son of
God.
Whereas the other Gospels tell the story of the baptism of Jesus as it was
happening, John tells this story to an unidentified company of his disciples
*after* it happens.  Hence, he could have told them about it well after the
fact.  The Gospel of John continues:
1:35 Again the next day after John stood, and two of his disciples; 1:36 And
looking upon Jesus as he walked, he saith, Behold the Lamb of God! 1:37
And the two disciples heard him speak, and they followed Jesus.
The second time that John designates Jesus as “the Lamb of God” to a
group of his disciples, they do what he evidently wanted them to do—they
followed Jesus.  The Gospel of John goes on to say:
1:38 Then Jesus turned, and saw them following, and saith unto them, What
seek ye? They said unto him, Rabbi, (which is to say, being interpreted,
Master,) where dwellest thou? 1:39 He saith unto them,  Come and see.
They came and saw where he dwelt, and abode with him that day: for it was

JESUS † The Complete Biography
about the tenth hour. 1:40 One of the two which heard John speak, and
followed him, was Andrew, Simon Peter's brother. 1:41 He first findeth his
own  brother  Simon,  and  saith  unto  him,  We  have  found  the  Messias
[Mashiach ben David], which is, being interpreted, the Christ. 1:42 And he
brought him to Jesus. And when Jesus beheld him, he said, Thou art Simon
[Shim’on] the son of Jona [Yona]: thou shalt be called Cephas [Greek for
Rock], which is by interpretation, A stone.
Jesus sojourns in the Galilee
The Gospel of John, as pointed out earlier, depicts Andrew as a disciple of
John  who  seeks  out  Jesus  when  John  calls  him  “the  Lamb  of  God”.
Andrew becomes convinced that Jesus is the Messiah and so he finds his
brother Peter and brings him to meet the Messiah.  The Gospel of John
does not say that Andrew and Peter began from that moment to follow
Jesus, nor that Jesus invited them to follow him.  It states that this was
their first meeting with him.  If this were the case, the *subsequent*
encounter of Jesus with Andrew and Peter on the shore of the Sea of
Galilee and their immediate abandonment of their vocation in order to
follow him makes much more sense.    After his first meeting with Andrew
and Simon Peter, the Gospel of John records:
1:43 The day following Jesus would go forth into Galilee, and findeth Philip,
and saith unto him, Follow me. 1:44 Now Philip was of Bethsaida, the city of
Andrew and Peter.
The Gospel of John does not record the election of Andrew and Peter…it
states that they came to him, not that he summoned them to follow him.
The Gospel of Matthew describes his summons to the two brothers:
4:18 And Jesus, walking by the sea of Galilee, saw two brethren, Simon
called Peter, and Andrew his brother, casting a net into the sea: for they
were fishers.  4:19 And he saith unto them, Follow me, and I will make you
fishers of men.  4:20 And they straightway left their nets, and followed him.
4:21 And going on from thence, he saw other two brethren, James the son
of Zebedee, and John his brother, in a ship with Zebedee their father,
mending their nets; and he called them.  4:22 And they immediately left the
ship and their father, and followed him.

JESUS † The Complete Biography
The Gospel of Mark tells the same story in its own fashion:
1:16 Now as he walked by the sea of Galilee, he saw Simon and Andrew his
brother casting a net into the sea: for they were fishers.  1:17 And Jesus
said unto them, Come ye after me, and I will make you to become fishers of
men.  1:18 And straightway they forsook their nets, and followed him.  1:19
And when he had gone a little farther thence, he saw James the son of
Zebedee, and John his brother, who also were in the ship mending their
nets.  1:20 And straightway he called them: and they left their father
Zebedee in the ship with the hired servants, and went after him.
The Gospel of Luke does not refer to the election of the disciples, but it
does name the disciples:
6:13 And when it was day, he called unto him his disciples: and of them he
chose twelve, whom also he named apostles; 6:14 Simon, (whom he also
named  Peter,)  and  Andrew  his  brother,  James  and  John,  Philip  and
Bartholomew, 6:15 Matthew and Thomas, James the son of Alphaeus, and
Simon called Zelotes, 6:16 And Judas the brother of James, and Judas
Iscariot, which also was the traitor.
Likewise, the Gospel of the Ebionites124 refers to the election of these
disciples:
Coming to Capernaum, he entered the house of Simon, who is called Peter,
and said, “As I passed by the lake of Tiberias, I chose John and James,
sons of Zebedee, and Simon, Andrew, Thaddaeus, Simon the Zealot,
Judas Iscariot; and you, Matthew, sitting at the tax office, I called and you
followed me.  You, therefore, I desire to be twelve apostles, as a witness to
Israel.”
While the Gospels of Matthew and Mark tell only the of the election of
Andrew and Simon Peter followed by that of James and John, the Gospel
of John refers to the election of Philip, and after him Nathanael:
1:43 The day following Jesus would go forth into Galilee, and findeth Philip,
and saith unto him, Follow me. 1:44 Now Philip was of Bethsaida, the city of
Andrew and Peter. 1:45 Philip findeth Nathanael, and saith unto him,  We

JESUS † The Complete Biography
have found him, of whom Moses in the law, and the prophets, did write,
Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Joseph. 1:46 And Nathanael said unto him,
Can there any good thing come out of Nazareth? Philip saith unto him,
Come and see. 1:47 Jesus saw Nathanael coming to him, and saith of him,
Behold an Israelite indeed, in whom is no guile! 1:48 Nathanael saith unto
him, Whence knowest thou me? Jesus answered and said unto him, Before
that Philip called thee, when thou wast under the fig tree, I saw thee. 1:49
Nathanael answered and saith unto him, Rabbi, thou art the Son of God;

Because I said unto thee, I saw thee under the fig tree, believest thou? thou
shalt see greater things than these. 1:51 And he saith unto him, Verily, verily,
I say unto you, Hereafter ye shall see heaven open, and the angels of God
ascending and descending upon the Son of man.
While Philip is mentioned as one of the twelve disciples in the synoptic
Gospels (Matthew 10:3; Mark 3:18; Luke 6:14), this is the only reference in
any of them to him.  Nathanael is only referred to in the Gospel of John,
where he is counted among the disciples (John 21:1-2).  The Gospel of
John continues with another story not found in the synoptic Gospels:
2:1 And the third day there was a marriage in Cana of Galilee; and the
mother  of  Jesus  was  there:  2:2  And  both  Jesus  was  called,  and  his
disciples, to the marriage. 2:3 And when they wanted wine, the mother of
Jesus saith unto him, They have no wine. 2:4 Jesus saith unto her, Woman,
what have I to do with thee? mine hour is not yet come. 2:5 His mother saith
unto the servants, Whatsoever he saith unto you, do it. 2:6 And there were
set there six waterpots of stone, after the manner of the purifying of the
Jews, containing two or three firkins apiece. 2:7 Jesus saith unto them, Fill
the waterpots with water. And they filled them up to the brim. 2:8 And he
saith unto them, Draw out now, and bear unto the governor of the feast.
And they bare it. 2:9 When the ruler of the feast had tasted the water that
was made wine, and knew not whence it was: (but the servants which drew
the water knew;) the governor of the feast called the bridegroom, 2:10 And
saith unto him, Every man at the beginning doth set forth good wine; and
when men have well drunk, then that which is worse: but thou hast kept the
good wine until now. 2:11 This beginning of miracles did Jesus in Cana of

JESUS † The Complete Biography
Galilee, and manifested forth his glory; and his disciples believed on him.
2:12 After this he went down to Capernaum, he, and his mother, and his
brethren, and his disciples: and they continued there not many days.
How did the “beloved disciple”, who purports to be the source of the
Gospel of  John know about this miracle, while  the sources  for  the
synoptic Gospels apparently knew nothing of it, as it is found nowhere
else?   If the “beloved disciple” was the caretaker of Mary, mother of Jesus
after his death, then she could very well have told him the story.  While his
disciples were invited to the wedding along with Jesus, it seems that those
who attended did not tell this story to their colleagues.
The Gospel of Mark takes up the story at that point, telling us about the
first preaching of Jesus in a synagogue, on the Sabbath following his
recruitment of Simon Peter and Andrew, James and John:
1:21 And they went into Capernaum; and straightway on the sabbath day he
entered into the synagogue, and taught.  1:22 And they were astonished at
his doctrine: for he taught them as one that had authority, and not as the
scribes.  1:23 And there was in their synagogue a man with an unclean spirit;
and he cried out, 1:24 Saying, Let us alone; what have we to do with thee,
thou Jesus of Nazareth? art thou come to destroy us? I know thee who
thou art, the Holy One of God.  1:25 And Jesus rebuked him, saying, Hold
thy peace, and come out of him.  1:26 And when the unclean spirit had torn
him, and cried with a loud voice, he came out of him.  1:27 And they were all
amazed, insomuch that they questioned among themselves, saying, What
thing is this? what new doctrine is this? for with authority commandeth he
even the unclean spirits, and they do obey him.  1:28 And immediately his
fame spread abroad throughout all the region round about Galilee.

Jesus returns to Judaea and baptizes

The  Gospel of John also reports that ultimately the disciples of Jesus
baptized more disciples than John:
4:1 When therefore the LORD knew how the Pharisees had heard that
