The Gospel of Luke tells of an encounter between Jesus and a Samaritan
man, as he journeyed from the Galilee to Jerusalem, indicating that, unlike
the  Jewish  populace  of  his  time,  Jesus  had  no  prejudice  towards
Samaritans, and praised a righteous Samaritan over an ungrateful and
unrighteous Jew:
17:11 And it came to pass, as he went to Jerusalem, that he passed
through the midst of Samaria and Galilee. 17:12 And as he entered
into a certain village, there met him ten men that were lepers, which
stood afar off: 17:13 And they lifted up their voices, and said, Jesus,
Master, have mercy on us. 17:14 And when he saw them, he said unto
them,  Go shew yourselves unto the priests. And it came to pass,
that, as they went, they were cleansed. 17:15 And one of them, when
he saw that he was healed, turned back, and with a loud voice
glorified God, 17:16 And fell down on his face at his feet, giving him
thanks: and he was a Samaritan. 17:17 And Jesus answering said,
Were there not ten cleansed? but where are the nine? 17:18 There are
not found that returned to give glory to God, save this stranger.
17:19 And he said unto him, Arise, go thy way: thy faith hath made
thee whole.
When he was teaching one day, according to the Gospel of Luke, he was
challenged to describe the meaning of “neighbor”  in the context of the
commandment to “love…thy neighbor as thyself”:
10:25 And, behold, a certain lawyer stood up, and tempted him,
saying, Master, what shall I do to inherit eternal life? 10:26 He said

answering said, Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart,
and with all thy soul, and with all thy strength, and with all thy mind;
and thy neighbour as thyself. 10:28 And he said unto him, Thou hast
answered right: this do, and thou shalt live. 10:29 But he, willing to
justify himself, said unto Jesus,  And who is my neighbour?  10:30
And Jesus answering said, A certain man went down from Jerusalem

JESUS † The Complete Biography
to Jericho, and fell among thieves, which stripped him of his raiment,
and wounded him, and departed, leaving him half dead. 10:31 And by

him, he passed by on the other side. 10:32 And likewise a Levite,
when he was at the place, came and looked on him, and passed by
on the other side. 10:33 But a certain Samaritan, as he journeyed,
came where he was: and when he saw him, he had compassion on

10:37 And he said, He that shewed mercy on him. Then said Jesus
unto him, Go, and do thou likewise.
In the Gospel of John we find Jesus accused of being a Samaritan, and of
being demonic:
8:48 Then answered the Jews, and said unto him, Say we not well
that thou art a Samaritan, and hast a devil? 8:49 Jesus answered, I
have not a devil; but I honour my Father, and ye do dishonour me.
Jesus returns to Jerusalem for Passover
The Gospel of Matthew speaks of the return to Jerusalem to celebrate the
festival of Passover:

apart in the way, and said unto them, 20:18  Behold, we go up to

priests and unto the scribes, and they shall condemn him to death,

JESUS † The Complete Biography
20:19 And shall deliver him to the Gentiles to mock, and to scourge,
and to crucify him: and the third day he shall rise again.  20:20 Then
came  to  him  the  mother  of  Zebedees  children  with  her  sons,
worshipping him, and desiring a certain thing of him.  20:21 And he
said unto her, What wilt thou? She saith unto him, Grant that these
my two sons may sit, the one on thy right hand, and the other on the

not what ye ask. Are ye able to drink of the cup that I shall drink of,
and to be baptized with the baptism that I am baptized with? They

to give, but it shall be given to them for whom it is prepared of my
Father.  20:24 And when the ten heard it, they were moved with

dominion over them, and they that are great exercise authority

will  be  great  among  you,  let  him  be  your  minister;  20:27  And
whosoever will be chief among you, let him be your servant: 20:28
Even as the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to
minister, and to give his life a ransom for many.  20:29 And as they
departed from Jericho, a great multitude followed him.  20:30 And,

son of David.  20:31 And the multitude rebuked them, because they
should hold their peace: but they cried the more, saying,  Have
mercy on us, O Lord, thou son of David.  20:32 And Jesus stood

The Gospel of John refers to this same time, and the appearance of Jersus

11:55 And the Jews' passover was nigh at hand: and many went

The synoptic Gospels report an event which most probably happened prior
to the entry of Jesus into Jerusalem at the time of this Passover.  So
triumphant was this arrival that it is unlikely that it would have occurred
simultaneously…the principal character would likely have lost his nerve if
he had personally witnessed the tumultuous enthusiasm of the masses.  It
was the defection of Judas Iscariot, reported in the synoptic Gospels, and
placed by Matthew and Mark immediately after this supper in Bethany:
26:14 Then one of the twelve, called Judas Iscariot, went unto
the chief priests, 26:15 And said unto them, What will ye give
me, and I will deliver him unto you? And they covenanted with
him for thirty pieces of silver.  26:16 And from that time he
sought opportunity to betray him. (Matthew)
14:10 And Judas Iscariot, one of the twelve, went unto the
chief priests, to betray him unto them. 14:11 And when they
heard it, they were glad, and promised to give him money. And
he sought how he might conveniently betray him.  (Mark)
22:3 Then entered Satan into Judas surnamed Iscariot, being
of the number of the twelve. 22:4 And he went his way, and

JESUS † The Complete Biography
communed with the chief priests and captains, how he might
betray  him  unto  them.  22:5  And  they  were  glad,  and
covenanted to give him money. 22:6 And he promised, and
sought opportunity to betray him unto them in the absence of
the multitude. (Luke)
The Gospel of John does not report this secret and traitorous transaction,
but in its telling of the supper story (which follows shortly) it records Judas
Iscariot  being  concerned  about  the  money,  the  financial  value  of  the
ointment.  Furthermore, it states “This he said, not that he cared for the
poor; but because he was a thief, and had the bag, and bare what was put
therein.”  By then, plainly, Judas Iscariot had already received the bag of
money from the chief priests in advance of his betrayal of Jesus.  This story
recalls the teaching of Jesus that “Ye cannot serve God and mammon”
(Matthew 6:24; Luke 16:13).    The Greek term translated as mammon is
mamOna  and this is derived from the Aramaic  mAmOnA.  Both words
mean “wealth”, in the sense of “material riches”.  The synoptic Gospel
accounts indicate that Judas Iscariot agreed to deliver Jesus to the chief
priests  when  they  promised  “to  give  him  money”  and  the  Gospel  of
Matthew even specifies that the price was “thirty pieces of silver”.  The
clear message of the Gospels is that Judas Iscariot valued money over
Jesus, and that he could not be a true believer in Jesus or in God because
“Ye cannot serve God and mammon.”  This uncompromising choice of
spiritual values over material values, and obedience to the voice of God
and detachment from the lure of material riches is one of the hallmarks of
Jesus’ message.  It was embodied in the lifestyle his precursor adopted, he
himself  adopted,  and  his  disciples  likewise  embraced—fewness  and
simplicity  of  possessions,  chastity  and  (for  many)  celibacy,  and
abandonment of worldly ambitions and pursuits.  He told his followers to
“let the dead bury their dead” (Matthew 8:22;  Luke 9:60), and “go and sell
that thou hast, and give to the poor” (Matthew 19:20; Mark 10:21).  He
expected  total  commitment  to  the  divine  from  his  followers,  but  still
praised the less drastic obedience to divine principle of others, as depicted
in this story recorded in the Gospel of Luke:
19:2 And, behold, there was a man named Zacchaeus, which was the
chief among the publicans, and he was rich. 19:3 And he sought to
see Jesus who he was; and could not for the press, because he was
little of stature. 19:4 And he ran before, and climbed up into a
sycamore tree to see him: for he was to pass that way. 19:5 And

JESUS † The Complete Biography
when Jesus came to the place, he looked up, and saw him, and said
unto him, Zacchaeus, make haste, and come down; for to day I must
abide at thy house. 19:6 And he made haste, and came down, and
received him joyfully. 19:7 And when they saw it, they all murmured,
saying, That he was gone to be guest with a man that is a sinner. 19:8
And Zacchaeus stood, and said unto the Lord: Behold, Lord, the

Jesus said unto him,  This day is salvation come to this house,
forsomuch as he also is a son of Abraham. 19:10 For the Son of man
is come to seek and to save that which was lost.

The  Gospel of Matthew tells this story as well, but he says that this
dinner took place in the house of Simon the leper (Matthew 26:6; Mark
14:3) or Simon the Pharisee (Luke 7:39-40), and there is no mention of
Martha, Mary or Lazarus.   In the Gospel of John, the owner of the house
in which the three siblings sup with Jesus is not identified.  Could it be that
Simon the leper was father of these three?   In that case, the Hebrew name
of Lazarus would have been Eleazar ben Shim’on, a priestly name to be
sure, and given the proximity of Bethany to Jerusalem, he may well have
been in service at the Temple.  Of course, there was another Eleazar ben
Shim’on, about whom we know considerably more.223  Even as the synoptic
Gospels make no mention of Lazarus, neither do the synoptic Gospels
name the woman who anoints Jesus with ointment:

told for a memorial of her.

This is the last mention of Lazarus by name in the Gospel of John, which

disciples, 11:2 And saith unto them, Go your way into the village over

against you: and as soon as ye be entered into it, ye shall find a colt
tied, whereon never man sat; loose him, and bring him. 11:3 And if any
man say unto you, Why do ye this? say ye that the Lord hath need
of him; and straightway he will send him hither. 11:4 And they went
their way, and found the colt tied by the door without in a place
where two ways met; and they loose him. 11:5 And certain of them
that stood there said unto them, What do ye, loosing the colt? 11:6
And they said unto them even as Jesus had commanded: and they
let them go. 11:7 And they brought the colt to Jesus, and cast their
garments on him; and he sat upon him. 11:8 And many spread their
garments in the way: and others cut down branches off the trees,
and strawed them in the way. 11:9 And they that went before, and
they  that  followed,  cried,  saying,  Hosanna;  Blessed  is  he  that
cometh in the name of the Lord: 11:10 Blessed be the kingdom of our
father David, that cometh in the name of the Lord: Hosanna in the

The Gospel of Luke likewise conveys all of these details:
19:29 And it came to pass, when he was come nigh to Bethphage and
Bethany, at the mount called the mount of Olives, he sent two of his
disciples, 19:30 Saying, Go ye into the village over against you; in the
which at your entering ye shall find a colt tied, whereon yet never
man sat: loose him, and bring him hither. 19:31 And if any man ask
you, Why do ye loose him? thus shall ye say unto him, Because the
Lord hath need of him.   19:32 And they that were sent went their
way, and found even as he had said unto them. 19:33 And as they
were loosing the colt, the owners thereof said unto them, Why loose
ye the colt? 19:34 And they said, The Lord hath need of him. 19:35
And they brought him to Jesus: and they cast their garments upon
the colt, and they set Jesus thereon. 19:36 And as he went, they
spread their clothes in the way. 19:37 And when he was come nigh,

JESUS † The Complete Biography
even now at the descent of the mount of Olives, the whole multitude
of the disciples began to rejoice and praise God with a loud voice
for all the mighty works that they had seen; 19:38 Saying, Blessed be
the King that cometh in the name of the Lord: peace in heaven, and
glory in the highest.
Once in the holy city on this fateful Passover, and the disciples have
gathered together, according to the Gospel of John and not found in the
synoptic Gospels, Jesus had another visitation from an angel:
12:23 And Jesus answered them, saying, The hour is come, that the
Son of man should be glorified. 12:24 Verily, verily, I say unto you,
Except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth
alone: but if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit.  12:25 He that loveth
his life shall lose it; and he that hateth his life in this world shall keep
it unto life eternal. 12:26 If any man serve me, let him follow me; and
where I am, there shall also my servant be: if any man serve me, him
will my Father honour. 12:27 Now is my soul troubled; and what shall I
say? Father, save me from this hour: but for this cause came I unto
this hour. 12:28 Father, glorify thy name. Then came there a voice
from heaven, saying, I have both glorified it, and will glorify it again.
12:29 The people therefore, that stood by, and heard it, said that it
thundered:  others  said,  An  angel  spake  to  him. 12:30  Jesus
answered and said, This voice came not because of me, but for your
sakes. 12:31 Now is the judgment of this world: now shall the prince of
this world be cast out. 12:32 And I, if I be lifted up from the earth, will
draw all men unto me. 12:33 This he said, signifying what death he
should die.
This angelic visitation has many special characteristics—whereas the voice
from heaven that spoke during the baptism of Jesus was heard only by
John the Baptist and a few others at the time; and the voice from heaven
that spoke on the mountain was witnessed by Peter, James and his brother
John; this voice from heaven is witnessed by “the people” in Jerusalem

JESUS † The Complete Biography
during the Passover festival, and the sound of this voice is described by
some saying “it thundered” while others said “an angel spake to him”.  The
people who witnessed this extraordinary spectacle were evidently curious,
and Jesus obliges their curiosity by explaining that this voice from heaven
spoke for the sake of the people, indicating that the Day of Judgment had
arrived, that Satan, the prince of this world would now be cast out, that he
wold be lifted up to the heavens from earth, and that he would “draw all
men unto me.”  These are stupendous statements, each one of them, and
they indicate that the “judgment” and “resurrection” are not future events,
but were fulfilled at that very time, when Jesus was in Jerusalem, two
millennia ago.  Jesus continues to answer their queries:
12:34 The people answered him, We have heard out of the law that
Christ abideth for ever: and how sayest thou, The Son of man must
be lifted up? who is this Son of man?  12:35 Then Jesus said unto
them, Yet a little while is the light with you. Walk while ye have the
light, lest darkness come upon you: for he that walketh in darkness
knoweth not whither he goeth. 12:36 While ye have light, believe in
the light, that ye may be the children of light. These things spake
Jesus, and departed, and did hide himself from them.
Instead of believing in his divine appointment, “the people” did not believe
in him, and so he left them and sought solace apart from them:
12:37 But though he had done so many miracles before them, yet
they  believed  not  on  him:  12:38  That  the  saying  of  Esaias  the
prophet might be fulfilled, which he spake, Lord, who hath believed
our report? and to whom hath the arm of the Lord been revealed?
12:39 Therefore they could not believe, because that Esaias said
again, 12:40 He hath blinded their eyes, and hardened their heart;
that they should not see with their eyes, nor understand with their
heart, and be converted, and I should heal them. 12:41 These things
said Esaias, when he saw his glory, and spake of him.
What is remarkable is that the common folk did not believe him at this
time but that there were nevertheless leaders of the people, most likely
Sadducees, Essenes or Herodians, or perhaps some of each, who believed
that he was divinely elected:

JESUS † The Complete Biography
12:42 Nevertheless among the chief rulers also many believed on him;
but because of the Pharisees they did not confess him, lest they
should be put out of the synagogue: 12:43 For they loved the praise
of men more than the praise of God.
The deep sorrow, the greatest sorrow of the world is the sorrow of the Son
of man, the prophet of God who knows what mankind’s crying need is, and
sees that mankind rejects the only means whereby that need may be met:
12:44 Jesus cried and said, He that believeth on me, believeth not
on me, but on him that sent me.  12:45 And he that seeth me seeth
him  that  sent  me.  12:46  I  am  come  a  light  into  the  world,  that
whosoever believeth on me should not abide in darkness. 12:47 And
if any man hear my words, and believe not, I judge him not: for I came
not to judge the world, but to save the world. 12:48 He that rejecteth
me, and receiveth not my words, hath one that judgeth him: the word
that I have spoken, the same shall judge him in the last day. 12:49
For I have not spoken of myself; but the Father which sent me, he
gave me a commandment, what I should say, and what I should
speak. 12:50 And I know that his commandment is life everlasting:
whatsoever I speak therefore, even as the Father said unto me, so I
speak.
The Gospel of Mark reports that immediately after his triumphal entry
into Jerusalem, Jesus immediately visited the Temple, and that he then
returned to Bethany with his disciples:
11:11 And Jesus entered into Jerusalem, and into the temple: and
when he had looked round about upon all things, and now the
eventide was come, he went out unto Bethany with the twelve.
This Gospel then says speaks of a first encounter between Jesus and a fig
tree the following morning, on his way back to Jerusalem:

JESUS † The Complete Biography
11:12 And on the morrow, when they were come from Bethany, he was
hungry: 11:13 And seeing a fig tree afar off having leaves, he came, if
haply he might find any thing thereon: and when he came to it, he
found nothing but leaves; for the time of figs was not yet.  11:14 And
Jesus answered and said unto it, No man eat fruit of thee hereafter
for ever. And his disciples heard it.
This first encounter with the fig tree is not reported in the other Gospels.
The Gospel of Mark continues with an account of Jesus in the Temple,
expelling the merchants:
11:15 And they come to Jerusalem: and Jesus went into the temple,
and began to cast out them that sold and bought in the temple, and
overthrew the tables of the moneychangers, and the seats of them
that sold doves; 11:16 And would not suffer that any man should
carry any vessel through the temple.  11:17 And he taught, saying
unto them, Is it not written, My house shall be called of all nations
the house of prayer? but ye have made it a den of thieves.  11:18 And
the scribes and chief priests heard it, and sought how they might
destroy  him:  for  they  feared  him,  because  all  the  people  was
astonished at his doctrine.  11:19 And when even was come, he went
out of the city.
The Gospel of Matthew likewise reports a visit to the Temple, and the
forcible removal of commerce from its sacred environs:
21:12 And Jesus went into the temple of God, and cast out all them
that sold and bought in the temple, and overthrew the tables of the
moneychangers, and the seats of them that sold doves, 21:13 And
said unto them, It is written, My house shall be called the house of
prayer; but ye have made it a den of thieves.  21:14 And the blind and
the lame came to him in the temple; and he healed them.  21:15 And
when the chief priests and scribes saw the wonderful things that he
did, and the children crying in the temple, and saying, Hosanna to

JESUS † The Complete Biography
the son of David;  they were sore displeased, 21:16 And said unto
him, Hearest thou what these say? And Jesus saith unto them, Yea;
have ye never read, Out of the mouth of babes and sucklings thou
hast perfected praise? 21:17 And he left them, and went out of the
city into Bethany; and he lodged there.
The  Gospel of Luke reverses the order of the account, first reporting
Jesus’ conversation with the priests and scribes and then his visit to the
Temple and eviction of the merchants:
19:39 And some of the Pharisees from among the multitude said unto
him, Master, rebuke thy disciples.  19:40 And he answered and said
unto them,  I tell you that, if these should hold their peace, the
stones would immediately cry out.  19:41 And when he was come
near, he beheld the city, and wept over it, 19:42 Saying,  If thou
hadst known, even thou, at least in this thy day, the things which
belong unto thy peace! but now they are hid from thine eyes.  19:43
For the days shall come upon thee, that thine enemies shall cast a
trench about thee, and compass thee round, and keep thee in on
every side, 19:44 And shall lay thee even with the ground, and thy
children within thee; and they shall not leave in thee one stone upon
another; because thou knewest not the time of thy visitation.  19:45
And he went into the temple, and began to cast out them that sold
therein, and them that bought; 19:46 Saying unto them, It is written,
My house is the house of prayer: but ye have made it a den of
thieves.
The next morning, Jesus has a second encounter with the fig tree, and he
tells a parable to his disciples, first in the Gospel of Matthew:
21:18 Now in the morning as he returned into the city, he hungered.
21:19 And when he saw a fig tree in the way, he came to it, and found
nothing thereon, but leaves only, and said unto it, Let no fruit grow

JESUS † The Complete Biography
on thee henceforward for ever. And presently the fig tree withered
away. 21:20 And when the disciples saw it, they marvelled, saying,
How soon is the fig tree withered away! 21:21 Jesus answered and
said unto them, Verily I say unto you, If ye have faith, and doubt
not, ye shall not only do this which is done to the fig tree, but also if
ye shall say unto this mountain, Be thou removed, and be thou cast
into the sea; it shall be done. 21:22 And all things, whatsoever ye
shall ask in prayer, believing, ye shall receive.
Then, in the Gospel of Mark, he tells the same story, with more detail:
11:20 And in the morning, as they passed by, they saw the fig tree
dried up from the roots. 11:21 And Peter calling to remembrance saith
unto  him,  Master,  behold,  the  fig  tree  which  thou  cursedst  is
withered away.  11:22 And Jesus answering saith unto them,  Have
faith in God. 11:23 For verily I say unto you, That whosoever shall say
unto this mountain, Be thou removed, and be thou cast into the sea;
and shall not doubt in his heart, but shall believe that those things
which he saith shall come to pass; he shall have whatsoever he saith.
11:24 Therefore I say unto you, What things soever ye desire, when
ye pray, believe that ye receive them, and ye shall have them. 11:25
And when ye stand praying, forgive, if ye have ought against any:
that your Father also which is in heaven may forgive you your
trespasses. 11:26  But if ye do not forgive, neither will your Father
which is in heaven forgive your trespasses.
Jesus on prayer
To digress from our telling of the story, in this discourse Jesus refers to the
manner in which prayer should be offered, and in words strikingly similar
to his model prayer, in the Gospel of Matthew:

JESUS † The Complete Biography
6:9 After this manner therefore pray ye: Our Father which art in
heaven, Hallowed be thy name. 6:10 Thy kingdom come, Thy will be
done in earth, as it is in heaven. 6:11 Give us this day our daily bread.
6:12 And forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors. 6:13 And
lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil: For thine is the
kingdom, and the power, and the glory, for ever. Amen. 6:14 For if
ye  forgive  men  their  trespasses,  your  heavenly  Father  will  also
forgive you: 6:15 But if ye forgive not men their trespasses, neither
will your Father forgive your trespasses.
And the same model in the Gospel of Luke:
11:2 And he said unto them, When ye pray, say, Our Father which art
in heaven, Hallowed be thy name. Thy kingdom come. Thy will be
done, as in heaven, so in earth. 11:3 Give us day by day our daily
bread. 11:4  And forgive us our sins; for we also forgive every one
that is indebted to us. And lead us not into temptation; but deliver
us from evil.
Jesus speaks to multiple audiences in Jerusalem
The Gospel of Mark then speaks about the challenge made by the priests
and scribes and elders to Jesus’ authority, because he spoke as one with
authority, and they were accustomed to being in charge and believed it to
be their exclusive right, and he follows this with a detailed acount of a day
in the Temple with Jesus teaching different groups of Jews:
1)chief priests, scribes, elders:
11:27 And they come again to Jerusalem: and as he was walking in the
temple, there come to him the chief priests, and the scribes, and the
elders, 11:28 And say unto him, By what authority doest thou these
things? and who gave thee this authority to do these things? 11:29
And Jesus answered and said unto them, I will also ask of you one
question, and answer me, and I will tell you by what authority I do
these things. 11:30 The baptism of John, was it from heaven, or of

JESUS † The Complete Biography
men? answer me. 11:31 And they reasoned with themselves, saying, If
we shall say, From heaven; he will say, Why then did ye not believe
him? 11:32 But if we shall say, Of men; they feared the people: for all
men counted John, that he was a prophet indeed. 11:33 And they
answered and said unto Jesus, We cannot tell. And Jesus answering
saith unto them, Neither do I tell you by what authority I do these
things. 12:1 And he began to speak unto them by parables. A certain
man planted a vineyard, and set an hedge about it, and digged a
place  for  the  winefat,  and  built  a  tower,  and  let  it  out  to
husbandmen, and went into a far country.  12:2 And at the season he
sent to the husbandmen a servant, that he might receive from the
husbandmen of the fruit of the vineyard. 12:3 And they caught him,
and beat him, and sent him away empty. 12:4 And again he sent unto
them another servant; and at him they cast stones, and wounded
him in the head, and sent him away shamefully handled. 12:5 And
again he sent another; and him they killed, and many others; beating
some,  and  killing  some.  12:6  Having  yet  therefore  one  son,  his
wellbeloved,  he  sent  him  also  last  unto  them,  saying,  They  will
reverence  my  son.  12:7  But  those  husbandmen  said  among
themselves, This is the heir; come, let us kill him, and the inheritance
shall be our's. 12:8 And they took him, and killed him, and cast him
out  of  the  vineyard.  12:9  What  shall  therefore  the  lord  of  the
vineyard do? he will come and destroy the husbandmen, and will give
the vineyard unto others. 12:10 And have ye not read this scripture;
The stone which the builders rejected is become the head of the
corner: 12:11 This was the Lord's doing, and it is marvellous in our
eyes?  12:12 And they sought to lay hold on him, but feared the
people: for they knew that he had spoken the parable against them:
and they left him, and went their way.

12:13 And they send unto him certain of the Pharisees and of the

Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the

3) Sadducees:
12:18 Then come unto him the Sadducees, which say there is no
resurrection; and they asked him, saying, 12:19 Master, Moses wrote
unto us, If a man's brother die, and leave his wife behind him, and
leave no children, that his brother should take his wife, and raise up

when they shall rise from the dead, they neither marry, nor are given

touching the dead, that they rise: have ye not read in the book of
Moses, how in the bush God spake unto him, saying, I am the God of
Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob? 12:27 He is

JESUS † The Complete Biography
not the God of the dead, but the God of the living: ye therefore do
greatly err.
4) Scribes:
12:28 And one of the scribes came, and having heard them reasoning
together, and perceiving that he had answered them well, asked him,
Which is the first commandment of all? 12:29 And Jesus answered

said unto him, Well, Master, thou hast said the truth: for there is one
God; and there is none other but he: 12:33 And to love him with all

with all the strength, and to love his neighbour as himself, is more
than all whole burnt offerings and sacrifices. 12:34 And when Jesus
saw that he answered discreetly, he said unto him, Thou art not far
from the kingdom of God. And no man after that durst ask him any
question. 12:35 And Jesus answered and said, while he taught in the

For David himself said by the Holy Ghost224, The LORD said to my

footstool. 12:37  David  therefore  himself  calleth  him  Lord;  and
whence is he then his son?

chief seats in the synagogues, and the uppermost rooms at feasts:

into the treasury: and many that were rich cast in much. 12:42 And
there came a certain poor widow, and she threw in two mites, which

more in, than all they which have cast into the treasury: 12:44 For all
they did cast in of their abundance; but she of her want did cast in
all that she had, even all her living.
The Gospel of Matthew reports these same discourses in even greater
detail, and, like the Gospel of Mark, Jesus speaks to several groups of
people:
1)chief priests and elders of the people:
21:23 And when he was come into the temple, the chief priests and
the elders of the people came unto him as he was teaching, and
said, By what authority doest thou these things? and who gave thee
this authority? 21:24 And Jesus answered and said unto them, I also
will ask you one thing, which if ye tell me, I in like wise will tell you by
what authority I do these things. 21:25 The baptism of John, whence
was it? from heaven, or of men? And they reasoned with themselves,
saying, If we shall say, From heaven; he will say unto us, Why did ye
not then believe him? 21:26 But if we shall say, Of men; we fear the
people; for all hold John as a prophet.  21:27 And they answered
Jesus, and said, We cannot tell. And he said unto them, Neither tell I
you by what authority I do these things. 21:28 But what think ye? A
certain man had two sons; and he came to the first, and said, Son,
go work to day in my vineyard. 21:29 He answered and said, I will not:
but afterward he repented, and went. 21:30 And he came to the

second, and said likewise. And he answered and said, I go, sir: and

That the publicans and the harlots go into the kingdom of God

another, and stoned another. 21:36 Again, he sent other servants

Before we leave this topic, we will consider an apocryphal report, of great
renown particularly among the Eastern Christians, of a communication
between Jesus and another king, in Syria.
Communication with King Abgar
Abgar/Abgarus V, was King of Osroene (what is currently part of Syria),
whose capitol city was Edessa and he reigned from 4 BCE to 15/50 CE.  He
was a contemporary of Jesus, and, according to some documentary sources
which are first described in the 4th century CE, they were in contact.
Eusebius, Bishop of Caesaria and prolific historian of early Christianity,
records a tradition, in his Historia Ecclesiastica, I, xiii, written in 325 CE,
concerning written communications exchanged between King Abgar of
Edessa  and  Jesus.   Eusebius  was  convinced  that  the  original  letters,
written in Syriac, were kept in the archives of Edessa.  Eusebius copies the
letter of Abgar and the response of Jesus into the text of his book.    In a
Syriac text called Doctrina Addai, which has been dated to the second half
of the 4th century CE, and which is attributed to Thaddeus of Edessa, one of

JESUS † The Complete Biography
the seventy-two disciples, the story is somewhat different from the version
found in Eusebius.  According to this work, while the communication of
King Abgar V was in writing, the response of Jesus was given verbally to
Abgar’s envoy, the court archivist Hannan/Ananias, and this occurred in
the year 32 CE.  According to Doctrina Addai, Hannan painted an image of
Jesus, the first portrait from life.  Greek versions of this story are found in
the  Acta  Thaddaei.   In  the  mid-5th century  CE  the  History  of  the
Armenians of Moses of Chorene reported the story and indicated that
Hannan’s portrait of Jesus was preserved in Edessa.
An English translation, by M.R.James, of the Greek text of Eusebius232,
cites “a copy of a letter written by Abgarus the toparch to Jesus, and sent to
him by means of Ananias the runner, to Jerusalem”:
Abgarus Uchama the toparch to Jesus the good Saviour that hath appeared
in the parts (place) of Jerusalem, greeting. I have heard concerning thee
and thy cures, that they are done of thee without drugs or herbs: for, as the
report  goes,  thou  makest  blind  men  to  see  again,  lame  to  walk,  and
cleansest lepers, and castest out unclean spirits and devils, and those that
are afflicted with long sickness thou healest, and raisest the dead.   And
having heard all this of thee, I had determined one of two things, either
that thou art God come down from heaven, and so doest these things or art
a Son of God that doest these things.   Therefore now have I written and
entreated thee to trouble thyself to come to me and heal the affliction
which I have or indeed I have heard that the Jews even murmur against
thee and wish to do thee hurt. And I have a very little city but (and) comely
(reverend), which is sufficient for us both.
The  version  of  this  letter  found  in  Doctrina  Addai,  translated  into
English233, is as follows:
Abgar Ouchama to Jesus, the Good Physician Who has appeared in the
country of Jerusalem, greeting:  I have heard of Thee, and of Thy healing;
that Thou dost not use medicines or roots, but by Thy word openest (the
eyes) of the blind, makest the lame to walk, cleansest the lepers, makest
the deaf to hear; how by Thy word (also) Thou healest (sick) spirits and
those who are tormented with lunatic demons, and how, again, Thou
raisest the dead to life. And, learning the wonders that Thou doest, it was
borne in upon me that (of two things, one): either Thou hast come down
from heaven, or else Thou art the Son of God, who bringest all these things
to pass. Wherefore I write to Thee, and pray that thou wilt come to me,
who adore Thee, and heal all the ill that I suffer, according to the faith I
have  in  Thee.  I  also  learn  that  the  Jews  murmur  against  Thee,  and
persecute Thee, that they seek to crucify Thee, and to destroy Thee. I
possess but one small city, but it is beautiful, and large enough for us two
to live in peace.

JESUS † The Complete Biography
From  the  English  translation,  by  M.R.James,  of  the  Greek  text  of
Eusebius234, “the answer, written by Jesus, sent by Ananias the runner to
Abgarus the toparch” reads as follows:
Blessed art thou that hast believed in me, not having seen me.   For it is
written concerning me that they that have seen me shall not believe in me,
and that they that have not seen me shall believe and live. But concerning
that which thou hast written to me, to come unto thee; it must needs be
that I fulfill all things for the which I was sent here, and after fulfilling
them should then be taken up unto him that sent me.   And when I am
taken up, I will send thee one of my disciples, to heal thine affliction and
give life to thee and them that are with thee.
The oral response and circumstances thereof reported in Doctrina Addai,
translated into English235, is as follows:
When Jesus had received the letter, in the house of the high priest of the
Jews, He said to Hannan, the secretary, "Go thou, and say to thy master,
who hath sent thee to Me: 'Happy art thou who hast believed in Me, not
having seen me, for it is written of me that those who shall see me shall not
believe in Me, and that those who shall not see Me shall believe in Me. As
to that which thou hast written, that I should come to thee, (behold) all
that for which I was sent here below is finished, and I ascend again to My
Father who sent Me, and when I shall have ascended to Him I will send
thee one of My disciples, who shall heal all thy sufferings, and shall give
(thee) health again, and shall convert all who are with thee unto life
eternal. And thy city shall be bleseed forever, and the enemy shall never
overcome it.'"
According to currently accessible information236, versions of this story and
of the purported communication between Abgar V and Jesus survive in
Syriac, Armenian, in two independent Greek versions (Eusebius and Acta
Thaddaei), and several inscriptions on marble and metal.  It was used as a
talisman, an amulet by many Christians, particularly in the East.  It is also
cited in Syrian liturgies, during Lent, and in at least one Celtic liturgy, as
found in the Liber Hymnorum, a manuscript preserved at Trinity College,
Dublin (E. 4,2).

The Apocalypses – After the Resurrection
The  Gospel of Mark gives an account of Jesus’ prophecies, called the
minor  apocalypse,  which  were  spoken  on  the  Mount  of  Olives  to  his
disciples:
13:1 And as he went out of the temple, one of his disciples saith unto
him, Master, see what manner of stones and what buildings are here!
13:2 And Jesus answering said unto him,  Seest thou these great
buildings? there shall not be left one stone upon another, that shall
not be thrown down. 13:3 And as he sat upon the mount of Olives
over against the temple, Peter and James and John and Andrew
asked him privately,  13:4 Tell us, when shall these things be? and
what shall be the sign when all these things shall be fulfilled? 13:5
And Jesus answering them began to say, Take heed lest any man
deceive you: 13:6 For many shall come in my name, saying, I am
Christ; and shall deceive many. 13:7 And when ye shall hear of wars
and rumours of wars, be ye not troubled: for such things must
needs be; but the end shall not be yet. 13:8 For nation shall rise
against nation, and kingdom against kingdom: and there shall be
earthquakes  in  divers  places,  and  there  shall  be  famines  and
troubles: these are the beginnings of sorrows. 13:9 But take heed to
yourselves: for they shall deliver you up to councils; and in the
synagogues ye shall be beaten: and ye shall be brought before
rulers and kings for my sake, for a testimony against them. 13:10 And
the gospel must first be published among all nations. 13:11 But when
they  shall  lead  you,  and  deliver  you  up,  take  no  thought
beforehand what ye shall speak, neither do ye premeditate: but
whatsoever shall be given you in that hour, that speak ye: for it is
not ye that speak, but the Holy Ghost. 13:12 Now the brother shall
betray the brother to death, and the father the son; and children
shall rise up against their parents, and shall cause them to be put to

JESUS † The Complete Biography
death. 13:13 And ye shall be hated of all men for my name's sake: but
he that shall endure unto the end, the same shall be saved. 13:14 But
when ye shall see the abomination of desolation, spoken of by
Daniel  the  prophet,  standing  where  it  ought  not,  (let  him  that
readeth understand,) then let them that be in Judaea flee to the
mountains: 13:15 And let him that is on the housetop not go down
into the house, neither enter therein, to take any thing out of his
house: 13:16 And let him that is in the field not turn back again for to
take up his garment. 13:17 But woe to them that are with child, and to
them that give suck in those days! 13:18 And pray ye that your flight
be not in the winter. 13:19 For in those days shall be affliction, such
as was not from the beginning of the creation which God created
unto this time, neither shall be. 13:20 And except that the Lord had
shortened those days, no flesh should be saved: but for the elect's
sake, whom he hath chosen, he hath shortened the days. 13:21 And
then if any man shall say to you, Lo, here is Christ; or, lo, he is
there; believe him not: 13:22 For false Christs and false prophets
shall rise, and shall shew signs and wonders, to seduce, if it were
possible, even the elect. 13:23 But take ye heed: behold, I have
foretold  you  all  things.  13:24  But  in  those  days,  after  that
tribulation, the sun shall be darkened, and the moon shall not give
her light, 13:25 And the stars of heaven shall fall, and the powers
that are in heaven shall be shaken. 13:26 And then shall they see the
Son of man coming in the clouds with great power and glory. 13:27
And then shall he send his angels, and shall gather together his
elect from the four winds, from the uttermost part of the earth to
the uttermost part of heaven. 13:28 Now learn a parable of the fig
tree; When her branch is yet tender, and putteth forth leaves, ye
know that summer is near: 13:29 So ye in like manner, when ye shall
see these things come to pass, know that it is nigh, even at the
doors. 13:30 Verily I say unto you, that this generation shall not

JESUS † The Complete Biography
pass, till all these things be done. 13:31 Heaven and earth shall pass
away: but my words shall not pass away. 13:32 But of that day and
that hour knoweth no man, no, not the angels which are in heaven,
neither the Son, but the Father. 13:33 Take ye heed, watch and
pray: for ye know not when the time is. 13:34 For the Son of Man is
as a man taking a far journey, who left his house, and gave authority
to his servants, and to every man his work, and commanded the
porter to watch. 13:35 Watch ye therefore: for ye know not when the
master of the house cometh, at even, or at midnight, or at the
cockcrowing, or in the morning: 13:36 Lest coming suddenly he find
you sleeping. 13:37 And what I say unto you I say unto all, Watch.
The  Gospel  of  Matthew gives  a  very  similar  version  of  the  minor

JESUS † The Complete Biography

Jesus anoints his disciples and outs his betrayer
The Gospel of John reports a meal shared prior to the feast of Passover,
and as he anoints his disciples and preaches to them, and neither the
actions nor the words are reported in any other Gospel, it will be treated
separately here:
13:1 Now before the feast of the passover, when Jesus knew that his
hour was come that he should depart out of this world unto the
Father, having loved his own which were in the world, he loved them
unto the end. 13:2  And supper being ended, the devil having now
put into the heart of Judas Iscariot, Simon's son, to betray him;
13:3  Jesus knowing that the Father had given all things into his
hands, and that he was come from God, and went to God; 13:4  He
riseth from supper, and laid aside his garments; and took a towel,
and girded himself. 13:5  After that he poureth water into a bason,
and began to wash the disciples' feet, and to wipe them with the
towel wherewith he was girded. 13:6  Then cometh he to Simon Peter:
and Peter saith unto him, Lord, dost thou wash my feet? 13:7  Jesus
answered and said unto him, What I do thou knowest not now; but
thou shalt know hereafter.  13:8  Peter saith unto him,  Thou shalt
never wash my feet. Jesus answered him, If I wash thee not, thou
hast no part with me. 13:9  Simon Peter saith unto him, Lord, not my
feet only, but also my hands and my head. 13:10  Jesus saith to him,
He that is washed needeth not save to wash his feet, but is clean
every whit: and ye are clean, but not all. 13:11  For he knew who
should betray him; therefore said he, Ye are not all clean. 13:12  So
after he had washed their feet, and had taken his garments, and

JESUS † The Complete Biography

13:14  If I then, your Lord and Master, have washed your feet; ye
also ought to wash one another's feet. 13:15  For I have given you an
example, that ye should do as I have done to you. 13:16  Verily, verily,
I say unto you, The servant is not greater than his lord; neither he

things, happy are ye if ye do them. 13:18  I speak not of you all: I

was leaning on Jesus' bosom one of his disciples, whom Jesus loved.
It should be noted that there is no naming of the disciple “whom Jesus
loved”,  either  here  or  elsewhere  in  the  canonical  and  non-canonical
literature.  It has been noted that the only man who is named as being
loved by Jesus was Lazarus, and that Jesus loved him so much that he
brought him back to life after he had been dead for four days.  Whether or
not this “disciple, whom Jesus loved”, referred to this way only in the
Gospel of John (John 13:23, 19:26, 20:2, 21:7, 21:20), was Lazarus, it is
evident that he was the “other disciple” also alluded to only in that Gospel
(John 18:16, 20:2-4, 20:8) and only subsequent to the resurrection of
Lazarus, whom he “loved” (John 11:5, 11:4-44).
13:24 Simon Peter therefore beckoned to him, that he should ask
who it should be of whom he spake. 13:25 He then lying on Jesus'
breast saith unto him, Lord, who is it? 13:26 Jesus answered, He it is,

Judas Iscariot makes a deal
The Gospel of Mark reports that Judas Iscariot made a deal to betray
Jesus to the authorities, immediately prior to the feast of Passover:
14:10 And Judas Iscariot, one of the twelve, went unto the chief
priests, to betray him unto them. 14:11 And when they heard it, they
were glad, and promised to give him money. And he sought how he

JESUS † The Complete Biography
might conveniently betray him. 14:12 And the first day of unleavened
bread, when they killed the passover…
The Gospel of Matthew tells virtually the same story:
26:14 Then one of the twelve, called Judas Iscariot, went unto the
chief priests, 26:15 And said unto them, What will ye give me, and I will
deliver him  unto you? And they covenanted with him for thirty
pieces of silver. 26:16 And from that time he sought opportunity to
betray  him. 26:17 Now the  first  day of  the  feast  of  unleavened
bread…
The Gospel of Luke tells the same story, but omitting the price:
22:3 Then entered Satan into Judas surnamed Iscariot, being of the
number of the twelve. 22:4 And he went his way, and communed with
the chief priests and captains, how he might betray him unto them.
22:5 And they were glad, and covenanted to give him money. 22:6
And he promised, and sought opportunity to betray him unto them
in the absence of the multitude.
The Passover seder with the Jesus and his disciples
The synoptic Gospels then tell the story of the “last supper”, the first meal

and there shall meet you a man bearing a pitcher of water: follow

the house, The Master saith, Where is the guestchamber, where I

JESUS † The Complete Biography
shall eat the passover with my disciples? 14:15 And he will shew you a

14:16 And his disciples went forth, and came into the city, and found
as he had said unto them: and they made ready the passover. 14:17
And in the evening he cometh with the twelve. 14:18 And as they sat
and did eat, Jesus said,  Verily I say unto you, One of you which
eateth  with  me  shall  betray  me. 14:19  And  they  began  to  be

Is it I? 14:20 And he answered and said unto them, It is one of the

goeth, as it is written of him: but woe to that man by whom the Son
of man is betrayed! good were it for that man if he had never been

brake it, and gave to them, and said, Take, eat: this is my body.
14:23 And he took the cup, and when he had given thanks, he gave it
to them: and they all drank of it. 14:24 And he said unto them, This
is my blood of the new testament, which is shed for many. 14:25
Verily I say unto you, I will drink no more of the fruit of the vine, until
that day that I drink it new in the kingdom of God.

14:26 And when
they had sung an hymn, they went out into the mount of Olives.
The Gospel of Matthew tells the same story with greater brevity:

In the Garden of Gethsemane, Mount of Olives
The Gospel of Mark tells the story of the last night of Jesus, before his
capture:
14:26 And when they had sung an hymn, they went out into the
mount of Olives. 14:27 And Jesus saith unto them,  All ye shall be
offended because of me this night: for it is written237, I will smite the
shepherd, and the sheep shall be scattered. 14:28 But after that I
am risen, I will go before you into Galilee. 14:29 But Peter said unto
him, Although all shall be offended, yet will not I. 14:30 And Jesus
saith unto him,  Verily I say unto thee, That this day, even in this
night, before the cock crow twice, thou shalt deny me thrice.
The only Gospel account that places Jesus’ prophecy regarding the three
denials of his disciple Peter at the Passover seder is the Gospel of Luke.  In
the Gospel of Mark (14:30), and the Gospel of Matthew (26:34), the
prophecy is told on the Mount of Olives, after Jesus and his disciples had
completed the seder.
14:31 But he spake the more vehemently, If I should die with thee, I

forward a little, and fell on the ground, and prayed that, if it were
possible, the hour might pass from him. 14:36 And he said, Abba,

me: nevertheless not what I will, but what thou wilt.  14:37 And he
cometh, and findeth them sleeping, and saith unto Peter,  Simon,
sleepest thou? couldest not thou watch one hour? 14:38 Watch ye
and pray, lest ye enter into temptation. The spirit truly is ready, but
the flesh is weak. 14:39 And again he went away, and prayed, and
spake the same words. 14:40 And when he returned, he found them
asleep again, (for their eyes were heavy,) neither wist they what to
answer him. 14:41 And he cometh the third time, and saith unto them,
Sleep on now, and take your rest: it is enough, the hour is come;
behold, the Son of man is betrayed into the hands of sinners. 14:42
Rise up, let us go; lo, he that betrayeth me is at hand.
The Gospel of Matthew tells the same story:

The  Gospel of Luke tells an abbreviated tale of their last visit to the

Delivered into captivity by Judas Iscariot
The Gospel of Mark tells the story of Jesus delivered into captivity by
Judas Iscariot:
14:43 And immediately, while he yet spake, cometh Judas, one of
the twelve, and with him a great multitude with swords and staves,
from the chief priests and the scribes and the elders. 14:44 And he

shall kiss, that same is he; take him, and lead him away safely. 14:45
And as soon as he was come, he goeth straightway to him, and
saith,  Master, master; and kissed him. 14:46 And they laid their
hands on him, and took him. 14:47 And one of them that stood by
drew a sword, and smote a servant of the high priest, and cut off his
ear. 14:48 And Jesus answered and said unto them,  Are ye come
out, as against a thief, with swords and with staves to take me?
14:49 I was daily with you in the temple teaching, and ye took me
not: but the scriptures must be fulfilled. 14:50 And they all forsook
him, and fled. 14:51 And there followed him a certain young man,
having a linen cloth cast about his naked body; and the young men
laid hold on him: 14:52 And he left the linen cloth, and fled from them
naked.

In the synoptic Gospels, when Jesus is apprehended, “Peter followed afar

The Gospel of Mark:

The Gospel of Luke:

The Gospel of John reports that Peter was not the only disciple who
followed Jesus.  This is the only account of this event that includes this
“other disciple”:
18:15 And Simon Peter followed Jesus, and so did another

disciple, which was known unto the high priest, and spake

Who is this unnamed disciple, if not the similarly unnamed “other disciple,
who Jesus loved” (John 13:23, 19:26, 20:2, 21:7, 20-24)?  And how did he
come to be “known unto the high priest”?  It is certainly possible that this
unnamed disciple was Lazarus, and that he was a kohen himself, as Eleazar
was the patronymic of a line of high priests239:  “The high-priesthood
remained in the family of Eleazar until the time of Eli, into whose family it
passed (Eli was a descendant of  Ithamar, Eleazar's brother[3]). The high
priesthood was restored to the family of Eleazar in the person of  Zadok
after  Abiathar was cast out by  Solomon.”  There are many reasons to
conclude that the “beloved disciple” so copiously referred to in the Gospel
and John,  and nowhere else, was not, as has been supposed  for  two
millennia, John of Galilee, but rather, Lazarus of Judaea.  More about that
later.

The three denials of Peter
The canonical Gospels tell a story which begins with a prophecy and ends
with a fulfillment.  According to the Gospel of Mark (14:30), the Gospel of
Matthew (26:34), the Gospel of Luke (22:34) and the Gospel of John
(13:38), Jesus prophesied that Peter would deny him three times before a
rooster crows.  The implication seems to be that this would take place on
one day, the very day that Jesus made the prediction.  In the Gospels of
Mark and Matthew, Peter emphatically denied that he would ever deny
Jesus.  All four Gospels describe the fulfillment of this prophecy.  First we
cite the Gospel of Mark:
14:66 And as Peter was beneath in the palace, there cometh one of
the maids of the high priest: 14:67 And when she saw Peter warming
himself, she looked upon him, and said,  And thou also wast with
Jesus of Nazareth. 14:68 But he denied, saying, I know not, neither
understand I what thou sayest. And he went out into the porch; and
the cock crew.  14:69 And a maid saw him again, and began to say to
them that stood by,  This is one of them.  14:70 And he denied it
again. And a little after, they that stood by said again to Peter,

JESUS † The Complete Biography
Surely thou art one of them: for thou art a Galilaean, and thy
speech agreeth thereto. 14:71 But he began to curse and to swear,
saying, I know not this man of whom ye speak. 14:72 And the second
time the cock crew. And Peter called to mind the word that Jesus
said unto him,  Before the cock crow twice, thou shalt deny me
thrice. And when he thought thereon, he wept.
The Gospel of Matthew tells the story in almost identical phrasing:
26:69 Now Peter sat without in the palace: and a damsel came unto
him, saying,  Thou also wast with Jesus of Galilee. 26:70 But he
denied before them all, saying, I know not what thou sayest. 26:71
And when he was gone out into the porch, another maid saw him,
and said unto them that were there, This fellow was also with Jesus
of Nazareth. 26:72 And again he denied with an oath, I do not know
the man. 26:73 And after a while came unto him they that stood by,
and said to Peter, Surely thou also art one of them; for thy speech
bewrayeth  thee.  26:74  Then  began  he  to  curse  and  to  swear,
saying, I know not the man. And immediately the cock crew.  26:75
And Peter remembered the word of Jesus, which said unto him,
Before the cock crow, thou shalt deny me thrice. And he went out,
and wept bitterly.
The Gospel of Luke tells the same story, except in this version Jesus is
present, and he looks upon Peter after Peter denies him three times:
22:54 Then took they him, and led him, and brought him into the
high priest's house. And Peter followed afar off. 22:55 And when
they had kindled a fire in the midst of the hall, and were set down
together, Peter sat down among them. 22:56 But a certain maid
beheld him as he sat by the fire, and earnestly looked upon him, and
said, This man was also with him. 22:57 And he denied him, saying,
Woman, I know him not. 22:58 And after a little while another saw

JESUS † The Complete Biography
him, and said, Thou art also of them. And Peter said, Man, I am not.
22:59 And about the space of one hour after another confidently
affirmed, saying, Of a truth this fellow also was with him: for he is a
Galilaean. 22:60 And Peter said, Man, I know not what thou sayest.
And immediately, while he yet spake, the cock crew. 22:61 And the
Lord turned, and looked upon Peter. And Peter remembered the
word of the Lord, how he had said unto him, Before the cock crow,
thou shalt deny me thrice. 22:62 And Peter went out, and wept
bitterly.
The Gospel of John likewise relates this fulfillment of prophecy, but with a
detail not noted by any of the other evangelists—he identifies the third
peson who asked Peter if he was one of the disciples; not surprising, since,
according to this Gospel, Peter was accompanied by “another disciple”, and
it is his version of the story that seems to be told here:
18:15 And Simon Peter followed Jesus, and so did another disciple:
that disciple was known unto the high priest, and went in with Jesus
into the palace of the high priest. 18:16 But Peter stood at the door
without. Then went out that other disciple, which was known unto
the high priest, and spake unto her that kept the door, and brought
in Peter. 18:17 Then saith the damsel that kept the door unto Peter,
Art not thou also one of this man's disciples? He saith, I am not. 18:18
And the servants and officers stood there, who had made a fire of
coals; for it was cold: and they warmed themselves: and Peter stood
with them, and warmed himself…
18:25  And  Simon  Peter  stood  and  warmed  himself.  They  said
therefore unto him,  Art not thou also one of his disciples? He
denied it, and said, I am not. 18:26 One of the servants of the high
priest, being his kinsman whose ear Peter cut off, saith, Did not I
see thee in the garden with him? 18:27 Peter then denied again: and
immediately the cock crew.

The visit to Pontius Pilatus and Herod Antipas
The Gospel of Luke indicates that Jesus was brought first to Pilatethen

The other three canonical Gospels report that Jesus encountered only the

priests moved the people, that he should rather release Barabbas

JESUS † The Complete Biography
unto them. 15:12 And Pilate answered and said again unto them, What
will ye then that I shall do unto him whom ye call the King of the
Jews? 15:13 And they cried out again, Crucify him. 15:14 Then Pilate
said unto them, Why, what evil hath he done? And they cried out the

the people, released Barabbas unto them, and delivered Jesus,
when he had scourged him, to be crucified.
A remarkable characteristic of these accounts in all but the  Gospel of
Luke  is  the  silence  with  which  Jesus  meets  the  accusations  of  his
antagonists.  Why didn’t he defend himself?  Why did he permit these
blasphemies to go unanswered?  There is immense wisdom demonstrated
by this behavior, which we will consider at length and in depth.  At the top
of the list, let us consider for a moment the hierarchy, and to whom a
response may be demanded.  When Job questions God’s judgment in
visiting plagues and tribulations upon him, God answers him: “38:1 Then
the LORD answered Job out of the whirlwind, and said, 38:2 Who is this
that darkeneth counsel by words without knowledge? 38:3 Gird up now
thy loins like a man; for I will demand of thee, and answer thou me. 38:4
Where wast thou when I laid the foundations of the earth? declare, if thou
hast understanding.”    In relation to the chief priest, to Pilate, and to
Herod,  Jesus  is  infinitely  higher  in  authority.   It  is  for  him  to  pose
questions and for them to reply, and not the inverse.  By questioning and
especially by challenging him to explain himself, they transgress their
boundaries, the violate their relationship with God.  Perhaps a little lower
on the list is the inevitability of this moment, faced in one fashion or
another by every Manifestation of God, for all of them are opposed by the
religious and secular authorities of their times, and without this opposition
their divine sovereignty and prophetic station would not be recognized.
Yet a little lower on this list is the danger which prolonged argumentation
could bring upon the intimates of Jesus.  At that moment his opponents
were asking for his head, but if he had dared to prolong the debacle and
challenge their power, they might well have sought to harm his family or
his followers.  The Manifestation of God does not think only of himself but
of everyone in the world.  Of what possible benefit would a prolongation of
his passion serve in any case?

Witnesses of the crucifixion
The Gospel of Mark reports that:
15:40 There were also women looking on afar off: among whom was
Mary Magdalene, and Mary the mother of James the less and of

Joses, and Salome; 15:41 Who also, when he was in Galilee, followed

The Gospel of Matthew reports:
27:55   And  many  women  were  there  beholding  afar  off,  which
followed Jesus from Galilee, ministering unto him;  27:56 Among
which was Mary Magdalene, and Mary the mother of James and
Joses, and the mother of Zebedee’s children.
The Gospel of Luke likewise reports:
23:49  And all his acquaintance, and the women that followed him
from Galilee, stood afar off, beholding these things.
The  Gospel of John reports the presence of “the disciple…whom he
loved”, along with his mother, his aunt and Mary Magdalene, but not “afar
off” but “by the cross”:
Now there stood by the cross of Jesus his mother, and his mother's
sister, Mary the wife of Cleophas, and Mary Magdalene. 19:26 When
Jesus therefore saw his mother, and the disciple standing by, whom
he loved, he saith unto his mother,  Woman, behold thy son! 19:27
Then saith he to the disciple, Behold thy mother! And from that
hour that disciple took her unto his own home.
The Gospel of John is the only account that points to the presence of one
of the male disciples at the crucifixion; it identifies who that disciple was;
and it reports that Jesus directed this disciple to take care of his mother as
if she were his own.  It has been pointed out that the crucifixion occurred
in Jerusalem, and that the home of Lazarus, whom Jesus loved, was only a
few  miles  away  in  Bethany;  while  the  home  of  John,  who  has  been
regarded for centuries as the “beloved disciple”, would have been located
in a small village on the shore of the Kinneret, the sea of Galilee, over 100
miles from Jerusalem.   While Lazarus had an established home, in which
Martha and Mary were also living, it seems from the Gospel narrative that,
as one of the twelve, John had been on the road nonstop since meeting

JESUS † The Complete Biography
Jesus.  As Jesus replied when “a certain scribe came, and said unto him,
Master, I will follow thee whithersoever thou goest.  And Jesus saith unto
him, The foxes have holes, and the birds of the air have nests; but the Son
of man hath not where to lay his head.”  (Matthew 8:19-20)  Another
reason for regarding Lazarus as the “beloved disciple”, and hence honoring
those traditions that identified her resting place as Jerusalem, rather than
others which erroneously paired her up with John and had both of them
die in the city of Ephesus (Turkish: Efes), many years later.
Miraculous signs after the Crucifixion
The  Gospel of Mark reports a miraculous event, the cracking of the
immediately subsequent to the crucifixion:
15:38 And the veil of the temple was rent in twain from the top to the
bottom.
The Gospel of Matthew writes the same, and adds details:
27:51 And, behold, the veil of the temple was rent in twain from the
top to the bottom; and the earth did quake, and the rocks rent;
27:52 And the graves were opened; and many bodies of the saints
which slept arose,  27:53 And came out of the graves after his
resurrection, and went into the holy city, and appeared unto many.
The Gospel of Luke writes the same and adds one detail:
23:45 And the sun was darkened, and the veil of the temple was rent
in the midst.
The only disciple who witnessed the crucifixion was the “beloved disciple”,
and the  Gospel of John which purports to be his testimony does not
report any of these events.  The “veil of the temple” to which all three
synoptic  Gospels  refer  is  καταπέτασμα,  ατος,  τό (transliterated
katapetasma) in the original Greek; according to Strong’s Concordance242,
it is  literally  “that which is spread  out downwards,  that which hangs
down”, a curtain, veil, of that which separated the Holy of Holies from the
outer parts of the temple at Jerusalem, also of an outer curtain at the
entrance to the Holy Place in the same temple.”  Any worshipping Jew
could have attested to this event, and it is surprising that it is not reported

JESUS † The Complete Biography
by Josephus or in the Talmud or any other Jewish-authored text of the
time.   The  eclipse  of  the  sun,  reported  in  the  Gospel  of  Luke,  the
earthquake  reported  in  the  Gospel  of  Matthew,  and  the  physical
resurrection of entombed saints reported in the Gospel of Matthew are also
unreported.  Attempts to buttress this account through the citation of
independent testimonies, notably the references in the works of Christian
apologists hundreds of years after the event, to a pagan author called
Thallus have been debunked as untenable243.
A Roman Witness to the Crucifixion
The  Gospel of Mark reports that a Roman centurion witnessed the
crucifixion and was converted by the experience:
15:39 And when the centurion, which stood over against him, saw
that he so cried out, and gave up the ghost, he said, Truly this man
was the Son of God.
The Gospel of Matthew writes the same:
27:54 Now when the centurion, and they that were with him, watching
Jesus, saw the earthquake, and those things that were done, they
feared greatly saying, Truly this was the Son of God.
The Gospel of Luke:
23:47 Now when the centurion saw what was done, he glorified God,
saying, Certainly this was a righteous man.  23:48 And all the people
that came together to that sight, beholding the things which were
done, smote their breasts, and returned.
The Gospel of John does not refer to the centurion, or to the miraculous
events to which the centurion seems to be responding.  While the “beloved
disciple” could not have witnessed the rending of the Temple veil, as he
was on Calgary watching the crucifixion, he could have experienced an
earthquake, and the physical resurrection of the saints from the graveyard
that is situation adjacent to the place of crucifixion…but he is silent.
The Last Words of Jesus

JESUS † The Complete Biography
Through the centuries there has been much discussion about the last
words of Jesus.  In the Gospels of Mark and Matthew the last words
spoken by Jesus are virtually identical.  The Gospels of Luke and John
cite entirely different last words.  There is agreement however between the
three synoptic Gospels that just before dying Jesus “cried with a loud
voice”—only the  Gospel of Luke records the actual words that Jesus
cried.  And then there is the Gospel of John, which only refers to Jesus
bowing his head and not to  cry before he died.   All versions are here cited,
without preference or disapproval.
The Gospel of Mark:
15:34 And at the ninth hour Jesus cried with a loud voice, saying,
Eloi, Eloi, lama sabachthani? which is, being interpreted, My God,
my God, why hast thou forsaken me? 15:35 And some of them that
stood by, when they heard it, said, Behold, he calleth Elias. 15:36
And one ran and filled a spunge full of vinegar, and put it on a reed,
and gave him to drink, saying, Let alone; let us see whether Elias will
come to take him down. 15:37 And Jesus cried with a loud voice, and
gave up the ghost.
The Gospel of Matthew:
27:46 And about the ninth hour Jesus cried with a loud voice,
saying, Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani? that is to say, My God, my God,
why hast thou forsaken me? 27:47 Some of them that stood there,
when they heard that, said,  This man calleth for Elias. 27:48 And
straightway one of them ran, and took a spunge, and filled it with
vinegar, and put it on a reed, and gave him to drink. 27:49 The rest
said, Let be, let us see whether Elias will come to save him. 27:50
Jesus, when he had cried again with a loud voice, yielded up the
ghost.
The Gospel of Luke:

JESUS † The Complete Biography
23:46 And when Jesus had cried with a loud voice, he said, Father,
into thy hands I commend my spirit: and having said thus, he gave up
the ghost.
The Gospel of John:
19:30 When Jesus therefore had received the vinegar, he said, It is
finished: and he bowed his head, and gave up the ghost.
Of these accounts, the one that comes from an alleged eye-witness is that
reported in the Gospel of John.  And it is the simplest.  If it be alleged that
the  “beloved  disciple”  perhaps  did  not  hear  the  last  words  of  Jesus
reported by the other Gospels, consider that all three indicate that he said
these last words “with a loud voice” (Mark 15:37, Matthew 27:50, Luke
23:46).  As the “beloved disciple” was standing right there, what likelihood
is there that he would not have heard and reported these last words?
The Day of Preparation
All four canonical Gospels report that Jesus died on the day before the
Sabbath, which, according to the Jewish calendar, begins with sunset on
Yom Shlishi (Thursday) and ends with sunset on Yom Shivi (Friday).  As
the accounts speak of the evening coming after the death of Jesus, and
state that “it was the preparation”, and as the friends and followers of
Jesus were in a hurry to transfer his body inot a sepulchre, it is evident that
the crucifixion took place on Yom Shivi (Friday) and that the body of Jesus
was removed from the cross and placed in a sepulchre on Erev Shabbat.

up with him unto Jerusalem. 15:42 And now when the even was come,
because it was the preparation, that is, the day before the sabbath,

waited for the kingdom of God, came, and went in boldly unto

The Sabbath after the Crucifixion
Only one of the Gospels tells us what happened on the Sabbath after the
crucifixion, the Gospel of Matthew:
27:62 Now the next day, that followed the day of the preparation,
the chief priests and Pharisees came together unto Pilate, 27:63
Saying, Sir, we remember that that deceiver said, while he was yet
alive,  After three days I will rise again.  27:64 Command therefore
that the sepulchre be made sure until the third day, lest his disciples
come by night, and steal him away, and say unto the people, He is
risen from the dead: so the last error shall be worse than the first.
27:65 Pilate said unto them, Ye have a watch: go your way, make it as
sure as ye can. 27:66 So they went, and made the sepulchre sure,
sealing the stone, and setting a watch.
The  Gospel of Luke tells us only that the women who followed Jesus
waited during the Sabbath:
23:55  And  the  women  also,  which  came  with  him  from  Galilee,
followed after, and beheld the sepulchre, and how his body was
laid. 23:56 And they returned, and prepared spices and ointments;
and rested the sabbath day according to the commandment.
Yom Rishon after the Crucifixion
The  Gospel of Mark begins the story again after the Sabbath, quickly
telling us about the disappearance of Jesus from his sepulchre and the
appearance of a young man clothed in a long white garment, all witnessed
by Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James, and Salome:

mother of James, and Salome, had bought sweet spices, that they

might come and anoint him. 16:2 And very early in the morning the
first day of the week, they came unto the sepulchre at the rising of
the sun. 16:3 And they said among themselves, Who shall roll us away
the stone from the door of the sepulchre?  16:4 And when they
looked, they saw that the stone was rolled away: for it was very
great. 16:5 And entering into the sepulchre, they saw a young man
sitting on the right side, clothed in a long white garment; and they
were affrighted. 16:6 And he saith unto them, Be not affrighted: Ye
seek Jesus of Nazareth, which was crucified: he is risen; he is not
here: behold the place where they laid him. 16:7 But go your way, tell
his disciples and Peter that he goeth before you into Galilee: there
shall ye see him, as he said unto you. 16:8 And they went out quickly,
and fled from the sepulchre; for they trembled and were amazed:
neither said they any thing to any man; for they were afraid.
The  Gospel of Matthew tells the story somewhat differently…with the

28:1 In the end of the sabbath, as it began to dawn toward the first

was like lightning, and his raiment white as snow: 28:4 And for fear
of him the keepers did shake, and became as dead men. 28:5 And
the angel answered and said unto the women,  Fear not ye: for I
know that ye seek Jesus, which was crucified. 28:6 He is not here:
for he is risen, as he said. Come, see the place where the Lord lay.
28:7 And go quickly, and tell his disciples that he is risen from the
dead; and, behold, he goeth before you into Galilee; there shall ye
see him: lo, I have told you.

The  Gospel of Luke differs even more…reporting two men in shining

24:1 Now upon the first day of the week, very early in the morning,

stone rolled away from the sepulchre. 24:3 And they entered in, and
found not the body of the Lord Jesus. 24:4 And it came to pass, as
they were much perplexed thereabout, behold, two men stood by

down their faces to the earth, they said unto them, Why seek ye the
living among the dead? 24:6 He is not here, but is risen: remember
how he spake unto you when he was yet in Galilee, 24:7 Saying, The
Son of man must be delivered into the hands of sinful men, and be
crucified, and the third day rise again.
The Gospel of John begins with these simple words:
20:1 The first day of the week cometh Mary Magdalene early, when
it was yet dark, unto the sepulchre, and seeth the stone taken away
from the sepulchre.
Consider how naturalistic and normal this account is, in comparison with
the others—one of the women who stood by Jesus as he was crucified, and
who is reported to have followed his body to its internment and kept watch
there, having apparently gone home to sleep, returns in the very early
morning and finds the stone that was sealing the cave tomb rolled removed
from its place.  No earthquake unattested by other witnesses, no young
man in linen or angel or two men in shining garments…just an unsealed
gravesite.
Jesus appears to Mary Magdalene and other women
The Gospel of Mark announces that on the first day of the week (yom
rishon in Hebrew parlance, corresponding to Sunday) after the crucifixion,

The opposition does not rest

JESUS † The Complete Biography
The  Gospel of Matthew is the only Gospel which tells the story of an
opposition that does not rest after the burial of Jesus.  It begins with his
appearance to Mary Magdalene and the other Mary, and then indicates
that some of the watchmen who were assigned to guard the sepulchre of
Jesus reported his disappearance.  It indicates that there was a cover up,
that  money  changed  hands,  and  that  a  story  was  fabricated  that  the
disciples of Jesus “came by night, and stole him away” while they slept:
28:10 Then said Jesus unto them, Be not afraid: go tell my brethren
that they go into Galilee, and there shall they see me. 28:11 Now when
they were going, behold, some of the watch came into the city, and
shewed unto the chief priests all the things that were done. 28:12
And when they were assembled with the elders, and had taken
counsel, they gave large money unto the soldiers, 28:13 Saying, Say
ye, His disciples came by night, and stole him away while we slept.
28:14 And if this come to the governor's ears, we will persuade him,
and secure you. 28:15 So they took the money, and did as they were
taught: and this saying is commonly reported among the Jews until
this day.

Ascension of Jesus
The Gospel of Mark reports the ascension of Jesus:
16:19 So then after the Lord had spoken unto them, he was received
up into heaven, and sat on the right hand of God.
The Gospel of Luke likewise refers to the ascension of Jesus:
24:51 And it came to pass, while he blessed them, he was parted
from them, and carried up into heaven. 24:52 And they worshipped
him, and returned to Jerusalem with great joy: 24:53 And were
continually in the temple, praising and blessing God. Amen.
The Acts of the Apostles likewise attests to the ascension of Jesus:

JESUS † The Complete Biography
1:1 The former treatise have I made, O Theophilus, of all that Jesus
began both to do and teach, 1:2 Until the day in which he was taken
up...
1:9 And when he had spoken these things, while they beheld, he was
taken up; and a cloud received him out of their sight. 1:10 And while
they looked stedfastly toward heaven as he went up, behold, two
men stood by them in white apparel; 1:11 Which also said, Ye men of
Galilee, why stand ye gazing up into heaven? this same Jesus, which
is taken up from you into heaven, shall so come in like manner as ye
have  seen  him  go  into  heaven.  1:12  Then  returned  they  unto
Jerusalem from the mount called Olivet, which is from Jerusalem a
sabbath day's journey. 1:10 And while they looked stedfastly toward
heaven  as he went up, behold, two men stood by them in white
apparel; 1:11 Which also said, Ye men of Galilee, why stand ye gazing
up into heaven? this same Jesus, which is taken up from you into
heaven, shall so come in like manner as ye have seen him go into
heaven.
The ascension of Jesus has direct parallels in the Old Testament…it is
neither unique to Jesus nor represent a borrowing from Greek or some
other Middle Eastern religious tradition.  The story of Enoch, son of Cain,
in the Book of Genesis ends;
5:24 And Enoch walked with God: and he was not; for God took
him.
The Epistle to the Hebrews refers to that ascension of Enoch:
11:5 By faith Enoch was translated that he should not see death; and
was not found, because God had translated him: for before his
translation he had this testimony, that he pleased God.

JESUS † The Complete Biography
Much more familiar, to Jews and Christians alike, is the ascension of
Elijah, as told in Second Kings:
2:11  And it came to pass, as they still went on, and talked, that,
behold, there appeared a chariot of fire, and horses of fire, and
parted them both asunder; and Elijah went up by a whirlwind into
heaven. 2:12  And Elisha saw it, and he cried, My father, my father,
the chariot of Israel, and the horsemen thereof. And he saw him no
more: and he took hold of his own clothes, and rent them in two
pieces.
Hence, the ascension of Jesus is not unique to the New Testament, and the
Jewish  understanding  (midrash)  of  such  an  extraordinary  event  is
germaine to our present comprehension of what the disciples witnessed,
what it meant to them, and what it can mean for us.
Those to whom he appears or speaks
The Acts of the Apostles report sightings of Jesus after his ascension.
The first is Stephen:

JESUS † The Complete Biography
